en: The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Therein, in the first part, the second section—the Pretakāṇḍa, known as the Dharmakāṇḍa—is now commenced.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva!
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim victory. (GarP 2.1 Mangala)

Victorious is the tree of Madhusūdana, whose roots are firmly established in Dharma, whose trunk is the Veda, which is rich with the branches of the Purāṇas, whose flowers are the sacrifices, and whose fruit is liberation.
In the Naimiṣa forest, the field of the Unblinking One, the lords of sages headed by Śaunaka spoke these words to Sūta as he sat at the conclusion of their sacrificial rites: GarP_2,1.2 //
O Sūta, by the grace of Vyāsa you know every matter;
therefore, you ought to sever the doubt of us who are perplexed.
Relying on the analogy of the leech on grass, some indeed speak thus regarding the acquisition of another body by the embodied being. GarP_2,1.4 //
Furthermore, some say that after experiencing the torments of Yama, there is the attainment of another body; is there indeed anything real in that? (GarP 2.1.5)
Sūta said:
Well asked, O highly fortunate ones! Listen again;
for those who inquire for the sake of the world, doubt should not arise. (GarP 2.1.6)
Therefore, O twice-born ones, I shall dispel the doubt of you whose souls are purified by means of the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Homage to the sage Kṛṣṇa,
who have taken refuge in him and easily cross the ocean of saṃsāra as if it were a small stream.
Once, Vainateya felt a desire to see the worlds;
he then wandered through them, chanting the name of Hari.
Having wandered through the netherworld, the earth, and heaven, his heart finding no peace and being deeply distressed by the suffering of the world, he returned once more to Vaikuṇṭha.
Neither passion nor darkness, nor even goodness mixed with those two, ever proceeds there; rather, it is goodness alone that proceeds.
Therein is neither illusion nor destruction, nor are there impurities such as passion;
[the beings there] are dark and fair-complexioned, of beautiful luster, with eyes like the hundred-petaled lotus.
There, the well-formed hosts of Viṣṇu, honored by gods and asuras,
wore garments and ornaments of golden hue and were adorned with jeweled neck-ornaments.
They had four arms, wore earrings, crowns, and garlands,
and were accompanied by radiant rows of celestial chariots belonging to those great-souled ones.
Where, shining with rows of radiant women,
Śrī joyfully worships the feet of Hari with various splendors.
She herself sang of Hari as he sat upon the swing while being sung to by his female companions;
there she beheld Śrī Hari, the Lord of Śrī and the Protector of the Sātvatas.
The Lord of the Universe, the Lord of Sacrifice, was incessantly attended by his attendants, chief among whom were Sunanda, Nanda, Prabala, and Arhaṇa.
His face was bright with favor toward his servants, his long eyes were reddish,
he wore a diadem and earrings, and he was marked by the Goddess of Fortune upon his chest.
Wearing yellow garments, four-armed, with a face of serene smiles,
seated upon a worthy throne, and surrounded by those Śaktis.
And likewise from Pradhāna and Puruṣa, from Mahat and Ahaṃkāra, as well as from the eleven sense organs and the five elements.
The son of Vinatā, his heart filled with the joy of beholding Him and the hairs on his body standing on end, approached that Lord who was delighting in His own essential nature.
Dropping tears from his eyes and immersed in love, he bowed down.
To his own vehicle, who had arrived and prostrated, Viṣṇu said:
"O bird, what land has been traversed by you in all this time?"
Garuḍa said:
"O Vaikuṇṭha, by your grace, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving..."
"O Lord, I have surveyed the entire world, both moving and stationary,
from the realm of Bhūrloka up to Satyaloka, with the exception of the city of Yama."
Among all worlds, the world of the earth (bhūrloka) is the most abundant in all living beings;
among all creatures, the human state is auspicious, being the abode of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, the world of those who have performed virtuous deeds has never existed, nor will it ever exist.

The gods indeed sing these songs: "Blessed are those men who, in the region of the land of Bhārata, repeatedly become human beings for the sake of attaining the fruits of heaven and liberation, rather than remaining as gods."
Why is the deceased being tossed about in the belly? How is there a five-jeweled ornament in the mouth? Why are the darbha grasses moved downward, and why are the feet positioned toward the south?
For what purpose do his sons and grandsons stand before him?
And for what purpose, O Keśava, is a gift given, even the gift of a cow? (GarP 2.1.29)
How is it that they seek forgiveness from both friends and enemies for sesame, iron, gold, cotton, and likewise salt? (GarP 2.1.30)
For what reason are the seven grains, the earth, and cows given as gifts?
How indeed does a living being die, and where does one who has died go? (GarP 2.1.31)
And how indeed does one then resort to the *ativāha* body?
A son may carry a corpse on his shoulder, and a grandson may be the one who offers the funeral fire. (GarP 2.1.32)
Why is there an anointing with clarified butter, and from where does the performance of a single oblation arise?
For what purpose is Vasundharā [invoked], and why is the word "woman" (strī) proclaimed? (GarP 2.1.33)
For what purpose should one recite the Yama-sūkta while facing the northern direction?
[One should perform] the looking at the solar disc with water in a single garment.
One should place barley, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, a stone, a neem leaf,
a cloth, a man, and a woman in alternating upper and lower positions.
Having come to the house for food, one should not eat together with other people;
and for what purpose do sons offer the nine rice-balls (piṇḍas)? (GarP 2.1.36)
For what purpose is milk poured at a crossroads, and cooked food in earthenware vessels,
after having fashioned three sticks bound together by the Gaṇas at a four-way junction at night?
A lamp is offered every single day throughout the year during the night;
for what purpose is the burning of the body with water performed, and for what purpose is it done together with people?
"O Blessed One, one should cause nine morsels of food to be offered along with the invocation 'bhagavann'.
How should these be given to the ancestors, and how is the invocation of the horse performed? (GarP 2.1.39)
O King, if this is done, why should one cause the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to be offered?
What is it that is offered to him immediately after the offering of the rice-balls and so forth? GarP_2,1.40 //
The collection of bones and likewise the breaking of the water-pot—how could there be a bath on the second day for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires on the fourth? (GarP 2.1.41)

On the tenth day, should a cleansing bath be performed by everyone together? And for what reason should one have the house carried on the shoulders after anointing with oil and rubbing it with unguents?
And they should also offer an ointment made of oil for massaging at a large body of water;
on the tenth day, one should offer that funeral ball (piṇḍa) together with meat.
And on the eleventh day, preceded by the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and other ceremonies,
one should give a vessel, sandals, an umbrella, garments, and a finger-ring.
On the thirteenth day, what is the purpose of giving the gift of land? Why are there these sixteen śrāddhas performed for the duration of a year? (GarP 2.1.45)
Every single day, three hundred and sixty pots of food and water must be given for the satisfaction of the deceased.
O Lord, human beings are impermanent; they die only when their time has come.
"I do not see any opening at all; how then did that living soul depart? Whence do the elements—earth, water, and mind—as well as fire, O Lord, tell me, and wind and space, go? (GarP 2.1.48)
Whence come the five organs of action here, and the five organs of cognition? And how do these five vital airs pass away? 1.49.
Greed, delusion, and the other five are thieves within the body;
O Janārdana, from where do thirst, desire, and egoism depart?
Whether it be merit or demerit, whatever good deed has been performed—once the body has perished, where do the various acts of giving go? (GarP 2.1.51)

For what purpose is the *sapiṇḍana* performed, whether at the completion of a full year or otherwise? With whom is the merging of the deceased effected, and of what nature should one cause it to be performed therein?
Whether from fainting or from falling down, if misfortune should occur—those men on earth who have been burnt, those who have not been burnt, and those who have fallen; [all these are saved].
And what would become of those other beings at the end—
those who are sinful, of evil conduct, and others whose intellects have departed?
A self-killer, a slayer of a Brahmin, a thief, a betrayer of trust, or a Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapilā cow—anyone who recites this syllable [is purified]. (GarP 2.1.55)
Or if one should wear the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), what would his fate be, O Mādhava,
when a Śūdra has taken a Brāhmaṇa woman as his wife?
"I am afraid of that sinner; tell me about him, O Lord of the World.
Furthermore, O Soul of the Universe, listen as I speak with impetuosity out of curiosity."
Surveying the worlds within the world, he plunged into the circle of the universe;
there, seeing people sinking into nothing but sufferings, he was moved with compassion.
In my heart there is an unbearable affliction, more grievous than that affliction caused by the sons of Diti in the third heaven, or by death, disease, and other evils on earth. (GarP 2.1.59)
O Lord, through separations from beloved objects, there is fear of my own [rebirth] in the netherworld;
thus, there is no place other than your feet that is free from fear.
Unreal like a dream or an illusion, it has been swallowed up by time;
even there, in the land of Bhārata, they are partakers of manifold suffering.
I have seen people overwhelmed by passion, hatred, delusion, and the like;
some are blind, some squint-eyed, some with faltering speech, and others are lame.
Lame, one-eyed, deaf, mute, afflicted with leprosy, and hairy;
overcome by various diseases, they yet possess pride regarding flowers that exist only in the sky.
Having seen the variety of their faults and even their falling within the domain of death, who would not become joyful? How could there be any wonder in death?
He for whom death occurs according to the prescribed rite,
and for whom the annual funeral rites (*abdadakriyā*) are performed according to the rule after his passing, shall not fall into an evil rebirth.
"I have previously heard it in general from the sages that 'it was by me [taught] before,' but, O Lord, I ask this for the sake of knowing its specific details."
"What should be done for one who is dying? What gift should be given, O younger brother of Vāsava?
What is the procedure during the interval between life and death, and what is the rite for cremation?"
Whether it occurs immediately or after a delay, does he attain another body?
For one being led along the path of Yama, what need is there for a funeral rite lasting a year?
What atonement is there for one of evil mind, or for one who has died during the five-day period and so forth?
Grant me grace; you ought to sever my delusion entirely.
I have asked about everything; speak it indeed for the benefit of the world.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Elaboration of Questions," in the *Pretakhaṇḍa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
*Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*— 2.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed one, for the benefit of human beings indeed!
Listen with an attentive mind to everything concerning the rites for the deceased."
It is free from correct differentiation, extracted from the Śruti and Smṛti,
and that which has not been seen even by the gods led by Indra, nor by yogis who contemplate yoga.
That which is more secret than the secret has never been told to anyone anywhere;
yet, O highly fortunate one, because you are devoted, I shall speak of Vainateya to you.
"For one who has no son, there is no destination; neither heaven nor even [liberation].
By whatever means possible, the birth of a son must indeed be accomplished."
If liberation is not attained, a son shall deliver one from hell;
for the funeral pyre must be prepared by a son, and the grandson is the one who offers the oblations into the fire.
By means of sesame seeds and darbha grass on the ground, she who is in her menses shall indeed become a hut;
and by placing the five jewels in the mouth, through which life sprouts forth.
When the flower has indeed perished, how then can there be the holding of a fetus?
Therefore, it is with great care that one holds the fetus within the earth.
The ground should be smeared with cow dung and one should scatter sesame seeds and darbha grass upon it;
on that very [ground], the afflicted person, being liberated, burns away all sin.
A mattress of darbha grass leads the deceased to heaven, of this there is no doubt;
one should either scatter darbha grass there, or place it between the mattress and the pillow.
Everywhere else the ground is purified where no smear exists;
where a smear remains, it is purified by applying a smear once again.
Yātudhānas, piśācas, and rākṣasas who perform cruel deeds—these beings of base birth enter one who is untainted, yet afflicted and liberated. (GarP 2.2.11)

Likewise, the daily fire-oblation, the ancestral rite (śrāddha), and the washing of the feet for a twice-born man—without the mandala on the ground, the afflicted person is certainly not liberated. (GarP 2.2.12)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and likewise Agni attend upon him in the mandala; therefore, one should construct a mandala.
Otherwise, whether he is a child, an old man, or a youth, the fool dies;
he does not go to another womb, but instead sports with the vital wind.
Thus, that very birth is exhausted when it is mixed with blood;
for one who has become wind, there is neither the rite of faith (śrāddha) nor the offering of water.
O Tārkṣya, these sesame seeds produced from my sweat are purifying;
likewise, by means of these sesame seeds, the asuras, dānavas, and daityas flee in all directions.
May white sesame seeds, black sesame seeds, and sesame seeds resembling cow’s urine burn away my sins committed indeed with this body. (GarP 2.2.17)
A single sesame seed offered is equal to a droṇa of gold;
when given during libations, gifts, or fire-offerings, it becomes inexhaustible.
Darbha grasses arise from body hairs and sesame seeds from sweat, not otherwise;
by means of the śrāddha, the deities, the dānavas, and likewise the ancestors are satisfied.
According to the rules of ritual application, Brahmā is the source of sustenance for the universe;
through the rite performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), Brahmā, the ancestors, and the gods of the deities are honored.
By that, those ancestors are satisfied when the rite is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
Brahmā stands at the root of the *darbha* grass, and the god Janārdana is in the middle.
One should know Śaṅkara to be at the tip of the darbha grass; the three gods are said to reside in the kuśa.
O Lord of Birds, the brāhmaṇas, the mantras, the káśa grass, the fire, and tulasī [are likewise present].
O bird, these do not become stale even when performed again and again:
Tulasī, Brahmins, cows, Viṣṇu, and the Ekādaśī.
For men sinking in the ocean of worldly existence, there are five means of transport:
Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, and brahminical cows.
In this worthless and difficult saṃsāra, the six-footed [Tulasī] bestows liberation;
likewise, sesame seeds are incomparable purifiers, as are darbha grass and tulasī.
And these [rites] ward off the miserable rebirth for one who is suffering and heading toward it;
one should lift up the darbha grass with both hands and sprinkle it upon the ground with water.
At the time of death, one should cast *darbha* grasses into the hands of the patient;
he who is cast with *darbha* grasses is indeed encircled by *darbha* grasses.
Even a man devoid of mantras goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu,
provided he makes a cushion of cotton, places his feet upon it, and remains seated on the surface of the earth.
As an expiation in this essence-less ocean of saṃsāra,
one should smear a pure fire-pit with cow dung and establish it upon a bed of darbha grass.
By giving a gift of a vehicle, one dispels all evil;
it is like divine salt-flavor, which grants all desires to men. (GarP 2.2.30)
Since all food essences are not intense without salt,
and since that which is pleasing to the ancestors is auspicious, it shall therefore bestow heaven.
Since this salty flavor has originated from the body of Viṣṇu,
yogis therefore praise this gift as being "with salt" (salavaṇa).
When the life-breaths of women of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes, as well as of the Śūdra people and of the sick, do not depart from the surface of the earth; GarP_2,2.33 //
Then salt should be given for the opening of the gate of heaven.
Listen further, O Lord of Birds, to the detailed description of the form of Death.
For whom there would not be a separation of life and body by time,
and for living beings, death at their own appointed time would be an absolute oblivion.
Just as the wind drags clouds hither and thither,
so too, O Tārkṣya, do beings follow the power of Time alone, like those clouds.
Whether they be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa),
all states of being, which are essentially temporal in nature, indeed manifest within living beings.
The sun, the moon, Śambhu, the waters, Vāyu, Śatakratu,
fire, space, earth, Mitra, the herbs, and likewise the Vasus.
O slayer of serpents, rivers and oceans, as well as existence and non-existence—
all are created by Time and withdrawn again by it.
And when death has arrived, O bird, men are gathered up by time; then, through the conjunction of destiny, some disease arises. (GarP 2.2.40)
There would be a deficiency of the senses and a loss of strength and vigor,
as if one were simultaneously stung by ten million scorpions and a hundred thousand gadflies.
Then, O bird, suffering born of death is inferred by that [sign];
thereafter, in an instant, consciousness becomes impaired and falls into a state of insensibility.
Then the vital breaths are drawn away by the messengers of Yama who stand nearby;
at that time, when the breaths have reached the throat, one's form becomes loathsome.
Then he vomits foam, and his mouth becomes covered with saliva;
a person the size of a thumb then emerges from the body, crying out "Alas! Alas! (hā hā).
At that very moment, O dear one, he is led away by the messengers of Yama while looking back at his own home; indeed, this state of death occurs repeatedly for the sake of [renewed] existence.
The earth element, provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind,
blazes forth without fuel and shatters the vital points (marmas).
The vital air named udāna moves upward from there;
it prevents the downward movement of those who have eaten and those who do not desire to eat.
He who has not spoken falsehoods, nor caused a breach of affection,
and who is a believer and full of faith, attains a happy death.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of passion, nor out of hatred;
he who acts according to what has been taught and is gentle—he attains death in happiness.
Those who impart false knowledge attain the greatest darkness, as do false witnesses, liars, and those who betray trust. (GarP 2.2.50)
Those who revile the Vedas likewise fall into delusion and death;
they are terrifying, foul-smelling, and carry staffs and clubs in their hands.
Then the evil-minded messengers of Yama arrive;
when such a terrible path is reached, trembling arises within him.
He too cries out incessantly, even for his father, mother, and children;
yet that speech of his, though indistinct, appears as a single syllable through great effort.
His vision indeed wanders due to terror, and his face withers from gasping;
then, overcome by that agony, he abandons that body.
It becomes untouchable and contemptible at that very moment.
Thus has the true nature of death been described; now, by way of digression, something else will also be told.
I shall now answer for you the second question regarding diversity:
it arises from the non-existence of past karmas, O blessed one. (GarP 2.2.56)
For wandering beings here, there may be a variety of enjoyments, such as the state of a god, an asura, or a yakṣa, which bestows happiness. (GarP 2.2.57)
O Lord of Birds, human birth, animal birth, and birth as a bird and so forth—which bring extreme suffering—occur here according to the gradations of one's karmas. (GarP 2.2.58)
In this regard, I shall proclaim to you the ripening of karmas, through the diversity of which this living being wanders in saṃsāra for the sake of manifesting its manifold variety. (GarP 2.2.59)
Having reached the terrible and dreadful hells born of great sins (mahāpātaka),
those who committed great sins are reborn on earth once their karma has been exhausted.
Listen, O best of beings, to those characteristics by which they are described:
a killer of a Brahmin enters the wombs of deer, horses, pigs, and camels. (GarP 2.2.61)
A stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a moth;
and one who violates the teacher’s bed shall gradually become grass or a shrub.
A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a stealer of gold, deformed nails; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
Whichever among these one dwells with, he is born bearing that person's characteristic; by associating with an outcast for a year, one becomes an outcast.

Sin is transmitted among men through conversation, touch, breathing together, traveling together, eating together, sitting together, officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, and sexual union. (Garuda Purāṇa 2.2.65)
Having gone to the wives of others and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one is born as a Brahma-rākṣasa in a desolate forest region.
One who steals jewels will be born into a low caste;
and a man who takes the leaves or branches of a tree, or its fragrances, becomes a musk-shrew.

By eating food without mantras, one becomes a mouse that steals grain; by stealing a vehicle, a camel; by stealing fruit, a monkey; and by stealing household utensils, a crow or a vulture. (GarP 2.2.68)
One who steals honey becomes bitten by bees; one who steals fruit becomes a vulture; one who steals a cow becomes an iguana; likewise, one who steals fire becomes a crane.
One who steals a woman's garment becomes afflicted with white leprosy, and one who steals flavors suffers from a loss of appetite.

One who steals bell-metal becomes a swan; a stealer of another's property becomes one afflicted with epilepsy; a killer of a guru becomes one with chronic fainting; and a doer of cruel deeds becomes a dwarf.
One who abandons his lawful wife becomes a creature on earth that pierces with sound;
one who steals the property of gods or Brahmins becomes a pale-skinned eater of human flesh.
One who steals consecrated offerings (nyāsa) is born with a goiter and suffers from a major disease;
one who steals [other property] becomes one-eyed, and one who lives off women becomes lame. (GarP 2.2.72)

One who abandons his wife while she is still in her maidenhood becomes unfortunate; furthermore, one who eats what is not desired, suffers from wind-tumors (vātagulma), or approaches the wives of Brahmins, shall become a jackal.
The one who steals a bed becomes a mendicant ascetic; the stealer of clothing becomes a moth; from envy, one becomes blind from birth; and the stealer of a lamp becomes a skull-bearer.

One who is a descendant of Kauśika, a betrayer of friends, one who suffers decay, a reviler of his father and others, one whose speech falters, a speaker of falsehoods, and a false witness, shall have dropsy.
Then that mosquito, with its lips severed, shall become an obstacle to the wedding;
or else, as a low-born man, he shall void excrement and urine in the public square.

One who causes difficulty in urination becomes a defiler of a maiden, and one who sells the Vedas incurs impotence; a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard, and one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice becomes a boar.
From that [state], one becomes a cat; from there, a firefly; then a consumer of burning [substances]; a worm that eats putrid things; and one who is envious becomes a bee.

One who extinguishes a fire shall become afflicted with leprosy; one who takes what is not given becomes a bull; a stealer of a cow becomes a serpent; and a stealer of food shall suffer from indigestion.
A female crane becomes a fish by stealing fish, and a heron by stealing milk;
one who gives stale food to a Brahmin shall go to a state of hunchbackedness. (GarP 2.2.80)
O bird, he who steals fruits sees his lineage perish;
indeed, that man who eats food without having given it away shall be childless.
O King, by abducting one who has gone forth into the religious life, one becomes a flesh-eating piśāca;
by stealing water, one becomes a cātaka bird; and by stealing a book, one is born blind.
Having promised wealth to the twice-born, if one does not give it, one becomes a jackal;
by slandering those of noble birth, one obtains the body of a tortoise.

One who sells fruit becomes unfortunate; a wolf becomes the husband of a low-caste woman; one who touches fire with his foot becomes a cat; and one who eats the flesh of others becomes diseased. (GarP 2.2.84)
That man who breaks a water conduit shall become a fish;
likewise, those who do not listen to the stories of Hari nor offer praise to virtuous people [shall suffer the same fate].
O Hari, let this [mantra] reach the root of the ear of those men, and not other people— that dull-witted one who seizes the morsel of food situated in the mouth of another.
If one seeks divine implements for this Gaṇḍamālin,
yet practices dharma through hypocrisy, he shall become Gajacarma.
Diseases such as headaches afflict one who betrays trust,
as well as one who causes pain to a linga, misappropriates the property of Śiva, or consumes the remains of offerings made to Śiva.
Women also, by taking [a child] through this path, incur guilt;
it becomes the wifehood of these very same beings.
"Understand that all this belongs to hell at the end of enjoyment.
O Khaga, having shown you this, I have spoken to you in brief;
for just as there are various kinds of material objects, so too are the species of living beings."

Thus, the diversity of human happiness, suffering, and even births is said to arise from their own diverse karmas; they declare that from virtuous action comes what is auspicious, and likewise from non-virtuous action comes what is inauspicious.
All this that I was asked by you here has been fully explained.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Rites for the Deceased and the Ripening of Karma," in the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*), the *Pratāpa-khaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
(Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa— 3)
Sūta said: Thus encouraged, the bird, having heard this description of the nature of hell, asked about the hells themselves, his heart filled with agitation.
Garuḍa said:
Tell me the true nature of the hells into which those who perform evil deeds are cast, abounding as they are in suffering; and proclaim their various divisions.
The Blessed One said:
"O younger brother of Aruṇa, thousands of hells indeed exist;
it is not possible to describe them in detail, so I shall speak of them according to their principal ones."
Understand from me that the principal hell is named Raurava;
in Raurava go the man who gives false testimony and the man who is a liar.
Indeed, Raurava is two thousand yojanas in extent;
there, however, is a pit of knee-deep depth that is very difficult to traverse.
There, a mass of glowing coals was made level with the earth;
there, the ground of coals was heated by an extremely fierce fire.
In the midst of that, the followers of Yama release the evildoer;
burning with intense fire, he runs about in all directions.
At every step, his foot bursts and is shattered again;
he travels by lifting his foot and placing it down throughout the day and night.
In this way, he is released from an expanse of a thousand yojanas;
thereafter, for the sake of purifying other sins, he goes to a similar hell.
Raurava has been described by me as the first hell;
now hear, O bird, about the hell named Mahāraurava.
It extends for five thousand yojanas all around;
there the ground is made of copper, and beneath it is fire.
Scorching with that [flame], she, possessing a brilliance like a flashing lightning bolt, appears as exceedingly terrible to sinners upon the mere sight of her. (GarP 2.3.12)
And with his hands and feet bound by the followers of Yama,
that evildoer is released from the midst [of the river] and proceeds, wallowing along.
While being devoured by crows, cranes, wolves, owls, mosquitoes, and scorpions, as well as by other fierce creatures, he is dragged along on the path.
Burning with grief, his mind lost and wandering, he cries out "O Father!
repeatedly in distress; overwhelmed, he finds no peace.
Thus, liberation is attained by those men who have transcended [worldly existence],
even if tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years of evil have been committed by them with corrupt minds.
Likewise, another named Atiśīta (Exceeding Cold) is by its very nature [cold];
it is as vast as Mahāraurava and likewise enveloped in blinding darkness.
Afflicted by cold, men are bound there in that dreadful darkness;
having encountered one another, they embrace and seek refuge in each other.
Their teeth break as they tremble from the affliction of cold;
moreover, O bird, there are calamities there characterized by the extreme power of hunger and thirst.
A cruel wind, carrying fragments of snow, shatters their bones;
there, possessed by hunger, they incessantly devour the marrow, blood, and marrow-fluids trickling from their bones.
Being embraced, they wander about in their mutual union;
even so, there too, a very great suffering exists for men in the darkness.
O best of birds, that which is reached by one who has accumulated many [evil deeds] is known as Nikṛntana; beyond that is another, the most excellent of hells.
O bird, there the wheels of potter's kilns revolve incessantly;
upon them, men are dragged along by the Kālasūtra cord.
"O best of birds, by means of the *yamānu* held upon his finger, [he touches] from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head; yet no loss of life occurs for them."
Their bodies are cut into hundreds of pieces and indeed joined back together;
thus do those who have committed evil deeds wander for thousands of years.
Listen as I speak until that evil has been entirely exhausted and he no longer falls into hell.
There, the hell-beings dwelling therein experience unbearable suffering;
those very same wheels and water-wheels [are found] there, and others as well.
Some men who have committed evil deeds, having become the cause of their own suffering,
are mounted upon wheels and whirled around there.
For as many as thousands of years there is no interruption to their existence,
like those bound in water-wheels or like those tied in a water-pot.
Men wander about, vomiting blood again and again,
with entrails protruding from their mouths and eyes hanging down with entrails.
Listen now to another hell, named Asipatravana, where beings encounter sufferings that are unbearable to living creatures in this world. GarP_2,3.31.
There, upon a ground of blazing fire extending for a thousand yojanas,
seventy fierce-rayed fires burn with intense and most dreadful heat.
There, the beings dwelling in hell are constantly scorched;
yet in their midst, a foot with cool, glossy leaves is said to appear.
O best of birds, where there are fragments of fruits upon the leaves,
there very powerful dogs roam about, feeding on the flesh.
With large mouths and large fangs, possessing great strength like tigers,
they then beheld a forest ahead with cool shade.
There, living beings go, tormented by hunger and heat, crying out in great misery, "O mother! O brother! O father! GarP_2,3.36 //
For those who have gone there, their pair of feet is being burned by the fire situated on the earth, yet even there, the wind is exceedingly cool.
By that wind they are blown, and thus their swords fall upon them;
severed, they fall to the ground into a mass of blazing fire.
And elsewhere, while the entire surface of the earth is being licked and heated,
those dogs quickly tear at his body.
O dear one, I have described this most terrifying Sword-Leaf Forest (Asipatravana) to you, where those who weep are cut into many pieces.
Beyond this, learn from me of the even more terrifying Taptakumbha hell;
there, heated cauldrons are situated on all sides, filled with flames of fire.
Filled with masses of blazing fire, heated oil, and iron dust,
those of evil deeds are indeed cast headlong into these by the servants of Yama.
With their limbs bursting open and marrow and fluids dripping away,
they are boiled while their skulls split apart and their bones are being hacked by terrifying beings.
Torn apart by vultures, they are released again only to be seized by them with even greater speed;
once more they are scorched until they become one with the oil.
Then, with their heads, limbs, sinews, flesh, skin, and bones liquefied,
they are quickly struck by the staffs of the men of Yama as they are stirred about.
In the Kṛtāvarta hell, which is filled with great oil, those who have committed evil deeds are boiled;
this Taptakumbha has been described by me to you in detail, O bird.
The first is said to be Raurava, the next is Mahāraurava;
the third is Atiśīta, and the fourth is indeed Nikṛntana.
The fifth is Apratiṣṭha, and another is Asipatravana;
the seventh is Taptakumbha—these seven are considered the hells.
Other hells as well are likewise heard of, O lowest of men;
for according to the gradations of their actions, they fall into those various places.
For they are as follows: Naraka, Rodha, Śūkara, and Tāla; Taptakumbha, Mahājvāla, Śabala, and Vimohana.
Krimi, Krimabhakṣa, Lālābhakṣa, Viṣañjana, Adhaḥśiras, Pūyavaha, Rudhirāndha, and Viḍrabhuj. (GarP 2.3.51)
Likewise, there is the Vaitaraṇī river, the forest of sword-leaves,
the most terrible blazing fire, the pincers, and the lack of food.
Tāmisra, Kālasūtra, Loha,
Abhida, Apratiṣṭha, Avīci, and other such hells.
All the hells situated within the domain of Yama are characterized by darkness;
indeed, those who have performed evil deeds fall into them individually.
All those beginning with Raurava are proclaimed to be beneath the earth;
a man who is a robber, a killer of cows, a destroyer of embryos, or an arsonist shall fall there.

A killer of a Brahmin shall immerse himself in a boar, a drinker of liquor or a thief of gold shall fall from a palm tree, a slayer of a Kṣatriya shall fall [from a height], and having killed a Vaiśya, one goes to a miserable state.

He who commits the murder of a Brahmin, he who violates the bed of his guru, he who has sexual intercourse with his sister, one who is in a heated cauldron, as well as a king's soldier and a liar; GarP_2,3.57.
The seller of heated metals, likewise the guard of a prison, the one who sells honey-wine (mādhvī), and he who abandons his food; GarP_2,3.58.
He who approaches his daughter or his daughter-in-law, he by whom the Veda is sold, and he who defiles the Veda—these are the Mahājvālis. (GarP 2.3.59)
Those who despise their guru and strike him with arrows of speech,
and the man who approaches a woman who should not be approached, shall go to the Śabala hell.
The hero who, falling into delusion, indeed breaks the moral boundary,
and he who performs a wicked deed, enters upon a state of being devoured by worms.
One who hates gods and Brahmins falls into the Lālābhakṣa hell;
likewise do one who makes sacrificial vessels, a potter, one who misappropriates a deposit, and a physician.
One who sets fire to groves and one who administers poison go to Viṣañjana; likewise, he who accepts gifts from the unworthy and he who performs sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice.
A man who lives by these means shall go headfirst downwards;
[he who consumes] milk, liquor, meat, lac, perfumes, juices, and sesame seeds.
One who sells such things as these shall fall into the terrible hell of Putrid Pus; likewise,
he who binds chickens, cats, pigs,
birds, deer, or goats shall go to that same hell.
A keeper of goats, a keeper of buffaloes, one who lives by a water-wheel, one who lives by a banner, a Brahmin who subsists on the stage, a fowler, and one who performs sacrifices for villages; 66.

One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel belonging to a degraded person, a seller of Soma, a drinker of liquor, an eater of meat, and likewise a slaughterer of animals— GarP_2,3.67.
"These people fall into the Rudhirāndha hell; indeed, they fall—so say the wise—those who, while seated in a single row, feed poison to one another."
They fall into the terrible hell Viḍbhuj, of this there is no doubt;
likewise into Madhugrāha, Vaitaraṇī, and the one called Mūtrasaṃjñaka for those who revile [the teacher].
In the Asipatravana hell, there is one who is impure and wrathful;
even there, he is made to eat flames of fire by crows, like a deer-hunter.
Due to a lapse in his vow during a sacrifice, he shall fall into the Sandaṃśa hell;
likewise, if ascetics or celibate students discharge their semen even in a dream.
Those who are taught by their sons, and those who are commanded by their sons—
all of them go to hell, to the abyss, and to a state without food.
But those who, filled with anger and joy, perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life— all of them are dwellers in hell.
Situated above is the great and terrible Raurava, which is hot by nature;
below it is known as Sudāruṇa, which is cold by nature and characterized by darkness.
In this very sequence, all [the hells] are situated one below the other;
and the intensity of suffering in all of them increases according to the causes of their respective karmas.
And there is an increase in happiness everywhere here through the cause of the Dharma;
for the gods behold the most dreadful hells with their faces turned downwards.
And those hell-beings also see all the gods situated above;
these and other hundreds of hells are situated in the sky.
Day after day he is cooked in hell and burned elsewhere;
in another place he withers and splits, and in yet another he is crushed and dissolved.
In another hell, one is boiled and scorched; likewise, in yet another, struck by the wind, a single day in that hell shall have the duration of a hundred years.
Then, having emerged from all [those states], the sinner experiences the condition of an animal among worms,
insects, moths, stationary beings, and single-hoofed creatures.
Having gone to those places abounding in wild elephants, as well as to the cow-pens,
there [he becomes] a donkey, a horse, a mule, a gayal, a śarabha, and likewise a yak.
These six are the single-hoofed animals; now hear from me about the five-clawed ones, as well as those other species which are full of great sin and are givers of suffering.
Even a hunchback, one who is despised, or a dwarf may attain human birth;
yet he is born into the wombs of men such as the Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas.
They dwell in the womb for a moment and die again and again,
accompanied by whatever remainder of merit and demerit they possess.
Thereafter, he may ascend to the womb of a Rohiṇī, or become a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a king, and so forth; and at some point, he even attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, a god, or an Indra.
Thus do those of evil deeds fall downward into the hells;
now hear from me as I describe how those who perform meritorious deeds proceed.
Those men, directed by Yama to a meritorious rebirth,
enter a womb where hosts of Gandharvas sing and which is filled with the festivities of dance.
Adorned with the sweetness of necklaces and anklets,
the stainless celestial chariots, radiant with divine perfumes and garlands, proceed swiftly.
And having fallen from that state, they are born in the homes of other high-souled kings as those who protect the livelihoods and the earth of the healthy.
They obtain fierce enjoyments, and from there they go upward;
otherwise, having reached the downward path, men descend as before.
For a living being born in the world of death, death is indeed certain;
for the most sinful, the soul certainly departs by way of the lower path.
The earth dissolves into the earth, and likewise the waters into the waters;
fire dissolves into fire, and the wind into the wind.
And in space there is likewise space, all-pervading in the moon;
therein are desire and anger, as well as the five sense-faculties within the body.
O Tārkṣya, these have been described as the thieves who dwell within the body;
desire, anger, ego, and the mind are their leader therein.
And that Time is indeed the dissolution, joined with merit and demerit,
endowed with the five senses, together with all the gods.
He would enter the new body just as a snake enters its old, worn-out skin;
likewise, all the seven constituent elements (dhātus) that reside within the body [would depart].
For this body consists of six sheaths; all the bodily winds of embodied beings, as well as urine, feces, and whatever other diseases arise from their conjunction.
Bile, phlegm, marrow, flesh, fat,
bone, semen, and sinew— all these, along with the body itself, are consumed by fire.
This destruction of all embodied beings has been told to you, O Tārkṣya;
now I shall further describe to you how their bodies come to be.
The body is a single pillar bound together by sinews, adorned with three columns, joined with the sense organs, and possessing nine gates. (GarP 2.3.100)
Overwhelmed by sense objects, agitated by desire and anger, filled with passion and hatred, and plundered by the thief of craving so difficult to cross; (GarP 2.3.101)
This city is partitioned by the net of greed, enveloped in the cloth of delusion; it is well-bound by illusion and presided over by greed.
Those men who do not know the Self, which is endowed with these qualities and resides within the bodies of all embodied beings, are considered to be mere cattle.
In this very way, the fourfold body has been described to you;
eighty-four hundred thousand species were fashioned in the past.
Those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb—
all this concerning the detailed description of hell has been told to you.
Or perhaps there is a desire to ask what comes next in due order.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of the Hells, Entry into Them, Exit from Them, and so forth," in the *Pretakalpa*, the second part of the *Dharmakāṇḍa* within the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—4.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly, whatever defilement has been committed by men—
for the sake of purifying that sin, an expiation must be performed by men.
At the outset, the wise person should perform the tenfold ablution with ashes and so forth;
furthermore, according to his capacity, he should practice the substitutes for the six-year vow and the rest.
Or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that half;
then, according to one's ability, one should perform the ten gifts—listen indeed.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, molasses,
silver, and salt— these indeed are known as the ten gifts.
A man should give ten [cows] to those who have arrived for the sake of expiation;
thereafter, he proceeds along the path to the gate of Yama, which is crowded with pus and blood.
To cross the river Vaitaraṇī, one should give a Vaitaraṇī cow;
she who has black udders and black limbs is indeed known as the Vaitaraṇī.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt,
as well as the seven types of grain, land, and cows— each one of these is traditionally held to be purifying.
These eight great gifts should be given to an excellent twice-born man by one who is afflicted; hear from me their forms and characteristics.
An umbrella, sandals, garments, a signet ring, a water-pot, a seat, a vessel, and a footstool—these are remembered as the eightfold [set]. (GarP 2.4.9)
A vessel of sesame seeds, a vessel of clarified butter, and a bed with its furnishings—
all this should be given, as well as whatever is dear to oneself.
A horse, a chariot, a queen, an ornament,
and even a garment should be given to the Brahmins by him himself, preceded by the Veda.
O bird, one should also offer other gifts according to one's own capacity;
for one by whom atonement has been performed, even ten gifts [are required] on this earth.
The gift of a cow, the gift of the Vaitaraṇī river, and likewise the eight other gifts:
the vessel of sesame seeds, the vessel of clarified butter, and similarly the gift of a bed.
And by giving land according to the prescribed rite, one does not enter the womb of hell;
moreover, the wise maintain that the gift of salt may also be given independently.
Since this salty taste has arisen from the body of Viṣṇu,
when the life-breaths of a sick person do not depart upon the surface of the earth, [he recovers].
Then salt should be given, as well as the opening of the gate to heaven;
and whatever gifts have been personally bestowed by men [should also be offered].
And all those [auspicious things] stand before him;
O bird, he alone is truly a man who has performed the expiation with all its constituent parts.
Having reduced sins to ashes, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
for the milk of cows is indeed nectar, O best of birds.
Therefore, he who gives a cow attains immortality;
indeed, by giving the eight gifts, one shall dwell in the abode of the Gandharvas.
For in that terrible place, the abode wherein a human being is burned,
by the gift of an umbrella, a beautiful shade is produced on the path that bestows satisfaction.
If one gives sandals, one indeed crosses the Asipatravana forest with ease even while mounted on a horse and proceeds along. (GarP 2.4.21)
By giving food and a seat, one indeed experiences happiness on the road;
by giving a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in a waterless region, the donor shall surely be happy.
The messengers of Yama, though exceedingly fierce, terrifying, and dark-brown in hue,
do not cause him pain out of courtesy, because he has given gifts of clothing and ornaments.
O bird, a sesame vessel given to a brahmin certainly destroys the threefold sin arising from speech, mind, and body. (GarP 2.4.24)
By the gift of a vessel of clarified butter, a man shall dwell in the world of Rudra;
likewise, by giving a bed equipped with all its furnishings to a twice-born man.
Crowded with various celestial nymphs, he ascends a divine chariot;
having sported for sixty thousand years in the abode of Śakra.
Falling from the world of Indra, he shall become a king in this world—
endowed with all necessaries, youthful, and free from defects.
O Lord of Birds, he who gives a horse to a Brahmin dwells in the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on that horse.
Indeed, they attain as many abundant, radiant worlds as there are horses yoked to that chariot, which is equipped with all necessary implements. (GarP 2.4.29)
Having given a chariot to a twice-born man, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Having given to an eminent brahmin a buffalo that yields abundant milk, which has the hue of a fresh cloud, whose young calf is well-satisfied with mouthfuls of grass, and which is beautiful of hip and adorned with a golden tilaka, he conquers the arising of the worlds; what wonder is there in this?
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one is fanned by a breeze on the road;
by the gift of a garment, one becomes endowed with beauty, fortunate, and glorious.
He who bestows a house furnished with flavorful food and household utensils upon a Brahmin, his lineage does not perish, and he attains the unsurpassed heaven. (GarP 2.4.33)
In this matter, O best of birds, there is a difference in the weightiness or lightness of the fruit,
depending on the distinction between faith and lack of faith, and due to the gravity or insignificance of the gift.
Then, O bird, he experiences such delight as when one obtains the gifts of water and likewise the various flavors here in times of distress. (GarP 2.4.35)
He by whom food has been given with a mind purified by faith attains satisfaction even then, even without food.
If one should perform renunciation according to the prescribed rule when death is near, he shall not return again; he is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
If one who is near death is led toward a sacred ford (tīrtha),
liberation shall occur upon reaching that ford; if he dies while on the way,
there is no doubt that for him it will be equal to performing a sacrifice at every step.
If he should undertake the vow of fasting unto death according to the prescribed rite when death has arrived, O twice-born one, he does not wander further in saṃsāra.
The answer to the fourth question, "What is giving? has been stated;
now hear the answer to the question, "What is between death and burning? (GarP 2.4.40).
Then, having ascertained that the life-force has departed, the son or other relatives should quickly bathe and wash that corpse with pure water without hesitation.
Having clothed [the deceased] in new, unwashed garments, one should sprinkle his body with sandalwood water;
then, indeed, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at the place where the dead person lies.
Just as there may be fitness for burning preceded by ritual application, so too there may be sitting and washing; yet this fourfold [set] might not exist.
The invocation, the worship, the touching of the vessel, the immersion,
the formal resolve regarding the gift of food, and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should always take place.

The five ritual items would not exist; there would be no drawing of lines or the sprinkling of water for washing; and furthermore, one would not offer the inexhaustible water—these three things would likewise not exist.
O best of birds, one should perform the recitation of the *svadhā*, the pronouncement of blessings, and the application of the *tilaka*;
one should give a water-pot, offer food with black gram (*māṣa*), and provide a gift of iron as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The moving of the *piṇḍas* has been prescribed, but this triad has not been prescribed:
namely, the concealing, the dismissal, and likewise the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*.
Among these six types of impure śrāddhas, the rule has been declared for you:
there are exactly six locations for death—namely, at the door and likewise at the crossroads.
O bird, when there is rest, a pile of wood, or a collection [of materials],
the deity Earth is satisfied at the place of death by that which is called a corpse.
By this, the traveler at the door shall be satisfied, and the deity of the site (vāstudevatā) shall be pleased;
by this, the sky-farer at the crossroads and the deities beginning with the Bhṛtas shall be gratified.
At rest, this one is known as a *bhūta* and is satisfied by that;
on the funeral pyre he is called a *sādhaka*, and when gathered together, he is called a *preta*. (GarP 2.4.51)
Taking sesame seeds, darbha grass, clarified butter, and fuel, the sons and other relatives indeed proceed while reciting the verses of Yama or the Yama-sūkta.
Day after day, even as he is led away— cattle, horses, men, and bulls—
the son of Vivasvat is never satiated, like a wicked man with liquor.
Having recited this verse, or having recited a well-spoken hymn on the road,
all the kinsmen should proceed toward the forest in the southern direction.
O bird, one should perform two *śrāddha* rites on the way according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thereafter, one should gently place the corpse upon the ground with its head facing south.
Having placed [the body] on the cremation ground, one should perform the previously mentioned *śrāddha* ceremony;
the sons and others themselves should carry the grass, wood, sesame, clarified butter, and other materials. (GarP 2.4.56)
Any rite performed with items brought by a Śūdra becomes entirely fruitless;
one should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and face the south.
O Bird, an altar should then be constructed there according to the scriptures;
having divided the cloth into two parts, one should cover it with half of it.
One should cast half [of the body] directly onto the ground for the purpose of dwelling in the cremation ground;
then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should place the *piṇḍa* in the hand of the deceased.
Anointing with clarified butter should be performed on all the limbs of the corpse;
now hear that rite for the funeral cake (piṇḍa) which takes place in the interval between death and cremation.
The corpse becomes fit for the oblation through the five funeral cakes (piṇḍa) previously mentioned;
otherwise, due to its defilement, it indeed becomes a rākṣasa or similar being.
Having swept and smeared [the ground], and having scraped and removed the debris from the altar,
one should sprinkle it with water and establish the fire there according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda with flowers and unbroken rice grains,
the wise man should cremate one who maintains the sacred fires according to the Vedic injunctions.

One should avoid the fire of a Caṇḍāla, the fire of a funeral pyre, and the fire of one who has fallen from his caste. You are the creator of beings, the source of the universe, and the protector of the world.
"Therefore, bestow upon him this nectar that leads to heaven.
Having thus honored the flesh-eater, one should perform the oblation of the body.
When the body is thus half-burnt, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter with this mantra:
"From this you were born; may he be born again from you."
Having said, "To this [deity], for the heavenly world, svāhā," by name,
he should thus offer an oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by the mantra.
Therefore, one should weep intensely; in this way, he will find happiness after performing the cremation and the funeral rites there immediately following the burning.
O Bird, one should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased to pacify the pain of cremation;
then, having performed a circumambulation, those who witnessed the departure from the pyre [should do so].
Those who have recited the *sūktas* should go for the sake of bathing, preceded by the youngest;
then, having gone near the water and washed their garments, they should proceed.
Having put that [garment] on again, they should then say to that man:
"O men, we shall now perform the water-libation ceremony along with the removal of our clothes."
If someone has died at least ten years ago,
the sons and other relatives, with the eldest first, should say, "Perform [the rites]," while wearing a single garment and with their topknots untied.

All, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), should enter the water silently, facing the direction of the ancestors, with the mantra: "Apanaḥ śośucadagham. (Garuda Purāṇa 2.4.73)
Those who perform the bath should not splash the water;
instead, having come to the bank and tied their topknots, they should take straight *kuśa* grass.
Then, having placed water with sesame seeds in his right hand and taking it up in his joined palms, the sorrowful man [should offer it] toward the south from the *paitṛka* tīrtha.
O Bird, all of them, restrained in speech, should throw [the offerings] upon the ground or upon a stone, either once, three times, or even ten times.
"May they be satisfied, or may those who are being satisfied be gratified; I offer this libation; may they approach.
When the words "O deceased one, belonging to such-and-such a lineage" have been uttered, one should recite [the mantra] in this manner.
After the water-offering with joined palms has been performed, the cleaning of the teeth should be undertaken;
all kinsmen remain away for nine days, O Kāśyapa.
Then, having emerged from the water and put on [fresh] garments,
they should wring out their bathing cloth once and enter upon a clean spot of ground.
One should not shed tears after offering the funeral libation of water for cremation;
for the deceased, being powerless, must consume whatever phlegm and tears are shed by the kinsmen.
Therefore, one should not weep; rather, rites should be performed according to one's own capacity.
Then, when they had all sat down, a certain well-versed performer of rituals, an expert in the Purāṇas, [spoke].
One should dispel sorrow by proclaiming the impermanence of saṃsāra;
for within this human state, which is like the pithless trunk of a plantain tree, one must seek out the essential core.
He who acts [with such attachment] is utterly deluded regarding this body, which resembles a bubble on water; for this body, though composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state.
What cause for lamentation is there in that regard over one's own body produced by [past] actions? Even the earth, the ocean, and the gods meet their destruction. (GarP 2.4.84)
"How can the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction?"—
thus one should cause those seated upon soft grassy ground to hear there.
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by children;
having bitten the leaves of the Arjuna tree, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, [he should touch] fire, water, cow dung, white mustard seeds,
young dūrvā shoots, a bull, and other auspicious objects.
Having touched [the body] and having placed their feet slowly upon a stone, they should enter;
for one who has maintained the sacred fires, the cremation of the body is performed according to the Vedic injunctions.
One should bury a child less than two years of age and should not perform the water-libation for it;
likewise for a devoted wife who follows her husband in death.
Having first performed the ritual practice and paid homage to her husband, she should ascend the funeral pyre;
but she who, through delusion, falls from the pyre, shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
She who follows her husband shall dwell in heaven for as long a time as there are hairs on three and a half crores of human beings.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
so too that woman, having been extracted, rejoices together with him alone.
There, devoted to her husband and being praised by hosts of apsarases,
she sports with her lord for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, a thief, or a betrayer of a friend,
a woman who is not a widow purifies him by following him in death.
That woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral pyre,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
As long as a woman does not cause herself to be cremated when her husband has died in the fire,
she is by no means released from that female body.
She who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and that of the one to whom she is given.
She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who dies when her husband dies— she is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
A beloved wife ought not to go by ascending a separate funeral pyre;
however, those of the Kṣatriya and other castes who are of the same varṇa may indeed ascend it here.
Starting from a Caṇḍālī woman up to a Brāhmaṇī woman, the rule is the same for all of them, provided they are not pregnant and are neither very young nor very old.
O bird, I have explained the procedure for cremation in general;
do you wish to hear some specific details regarding it as well?
Garuḍa said: "O Lord of the World, tell me how the cremation should be performed when the master has gone abroad, or is dead, or when his bones have perished."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
If the bones of a man who has gone abroad cannot be found,
I shall describe to you their destination, location, and the prescribed rite.
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to that which is supremely secret regarding the difficult deaths of husbands:
those who have died from fasting or have been struck down by fanged beasts. GarP_2,4.104 //

Those who cling to the neck during an embrace, those who are emaciated, those who strike with the beak, those killed by poison, fire, bulls, or Brahmins, and those who commit suicide through cholera—[these do not attain the merit of the gift]. // GarP_2,4.105 //
Listen to the state of those who have died by falling, by hanging, or by water,
or by serpents, tigers, horned beasts, calamities, stones, or floods.
By means of Brahmins, beasts of prey, falls, trees, lightning, claws, iron, falling from mountains, the collapsing of walls, and likewise from cliffs; // GarP_2,4.107 //
In the Kaṭvāya forest and in the intermediate space, there were thieves, outcasts, women in their courses,
female dogs, Śūdras, washermen, and others who were adorned [with such things].
Those who die leaving remnants of food above, below, or both;
those who die by the blows of weapons; and likewise those touched by the breath from the mouth [of a corpse].
That should be known as an untimely death, occurring without the prescribed rites;
through that sin, having experienced the hells, they partake in the state of hungry ghosts.

One should not cause their cremation, nor the birth-impurity rites, nor the water-libation ceremony; one should not perform the funeral arrangements, nor conduct the post-mortem rites for the deceased.
One must not offer the gift of alms-food; for if one does so out of negligence, it all fails to reach its destination and perishes in the intermediate space.
Therefore, O bird, his sons, grandsons, and sapindas who desire their own welfare must perform the Nārāyaṇabali out of fear of public reproach. (GarP 2.4.113)
Yama declared that their purification shall occur in this manner and not otherwise;
once the Nārāyaṇa-bali has been performed, they become fit for the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika).
The rite that purifies him shall not be otherwise;
one should duly perform the entire Nārāyaṇa-bali at a sacred ford.
O Brahmin, one should have the rites performed before Kṛṣṇa by means of which a man becomes purified;
first, however, a libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed by Brahmins learned in the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
One should offer libations intended for Viṣṇu with all medicinal herbs mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata),
using either the Puruṣasūkta or Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Facing the south and recollecting the deceased as Viṣṇu— [thinking],
"The Lord is without beginning or end, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace"— GarP_2,4.118.
O inexhaustible one, lotus-eyed one, be the bestower of liberation from the state of a preta;
at the conclusion of the libation, may you be free from passion and devoid of envy.
Having become one whose senses and mind are conquered, pure, and devoted to dharma,
he should perform there exactly eleven śrāddhas with devotion.
In the performance of all ritual acts, being one-pointed and composed, one should offer water, rice, barley, wheat, and *priyaṅgu* grains. (GarP 2.4.121)
One should cause auspicious sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), ritual hand-gestures (mudrā), a parasol, and a turban to be offered;
one should cause all kinds of offerings to be presented, including milk mixed with honey.
One should give the eightfold gift accompanied by clothing and sandals;
one should liberate [the recipient] from all sins and must not practice deception regarding the row [of guests].
When the rice balls have been placed upon the ground, everything accompanied by perfumes, flowers,
and unbroken grains should be given to all the Brahmins according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Śāstras.
Whether in a conch, a sword, or a copper vessel, one should perform the libations separately,
while remaining joined in meditation and concentration and having descended to the ground upon one's knees.
One should indeed cause the arghya to be offered with a ṛc verse, each offering separately,
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, and the deceased as the fifth.
Then, they should be placed in separate jars together with the five jewels,
along with garments, sacred threads, mung beans, and footprints.
One should perform the five offerings to the deities according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should offer a stream of water separately for each individual rice-ball (piṇḍa).
In a conch shell, or a copper vessel, or even one made of clay if those are unavailable,
one should take water mixed with sesame seeds and all medicinal herbs.
One should give a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, together with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa; likewise, one should perform the gift of a footstep.
Then one should offer sesame seeds dedicated to Yama and an iron vessel as a sacrificial fee;
having thus offered the Viṣṇu-bali according to the rules and according to one's capacity.
It swiftly rescues [the victim]; there is no need for deliberation here. Now hear from me the special case regarding one who has died from the bite of a snake.
Having fashioned a Nāga out of a bhāra of gold and likewise a cow,
and having given them to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father.
Having thus offered the snake-oblation, one is liberated from the affliction caused by snakes;
thereafter, an effigy should be fashioned, provided with all medicinal herbs.
And hear, O Kāśyapa, the procedure for the arrangement of the Palāśa stalks:
having spread out a black antelope skin and Kuśa grass in the shape of a human being.

The collection of bones is said to consist of three hundred and sixty stalks; having placed those stalks individually upon these various limbs: śatatrayeṇa ṣaṣṭyā ca vṛntaiḥ prokto 'sthisañcayaḥ / vinyasya tāni vṛntāni aṅgeṣveṣu pṛthak pṛthak // GarP_2,4.136 //
One should place forty [syllables] on the head, ten on the neck;
one should apply twenty on the chest and likewise twenty on the abdomen.
One should place one hundred [units] on the two arms, twenty on the region of the hips,
one hundred on the two thighs, and thirty on the two shanks.
One should place four bones on the penis, six on the two testicles, and ten on the toes; in this manner, one should arrange the bones.
One should place a coconut in the position of the head and a gourd on the palate;
one should place the five jewels in the mouth and a plantain fruit on the tongue. (GarP 2.4.140)
One should place *nālika* in the intestines, and likewise *vālukā* in the nose; one should apply clay to the fat, and *haritāla* and *manaḥśilā* [to the blood]. (GarP 2.4.141)
Mercury is placed in the place of semen, gallstone in the feces, realgar on the limbs, and sesame oil in the joints. (GarP 2.4.142)
Just as barley flour is [placed] upon meat, honey upon blood, a mass of matted hair upon the head-hair, and the skin of a deer upon the hide; GarP_2,4.143 //
A palm leaf on the ears, guñjā berries on the breasts,
a śatapatra lotus on the nose, and a lotus on the region of the navel.
A pair of eggplants should be placed upon the testicles, and a gṛñjana root is auspicious for the penis;
clarified butter should be applied to the navel, and a trapusa fruit is prescribed for the two buttocks.
She is like a pearl upon the breasts, or a smear of saffron upon the head;
she is adorned with auspicious incense of camphor and aguru, and with fragrant, beautiful garlands.
One should place a silk thread as a lower garment upon the heart;
one should place prosperity and growth upon the two arms, and a cowrie shell upon the two eyes.
Pomegranate seeds on the teeth, campaka flowers on the fingers, vermilion at the corners of the eyes, and offerings such as betel leaf—[these are the ornaments]. (GarP 2.4.148)
Having prepared the deceased with all medicinal herbs and performed the worship as prescribed,
one should also place the sacrificial vessels in their proper order according to the ritual involving fire.
"May women purify my head; may this [head] of mine be purified by Varuṇa as well. Having thus performed the purification for the deceased with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone, GarP_2,4.150.
A well-behaved, milk-yielding cow, sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, and likewise salt, should be given with Viṣṇu in mind.
The seven types of grain, land, and cows—each one is remembered as purifying;
therefore, one should give a vessel of sesame seeds, and likewise the gift of a footstep.
One should perform the Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha for the sake of one's own liberation from the state of a preta;
then, having envisioned Viṣṇu within the heart, one should effect the release of the preta.
Having thus fashioned an effigy, one should burn it according to the prescribed ritual;
for its purification, the performer of the rite, such as a son or other relative, should perform an expiation.
Three, six, twelve, and likewise fifteen kṛcchra penances are prescribed for him,
according to the specific cause requiring expiation, just as for a Brahmin.
If one is unable [to perform the primary rite], one may instead perform a substitute offering (pratyāmnāya) such as a cow, gold, or other items;
likewise, if one lacks the qualification for it oneself, a kinsman should perform the purification in this manner.
But that which is given by an impure person, or intended for one who is impure—none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.
Having accomplished purification, the cremation and other post-mortem rites (aurdhvadehika) must be performed;
he who performs the cremation and so forth without first performing the expiation (niṣkṛti), [incurs sin].
Listen now to the expiation for those acts performed intentionally and unintentionally, respectively:
having touched fire, water, a ritual bath, [a corpse], carrying it, or speaking about it.
One who carries the corpse of any of these deceased persons, or burns it, is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, as well as by [the rites for] severing the cord and shedding tears.
Having performed the water-libation rite with the sacred grass, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance;
for a minor cause, the penance should be small, and for a great cause, it should be great.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, O you of noble vows, tell me the characteristics of the three: the Kṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Sāntapana."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Eating in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and eating food obtained unasked for three days, followed by three days of fasting— this is declared to be the Kṛcchra penance.
One should drink hot milk, hot ghee, and hot water, each for one day respectively, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
one should fast on the following day while performing the *Sāntapana* penance.
O bird, I have fully explained this procedure for one who has died an evil death;
then one should recognize him as truly dead when he has reached the extinction of the lamp.
Then one should perform the cremation with fire and observe impurity for three days;
for ten days, the ritual of the pit and the *piṇḍa* offerings must be performed, preceded by rites for the deceased.

One should then perform the ritual in this manner; thereafter, the deceased becomes a partaker of liberation, provided that the cremation was performed upon a substitute image due to the mistaken belief that he was dead.
Therefore, he must come and perform an immersion in a pit of clarified butter;
furthermore, the purificatory rites beginning with the birth ceremony (jātakarman) must be performed once again.
A man, O bird, should marry his own wedded wife according to the prescribed rites when the fifteenth year has passed, or the twelfth.
For one who is unknown or absent, one should perform a funeral rite using an effigy;
now hear the specific rule regarding the death of a woman in her menses or one who has recently given birth.
When the woman who has given birth has died, the performers of the sacrifice act in this manner:
they take water in a jar, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having consecrated the water with meritorious mantras through speech,
one should first bathe [the person] according to the prescribed rite with water from a hundred winnowing baskets.
Having bathed her with that very [water], O Lord of the Self, one should perform the cremation;
having bathed the deceased woman in her menses with the five products of the cow.
Having fashioned the form [of the deceased] within a cloth, one should cremate it according to the prescribed rite;
I shall now describe the cremation ritual for one who has died during the *pañcaka* period—listen to me.
Beginning with the half of Dhaniṣṭhā, this group of five constellations ending with Revatī is always defiled; it shall always be inauspicious.
No cremation should be performed there, nor should there be despair regarding any living beings;
water should not be offered to them, for it would always result in inauspiciousness.
Immediately after the five [rites], all other duties must be performed;
otherwise, suffering arises for his sons and kinsmen.
In these constellations, loss certainly occurs in the home of one who has died;
or else, the cremation must be performed according to the prescribed rites on the very same day of death.
That [rite] for human beings is preceded by oblations;
therefore, the Brahmins should perform this procedure according to the rules, accompanied by mantras.
Then, four effigies fashioned from darbha grass and consecrated with the Ṛkṣa-mantras should be thrown near the place where the corpse is located.
Then, a cremation should be performed together with those effigies;
at the end of the period of impurity, the sons should then perform rites for pacification and prosperity.
For that man who has died among the five [categories of sinners] and finds no peace,
one should offer sesame seeds, a cow, gold, and clarified butter on his behalf.
One should cause gifts to be given to the Brahmins that destroy all obstacles:
food, sandals, an umbrella, a golden seal, and two garments.
A sacrificial fee is given to the Brahmin as a means of liberation from sin.
Thus has this procedure, which removes the five [sins], been fully described by me; as well as the journey to Saṃyaminī, the duration of the stay, and the funeral rites.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rites for Cremation, the Characteristics of Kṛcchra Penances, the Return of the Deceased, the Death of a Woman in Her Menses, and the Expiations for the Five Types of Death," in the Pretakalpa of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 5.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having thus cremated the deceased man and having bathed and offered water with sesame seeds,
the women should go in front, while the men should follow behind.
One should have him eat neem leaves while weeping, addressing him by name;
and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed while he is standing upon a stone.
Having entered the house, O bird, all those who are sapinda relations, including sons and others, shall indeed remain in a state of impurity for ten nights. (GarP 2.5.3)
Having obtained their food by purchase, they should all sleep separately;
they should consume food free from pungent and salty seasonings, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days.
They should abstain from eating meat, sleep on the ground, remain celibate,
not touch one another, and refrain from giving gifts or studying.
Stained, with faces cast downward, wretched and deprived of enjoyments,
they avoid the massaging of their limbs and the combing of their hair.
They should eat from vessels made of clay or leaves;
they should stay there for one day or even three days.
Garuḍa said: O Lord, regarding that which is called "impurity" (āśauca),
what is its definition, for how long must it be maintained, and by what kind of men is it to be observed?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
This [sin] is quickly removed by means of time and other such factors;
for that which obstructs the offering of funeral cakes, study, giving, and so forth, is indeed a great excess arising from the person.
Impurity on account of death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it shall be exactly the same in the case of a birth for those who desire complete purification.
For those who offer water for a single birth, purification is desired after three nights;
those who offer water for the remainder of a death impurity are purified after three days.
Until the eruption of teeth, impurity is declared to last for one day;
until the tonsure ceremony (caula), it lasts for one night; until the initiation into Vedic study (vratādeśa), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, for ten nights.
Impurity has been fully explained to you; now I shall speak of the subject at hand in brief:
water should be placed in the third heaven and in the sky, and milk should be placed in an earthen vessel.
"O Kāśyapa, with this mantra, 'Bathe here,
drink here,' one should [offer it] at night at a crossroads where three pieces of wood are bound together by cords, for the sake of joy."
On the first day, or the third, or likewise the seventh or ninth,
the collection of the bones should be performed by those of the same lineage together with him.
After that time, touching the limbs of the sapinda relatives is prescribed;
likewise, those who share the same water (samānasalila) become eligible for all ritual acts.
Having bathed with a restrained mind, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the northeast and offer the piṇḍa for the pretas outside, omitting only the darbha grass.
On the ground for the unconditioned ones, and on kusha grass for the conditioned ones,
one should, with a concentrated mind, offer nine balls of rice over nine days.
Having offered the tenth ball of rice, one becomes pure during the remainder of the night,
whether it be a person of a different lineage or the same lineage, a woman or a man.
Whoever should offer [the funeral cake] on the first day must complete it for ten days;
he should perform the offering with rice, or with barley meal, or even with vegetables.
