Whatever substance was used on the first day shall remain the same for the ten-day period;
it is prescribed that the offering of a single handful [of water] continues for as long as the impurity lasts.
Alternatively, on the day the gift is given, one should offer handfuls of water according to the number of days elapsed:
ten handfuls within ten days, fifty within a fortnight, and at the end [of the year], one hundred and fifty.
Or, O bird, it may be a hundred añjalis increased by two;
for when the impurity lasts for three days, then there are ten añjalis.
On that first day, there were three añjalis;
on the second day, four; and likewise, on the third day, there were three.
O bird Śatāñjali, when there are thirty [breaths] on the first day, there are forty on the second day, and thirty on the third day. (GarP 2.5.25)
In this manner, the handfuls of water are to be distributed during both fortnights;
in all ancestral rites, the son is the primary person possessing the authority.
The scattering of rice-balls should be done silently, as well as the offering of flowers, incense, and so forth;
when the tenth day has arrived, one should perform a bath outside the village.
In that case, the clothes, hair, beard, and nails must be discarded;
a Brahmin becomes pure by touching water, and likewise a Kṣatriya by touching his mount.
A Vaiśya [should carry] a goad or reins, and a Śūdra who has performed his duties [should carry] a staff;
the shaving of the hair is performed by the sapinda relatives, including those younger than the deceased.
The rite for the sixteenth day, however, is performed with sixteen and ten funeral cakes;
indeed, by these, the first impurity caused by death lasts until the tenth day.
O best of birds, for ten days the sons and others there prepare morsels of food, which are divided into four portions every day.
With two parts the body [is sustained], with the third the followers of Yama are satisfied,
and with the fourth one sustains oneself as well.
Within nine days and nights, the body shall attain completion;
likewise, the head of the deceased is fashioned by the first lump [of clay].
But with the second [mark], one should briefly mark the ears, eyes, and nose;
and with the third, likewise in sequence, the throat, shoulders, arms, and chest.
With the fourth morsel, one should likewise [satisfy] the navel, the genitals, and the anus;
with the fifth, however, the knees, the shanks, and the feet at all times.
All the vital points [are struck] by the sixth [finger], while the channels are struck by the seventh;
the teeth and hair by the eighth, and virility by the ninth.
By the tenth [breath], however, there is fullness, a state of satisfaction, and the cessation of hunger.
O Vainateya, listen to me as I describe the middle one, the sixteenth.
O Bird, there are eleven [deities] beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Viṣṇu, as well as five Śrāddhas for the gods; among these, the sixteenth is the middle one.
If Bali Nārāyaṇa is made the object of the rite with a mental image,
then indeed the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) must also be performed on that eleventh day.
If a bull is not released on the eleventh day for a deceased person,
his state as a preta remains firmly established, even by the performance of hundreds of śrāddhas.

If the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) has not been performed when the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍapātana*) is made, one should know that everything is fruitless; it does not accrue to the deceased.
On this earth, there is nothing else at all— neither a son, nor a wife, nor a grandson, nor a father, nor a daughter— that exists [to save one] apart from the rite of releasing a bull.
Immediately after his death, the bull festival (vṛṣotsarga) must certainly be performed for him,
accompanied by four young heifers, or else a bull should be set free.
If, when the eleventh day has arrived, the acquisition of a bull occurs, his state as a preta shall not exist provided he is adorned according to the prescribed rite.
Having fashioned that bull out of *darbha* grass and flour,
the wise man should release it at the time of the bull's consecration (*vṛṣotsarga*), should he be unable to obtain a bull by any means.
Having fashioned a bull out of either clay or *darbha* grass, one should release it;
on the eleventh day, one should give whatever was desired by that person while he was alive.
One should likewise give a bed, a cow, and other such gifts intended for the deceased;
one should feed many Brahmins for the sake of pacifying the hunger of the departed spirit.
O Vainateya, listen as I describe the third, the sixteenth [chapter]:
the twelve monthly [rites] and likewise the first six-monthly one.
The sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is considered the third of the sixteen [śrāddhas],
performed on the twelfth day, at the end of three fortnights, at six months, monthly, and at the end of the year.
Due to differences of opinion, they speak of this sixteenth [offering] as the third;
for him by whom these sixteen funeral offerings (śrāddha) for the deceased have not been given— GarP_2,5.50.
Even by performing hundreds of śrāddha rites, his state as a piśāca remains firm;
it is proclaimed that the first [śrāddha] should be performed on either the eleventh or the twelfth day.

O son of Vinatā, O bird, on the anniversary of death, one should perform the purification every month starting from the first month; however, this may be done with a reduction of either one day or three days.
Indeed, Śrāddha rites are performed at the end of a month, six months, a year, or three fortnights; likewise, the Sapiṇḍana rite occurs when a full year has passed or at its half.
For men, [the rite] may be performed after three fortnights, or at a time of prosperity, or on the twelfth day;
for family customs are infinite, and the lifespan of men is subject to decline.
Because of the instability of the body, the performance on the twelfth day is praised;
O Lord of Birds, hear from me the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rites as well.
O Kāśyapa, that too should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
one should prepare four vessels provided with sesame seeds, perfumes, and water.
O Bird, there is one vessel for the deceased (preta) and likewise three vessels for the ancestors (pitṛ);
one should pour the contents of the preta-vessel into those three ancestral vessels.
One should offer four piṇḍas and complete them at the eastern ends;
from that point onward, the deceased indeed attains equality with the ancestors.
Then, O Lord of Birds, when that deceased one has attained the status of an ancestor,
one should worship his preceding ancestors with all the rites of the śrāddha.
In the case of ascending the same funeral pyre, as well as when death occurs on the same day, there is no *sāpiṇḍya* for a woman;
rather, upon the death of her husband, the woman's [lineage] becomes his.

O bird, in the case of a husband and wife, there is no doubt that the unity of the funeral rite, the unity of time, and the unity of the performer occurs together during the śrāddha and other rites, as well as at the cremation.
If she ascends the funeral pyre on a day other than the anniversary of her husband's death,
then when that anniversary arrives, she should be joined with him by means of a separate rice-ball offering.
And one should complete [the ritual] every year simultaneously.
For one whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite occurs before the completion of a year,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (udakumbha) must also be given for that entire year.
The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the sixteen *śrāddhas* should be performed by a single person alone, even among those whose wealth has been divided.
Sapiṇḍya with the paternal grandmothers, as well as with the maternal grandfathers, has been stated;
sapiṇḍya with the husband of the woman is also mentioned due to the distinction of dress and appearance.
I shall tell you the timing for the *navaśrāddha*; listen, O Kāśyapa!
On the day of death, at the place of death, one should arrange the *śrāddha* for the bird.
And then, the second [śrāddha] is that which is performed at the place where rest was taken on the way;
thereafter, the third śrāddha is said to be at the site of the funeral pyre.
O bird, there are indeed nine Śrāddhas: on the fifth, the seventh, likewise on the eighth, the ninth, and also on the tenth and the eleventh.
These nine types of ancestral rites (śrāddha) are recorded; the third is known as the ṣoḍaśī.
These should be performed by men according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
The nine-fold śrāddha is proclaimed for the first day, as well as the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh days. (GarP 2.5.71)
These six are spoken of here, yet they become nine through sacrifice;
I have explained them to you according to the differing opinions of the sages.
The position of conventional usage is my preferred view, though some here maintain that it is a formal application (*yoga*).

The sages said:
"Listen, child; we shall speak for your benefit, O boy. (GarP 2.6.89)
Indeed, by that which is maintained, there shall be happiness both here and in the hereafter for the various beings in saṃsāra— gods, animals, humans, and all other folk.
Bound by the snares of karma, they experience various kinds of enjoyments;
through the quality of *sattva* one attains the state of a god, and through *rajas*, the state of a human.
Driven by ignorance and following the impressions of his latent tendencies, the living being falls into the state of an animal due to darkness;
having obtained rebirth from a mother, he dies again and again.
Having thus passed through countless wombs, even those lands of karma,
one may at some point, by the turn of fate, obtain a human birth which is so difficult to find.
By the great grace of the Great Ones, having known Hari,
one is liberated from the crocodile of disease, the net of delusion, and the shoreless ocean of existence.
I see no other means for one desiring to cross over than the remembrance of Rāma, just as butter is not found in curds, nor light anywhere within wood.
By means of such churning practices, having thus known the Supreme, one shall become happy;
the Self is eternal, imperishable, true, all-pervading, the sustainer of all, and great.
He is immeasurable, self-luminous, and ungraspable even by the mind; consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, He dwells in the heart of every living being.
Even when all things perish, space never perishes;
it remains within all beings, as well as in fire and water.
The Self is everywhere untainted, like the wind among earthly things;
the Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees and acts for the protection of the virtuous.
Just as a jewel becomes manifest in the world yet is not perceived by the ignorant,
so too is that which you should cultivate in the heart through discernment by means of the intellect.
The Unborn One, satisfied by the yoga of devotion, reveals Himself;
thereupon, one becomes fulfilled and forever free from desire for anything anywhere.

Therefore, having abandoned the ego-sense regarding the body and its attachments, one should move through the worlds— worlds which are like a dream— free from attachment and devoid of the sense of "mine."
Where is constancy in a dream, and where is truth in a magical illusion?
Where is permanence in an autumn cloud, or where is reality in this physical body?
Having understood that all that is seen, whether moving or unmoving, is produced by ignorance and karma, the yogi who has mastery over his conduct will thereby attain perfection.
Having spoken thus, all those virtuous ones, who are compassionate toward the distressed, departed;
and I, following the path they had described, practiced exactly in that manner every day.
Then, before long, I beheld within myself this wonder:
consisting of light, eternally blissful, and as pure as the autumnal moon.
Having drenched me with floods of bliss and made me intensely longing,
that great splendor vanished like lightning in the sky.
Meditating with devotion upon that very wonder in my mind,
I cast off my body in due time and went to the imperishable Hari.
Furthermore, O Brahmā, by his will, my birth as Brahmā occurred through the grace of the Blessed One,
even though I was free from desire for the three worlds.
"Pressing the lute repeatedly, I wander about singing," having said this and shared his own experience with me, the wandering sage departed.
For me, too, there arose supreme wonder and great satisfaction;
therefore, through association with the virtuous and through devotion to the Supreme Self.
The mind, purified, stainless, and tranquil, shall attain liberation;
even the sin produced over many lifetimes [is destroyed] through association with the virtuous.
"O knower of dharma, it perishes quickly, like autumn waters.
The Vaiśya said:
"Having drunk the nectar of your words, my heart has attained peace."
"By the sight of you, the fruit of all sacred fords has been produced within me.
Having heard these words of his, the best of sages spoke:
Lomaśa said:
O Indra among kings, for your own benefit and because you desire the fruits of the three goals of life,
that which has been well-performed by you would have been even more abundant had it been done with the ritual release of bulls.
I consider everything else to be as ineffective as water from the frost;
there is no means on the surface of the earth that is equal to the rite of releasing a bull.
They go with ease to the destination of those who perform meritorious deeds—
he by whom the release of a bull was performed and who acted as the officiant for the horse sacrifice.
"I have seen both of them as equal and divine in the presence of Śakra;
therefore, having gone to Puṣkara and performed the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), [you shall attain your goal]."
"Therefore, O virtuous one, go home so that everything may be accomplished.
Vipaścit said:
"Then he returned once more to the excellent Puṣkara on the full-moon day of Kārttika."
Where the Blessed One, in the form of a boar and the fulfiller of sacrifices, resides,
he performed everything according to the rules together with the best of sages.
Many sacred fords have been visited, and thereafter there was the meeting with Lomaśa;
yet the merit born from the marriage of Nīla became even greater than that.
Having enjoyed divine sense-objects and having ascended to an excellent celestial mansion,
he was born by virtue of his merit into the royal family of Vīrasena.
For those who perform the rite of releasing a bull— which is proclaimed by Vīrapañcānana as the sole means of accomplishing the four aims of life— and for those who serve therein:
Touched by the spray of water from the cow's tail, they became divine in form;
standing at a distance, they beheld themselves with beautiful forms and well-nourished bodies.
And those people who appear even further away— unfortunate, soiled, coarse, emaciated, and lacking clothing— [should be known as those who have committed grave sins].
Those who, not seeing the bull-sacrifice, harbor malice—
all this conduct of the king from his previous birth was reported.
"I have heard from Parāśara this wonderful narrative concerning the Dharma;
therefore, out of compassion for me, please go to your own home."
Having heard the words of Vipaścit, that brahmin, filled with supreme wonder,
went home, escorted by the king’s servants.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Therefore, O King, if you are afraid even of Yama, perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), the most excellent of all rites, according to the prescribed injunctions.
O best of kings, there is no practice superior to the release of a bull; thus, the secret of Dharma has been told to you by me. (GarP 2.6.130)
If a woman who has sons dies before her husband,
she should not perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), but she should give a milch cow as a gift.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O bird, having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, the king went to Madhupurī and performed the entire rite of vṛṣotsarga according to the prescribed rules.
Having returned home, he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose;
in due time, he met his end and was led away by the followers of Vaivasvata.
Leaving Kālanagara, he traveled a great distance along the road and asked his messengers, "Where is the city of Śrāddhadeva?"
Wherein the sinners are cast down by the servants of Yama for the purification of their sins,
there dwells that god who discerns between dharma and adharma.
"That city of sin has already passed; it should not be looked upon by those such as you.
Having seen King Dharma before them, they spoke with the utmost reverence:
Then the god, possessing a divine form and accompanied by gods and gandharvas,
revealed himself to that high-souled king.
Having prostrated himself like a staff, the king stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
his mind filled with joy, he praised the God in many ways.
The King of Dharma also praised the king and spoke these words:
"Let him be led to the world of the gods, where enjoyments are most abundant."
Having heard that, Vīravāhana questioned Yama, the Lord of Justice: "O Lord, I do not know by what merit you are leading me to heaven."
The King of Dharma said:
"Meritorious deeds were performed by you—gifts and sacrifices in full detail;
indeed, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, the rite of releasing a bull was performed in Mathurā."
O King, even a very small amount of dharma, if practiced correctly, expands into great abundance through the grace of the twice-born and the gods. (GarP 2.6.142)
Having spoken thus, the brother of Yamunā vanished in an instant;
Vīrabāhu went to heaven and rejoiced together with the gods.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O bird, I have described to you in great detail the sacrifice of the bull (vṛṣayajña).
By hearing how it effects the removal of the karma of living beings, one is liberated from sins.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Release of a Bull," in the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the *Dvidṛgdṛ Pretakalpa*, during the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*— Chapter 7—
Garuḍa said:
O Hari, I have heard this great narrative concerning the fruit of the ritual release of a bull;
now tell me another story in which your wondrous majesty is revealed.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Today I shall relate to you a most wonderful dialogue between Santaptaka and the pretas, for the purpose of making his true nature known.
A certain Brahmin, intensely heated by his asceticism and with his sins burnt away by penance,
having realized the worthlessness of cyclic existence, wandered indeed in the forests.
Once, that twice-born man set out on a pilgrimage, his eyes fixed upon the prostrations made by the multitudes of Vaikhānasa sages.
And because his senses were withdrawn, he was one who suppressed outward activity;
moving by means of mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), he indeed became one who had strayed from the path.
While walking thus at the time of midday bathing, he, being desirous of water,
opened his eyes and gazed toward all the directions.
Then he beheld a dense forest, thick with hundreds of shrubs, creepers, and trees,
crowded with bark-covered trunks and spreading branches.
There were palm trees, *tāla* trees, *tamāla* trees, *priyāla* trees, and likewise *panasa* trees;
as well as *śrīparṇa*, *śāla*, *śākhoṭa*, *syandana*, and *tinduka* trees.
Sarja, arjuna, āmrātaka, śleṣmātaka, abhītakas, picumarda, ciñciṇī, karkandhū, and karṇikāras; GarP_2,7.9 //
Among these and many other trees, not even the path of birds is seen; how much less, then, that of a human?
In that most terrible forest, crowded with lions and tigers,
and inhabited by hyenas, gavayas, bears, and buffaloes.
It was surrounded by cuckoos, uru deer, elephants, monkeys, and likewise by wild beasts,
as well as by other carnivorous animals, piśācas, and rākṣasas.
The twice-born Santaptaka, his mind somewhat terrified by fear, became bewildered as to what to do; Yadbhavishya, however, departed once again.
Even amidst the humming of crickets and the hooting of owls,
Kunīlāṅga, lending his ear, moved forward five steps.
There, at the top of the banyan tree, he saw a corpse bound with tendons, as well as five extremely dreadful *preta*s with arms like those [of the corpse].
O bird, their limbs were reduced to nothing but veins, bones, and skin, with their bellies clinging to their backs,
as if they had abandoned their noses out of fear of falling into the hollows of their own eyes.
Their bones were shattered by the blows of swarms of needles, hooks, and saws;
they held constant great festivals for tasting marrow, fat, and fresh brains.
Seeing those [beings] whose bones were crushed by the friction of great tusks with clashing tips, his heart was terrified; he stood there, his gait faltering.
Seeing that a brahmin had arrived in the deserted forest, they ran away, each saying, "I will go first! I will go first! (GarP 2.7.19).
Among them, two by two seized his hands;
then others, two by two, seized his feet, and a fifth seized his head.
Intent on plowing, they spoke with words appropriate to their own kind, using clear articulation: "I shall eat," "I shall devour. (GarP 2.7.21)
Suddenly, taking him along with her, she departed; she looked about, wondering, "How much meat remains for the young brahmin, and what is to be done? (GarP 2.7.22)
They beheld this corpse, its intestines ripped out by their own iron-like fangs;
then, descending from the sky, they seized it with their feet.
But with their bodies mangled, they returned once more to the very sky;
seeing himself being carried away through the air, that twice-born one— GarP_2,7.24.
Overwhelmed by fear, he went to me in his mind for refuge;
with his heart, he mentally offered salutations to the Discus-bearer, who is equal to the one composed of consciousness.
May Mukunda— who, by the stroke of his discus, cast the crooked crocodile far away and removed its suffering,
thereby liberating the elephant from the crocodile’s maw— cut through the bonds of my karma.

May that Discus of mine, which the enemy of Mura released for the sake of Bharga’s sacrifice after having had King Śuddhoda imprisoned by Bhīma of Magadha and then himself liberated from his bonds, cut asunder this noose of karma.
"In this world, he praised me with his mind alone; being thus praised, I arose and went suddenly to that place where he was being led by the pretas."
"O bird, upon seeing us being led away by them, curiosity arose within me; I asked: for how long indeed did I follow behind them? (GarP 2.7.29)
O slayer of serpents, by my mere presence, that twice-born man instantly experienced the same bliss as the king who was sleeping in the palanquin.
Then, as Maṇibhadra was going toward Mount Meru, he was seen by me on the path;
having narrowed my eyes, I was indeed led to his side by that king of the Yakṣas.
I said to that great yakṣa: "Be indeed my adversary!
Destroy those hungry ghosts once more, and carry away the corpse located there. (GarP 2.7.32)
Thus addressed, he gave way to a most terrible and unbearable rage and assumed that preta-form which brings suffering even to other pretas.
Stretching out his two arms and licking the corners of his mouth,
he advanced toward those hungry ghosts, scattering them with a great wind from his loins.
With his two arms he seized two by two, and with his feet one from the head;
then he suddenly struck the pretas with a firm fist.
With all their faces pale, they each seized that brahmin and the corpse by the hands and feet, and began to fight.
With their claws, slaps with the palms of their hands, kicks,
and likewise with the strikes of their fangs, they all tore apart that single preta.
Having rendered their blows fruitless, he then seized them—
living men, not corpses— just as Death seizes the life-breath.
As soon as the corpse was taken away, those most cruel ones, having released a single bird on Mount Pāriyātra, were exceedingly delighted.
That preta, traveling with the speed of the wind, reached them in a mere instant;
he then became invisible, and they returned, their hopes shattered.
As soon as the Brahmin began to recite there on that mountain,
at that very moment, by the mere majesty of my abode and of the Brahmin, [the mountain was split].
Immediately, the memory of their former birth arose within them;
having circumambulated that brahmin, the bull among the twice-born, they then spoke.
Having said, "Today you ought to forgive us," those hypocritical gods— [an act] as impossible as the overturning of a mountain or the drying up of the ocean— GarP_2,7.43.
Having heard those words of theirs, he then asked:
"Who are you? Is this an illusion, or a dream, or perhaps a mental delusion?"
The pretas said:
"Understand this very truth: we pretas are indeed born of our own karma.
The brahmin said:
What are their names, what is their conduct, and how have they come to this state?
"How were you previously undisciplined, and how have you now become disciplined?
The pretas replied:
"Listen, O chief of brahmins; we shall explain your questions in due order."
O Great Yogi, through the sight of you, my sins have been removed;
I am known by the name Paryuṣita, and this one is remembered as Sūcīmukha.
"The third is Śīghraga, the fourth is Rodhaka, and the other is Lekhaka.
The Brahmin said:
"How indeed can there be anything meaningless for the pretas born of their own karma?"
"O hungry ghosts, speak without delay the etymological derivation of these names.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Thus addressed by the brahmin, they each gave their respective answers. (GarP 2.7.49)
Paryuṣita said:
"Once, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, I indeed invited a brahmin."
Having delayed, that old man arrived at my house; since I had not yet performed the śrāddha rite, I ate that cooked food out of hunger. (GarP 2.7.51)
Having drawn out some stale food and given it to a brahmin,
that sinner, upon death, went indeed to a loathsome womb because of that sin.
Because it was given as something that had stood overnight, it is therefore remembered as "paryuṣita" (stale).
Sūcīmukha said:
Once, a certain Brāhmaṇī went to the holy ford of Bhadravaṭa.
An old woman, whose only life was her five-year-old son, was obstructed by me, an heir to the Kṣatriya lineage. (GarP 2.7.54)
But there, in that desolate forest, having followed the path of wicked travelers,
he took her provisions along with her clothes and the garments of her son.
O Brahmin, I took them, pressing them to my head with my fist;
at that moment, the boy, afflicted by thirst, drank the water contained in the vessel.
In that place where there was only so much water, I warded him off with a roar of "huṃ";
then, like one parched with thirst, I drank all the water from my vessel.
Terrified by fear and parched with thirst, a child fell down, lifeless;
his mother, having died from grief for her son, cast her own body into the well.
O Brahmin, because of this sin, I have attained the state of a preta;
my body is as large as a mountain, yet the opening of my mouth is like the tip of a needle.
Even though I might obtain food, it cannot be eaten;
for even as I am burning with the fire of hunger, my mouth remains clenched shut.
Therefore, O Brahmin, because there was an opening in my mouth equal to the point of a needle, for this reason I am known by the name Sūcīmukha (Needle-mouth).
Śīghraga said:
"Formerly, belonging to the Vaiśya caste and possessing great wealth, I went with a certain friend to another land to engage in trade."
I had a friend with great wealth, and because of him, a great greed arose in me; yet, due to my aversion toward the unseen [truth], even my very root was destroyed. (GarP 2.7.63)
Then, having departed from there by boat, we both began to cross the river flowing along our path as the sun was turning red.
"And that friend of mine, exhausted by the fatigue of the journey, fell asleep in my lap; at that moment, an exceedingly cruel thought arose within me, who am so wicked."
When the hero had perished in the flood, I then cast him onto my lap;
as I was performing his funeral rites on the boat, he was not even noticed by the people.
Taking all the goods he had there— jewels, pearls, gold, and so forth— he quickly departed from that place and returned to his own home.
Leaving all that in my own home, I informed his wife:
"My brother was indeed slain by bandits on the road after they had plundered his wealth. (GarP 2.7.68)
"O mother of children, I have fled; do not weep," I said to her at that time; yet she, afflicted by grief, still felt a sense of "mine-ness" toward her household and kinsmen.
Having renounced even his most beloved life-breaths, he offered them into the fire according to the prescribed rite;
then, seeing that [kingdom] indeed free from thorns, he went home filled with joy.
Having come here, I have consumed all that wealth throughout my life;
indeed, I quickly returned after having cast my friend into a pit. (GarP 2.7.71)
"For this reason, I am a preta known by the name Śīghraga.
Rodhaka said: "O Lord of Sages, in the past I was of the Śūdra caste. (GarP 2.7.72)
Having obtained through royal favor the authority over a hundred great villages,
my parents were aged, and I had one younger uterine brother.
And that brother of mine was quickly separated from me by a single hunter;
deprived of his clothes and ornaments, he experienced supreme suffering.
His parents secretly gave him various small things that had not been given;
I have heard from his parents what was given to him by their trusted attendants.
Having understood all that in its true nature, I caused my parents to be imprisoned;
having bound them with firm shackles in a solitary, empty chamber.
Then, afflicted by grief, the two of them gave up their lives by drinking poison;
O twice-born one, even that boy wandered about, deprived of his parents.
O Brahmin, having died of hunger while wandering through cities, towns, villages,
and hamlets, I have, because of this sin, passed away and entered the state of a hungry ghost (preta).
"Since my parents were imprisoned, I am therefore named Rodhaka.
The scribe said:
"O Brahmin, in former times I was a most excellent twice-born man in Avantī."
"For I was appointed by King Bhadra to the worship of the gods;
there were many images there, bearing many names."
Then, as I performed worship for them, there was indeed much gold and a multitude of jewels upon their limbs; yet, while doing so, a sinful thought arose within me.
Having shattered their entire bodies with sharp iron, I also performed the gouging out of the jewels from their eyes and other parts. (GarP 2.7.82)
And seeing the limbs of the statues fashioned otherwise than they should be,
and their eyes devoid of jewels, the king blazed with anger like fire.
Afterwards, that bull among Brahmins, the king, made this vow:
"Whosoever shall have stolen these jewels and gold..."
"Once he is known by me, he will undoubtedly become one to be slain.
Having learned all of that, I shall go to his house at night, bearing a sword."
Having entered the king's palace, I killed the king like a sacrificial animal;
then, taking the jewels and gold, I departed elsewhere at nightfall.
In the great forest, by a tiger, it was carved with its claw-blades—
that which I had fashioned from iron for the purpose of drawing a likeness.
"O twice-born one, because of this sin, I am a preta; my name is Lekhaka. After the exhaustion of my experience in hell, I have attained this state of a preta. (GarP 2.7.88)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Such signs have been described by you regarding these ten states;
now let them tell me of their conduct alone, as well as their food, O Pretas."
The pretas said:
"Where there is no following of the Vedic path, no modesty, no dharma, no self-control, no forbearance, no fortitude, and no knowledge— we do not dwell there."
We inflict suffering upon him who, in his house, [eats] flesh and blood from its limbs in succession; for him, there shall be neither *śrāddha* nor *tarpaṇa*. (GarP 2.7.91)
"Eating and drinking—this is the conduct prescribed for us;
now hear of our food, which is despised by all the world."
"O sinless one, have you seen anything? Tell us; has anything been perceived by you?
[We see] vomit, feces, and rheum of the eyes, as well as phlegm, urine, and tears."
"O twice-born one, do not ask us further about this food and drink; O Master, shame arises in us as we speak of our own sustenance. (GarP 2.7.94)
"O Lord, we are ignorant, dull-witted, and overcome by darkness;
yet, O Brahmin, a memory of our former births has suddenly come to us. (GarP 2.7.95)
"O Lord, we do not know at all whether they are disciplined or undisciplined.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"While the deceased were speaking thus, and while the twice-born man was listening accordingly..."
Then I showed him this very form of mine, O Tārkṣya;
and that best of the twice-born, having seen the Person standing before him within his own heart, [was filled with wonder].
The lord of birds praised me with hymns and prostrated like a staff;
those hungry ghosts (pretas) also performed penance thereafter, their eyes wide with wonder.
O bird, those whose speech falters due to affection did not say anything at all; yet,

salutations be to you who, out of compassion, truly effect the deliverance of those whose minds are darkened by passion, whose hearts are agitated by greed, and whose intellects are deluded by ignorance.
While the twice-born was speaking thus,
that mountain then shone brilliantly on all sides from six celestial chariots of great luster, moving through the sky, adorned with magnificent garments, and produced by my will.
Thus, having traveled by celestial chariot to my world, that best of brahmins was followed by those five pretas;
through the power of association with the virtuous, they went to heaven, a realm of immeasurable merit, like the Suparṇas.

The hungry ghosts descended to heaven through the power of their association; among them was a Brahmin named Viṣvaksena, known as Taptaka, who possessed great renown. All this has been narrated by me to you; indeed, the man who recites this or who hears it shall not fall into the state of a hungry ghost.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Five Pretas," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[From] the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, who has the authority here for all these post-mortem rites?
How many kinds of rituals are prescribed? Tell me all of this."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O bird,
the son, the grandson, the great-grandson, his brother, the offspring of his brother,
or even the offspring of a *sapiṇḍa*— these kinsmen are worthy of performing the funeral rites."
In the absence of all those, O Bird, the rites should be performed by the sapinda descendants; and when both lineages are extinct, they should be performed by the women.
And the king, having severed his bonds by his own will,
should perform the preliminary rites, the intermediate rites, and likewise the subsequent rites.
Every year, O bird, a śrāddha must be performed there according to the rules for the ekoddiṣṭa rite; hear from me the fruit thereof.
Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Nāsatyas, Sūrya, Agni, Vasu, and the Maruts;
the Viśvedevas, the hosts of ancestors, the birds, human beings, and animals.
By performing a śrāddha endowed with faith for the crawling creatures, the hosts of mothers, and whatever else is designated as "beings," one gratifies the entire world.
Satisfied themselves, they in turn satisfy him with sons, wives, and wealth;
thus, the distinction between authority and ritual action has been briefly described.
Garuḍa said: O Supreme God, O Viṣṇu, if not even one among those mentioned should be eligible,
what then ought a wise man to do?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When there is no eligibility and when there is no certainty [of the deceased's state],
a man himself should offer the śrāddha for the sake of the living being while that being still lives.
Having observed the fast, well-bathed, united with Kṛṣṇa, and composed in mind,
he should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, who is both the agent and the enjoyer.
Accompanied by ritual fees and sesame seeds, he should, being well-composed, offer three water-cows to the ancestors with the words "Svadhā."
Recalling [the mantra], "To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svadhā! Homage! and recalling, "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage!"—thus he should remember.
To the south, however, one should offer the third oblation accompanied by a sacrificial fee, while recollecting: "Svadhā! Obeisance to Yama, the son of Aṅgiras! (GarP 2.8.14).
Having placed the Brahmins between those two and consulted with them, he should feed them;
having positioned the first [line] in the north, he should place the second in the south.
Having placed the third [offering] in the middle, one should thereafter perform the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth;
having first worshipped the Viśvedevas with the invocation and other rites.
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Rudras;
O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas"—thus he should say to them.
One should perform the remaining rites, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), as in the case of the ancestors;
then, one should give a cow to a twice-born man, dedicating it to the Vasus.
Then, one should offer a vessel of sesame seeds to Agni in the southeast, to Rudra in the south, to Sūrya and the twice-born in the southwest, and to the Viśvedevas in the west. (GarP 2.8.19)
Having thus offered inexhaustible water while saying "Svasti," he should then dismiss those twice-born brahmins while recollecting the eight-syllabled Lord Viṣṇu.
Then one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī, the Mistress of the Family, Śiva, and Nārāyaṇa;
thereafter, on the fourteenth day, one should go to whichever excellent river may be found.
Muttering the mantra "Victory to you! over garments and pieces of iron, he himself should kindle the fire there, facing the south.
Having fashioned an image of Brahmā with fifty blades of *kuśa* grass,
one should burn it after performing the cremation-ground fire-offering (*śmāśānika-homa*), concluding indeed with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Or else, one should meditate upon Niragni, Bhūmi, Yama, and Rudra;
having offered oblations in the primary location, one should subsequently invoke him.
Then, one should cook another *caru* mixed with mung beans in the fire,
and a second one mixed with sesame seeds and rice, along with a *pavitraka*.
One should offer the first [oblation] with "Oṃ, salutation to you, Pṛthivī," and immediately thereafter the second with "Oṃ, salutation to Yama. (GarP 2.8.26)
"Oṃ, salutations! Now, salutations to Rudra, the lord of the cremation grounds.
Then, [he offered it] into the blazing, kindled fire upon the ground that was naturally formidable.
One should offer seven handfuls of water to the seven known as the Yamas:
to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, and Antaka.
To Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to the one who takes away the life of all beings—
[one should offer oblations] seven times, together with the utterances of *svadhā*, *namas*, and the *praṇava*.
"O you of such-and-such lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you.
He should then offer ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by water-offerings (argha) and flowers.
"May incense, lamps, offerings, and perfumes be inexhaustible for all [the ancestors].
Having offered ten rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should meditate upon the gentle face of Viṣṇu. (GarP 2.8.31)
And one should perform the monthly *māsika* rites every month; thereafter, at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for oneself or for the deceased.
Knowing that power, health, wealth, and lifespan are unstable, one should perform [the rite] according to one's ability.
O Bird, I have thus explained all this to you regarding the *jīvaśrāddha*.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the second part, the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, in the *Pretakalpa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the eighth chapter titled "The Description of the Performer of the Śrāddha and the Śrāddha for Oneself. Śrī Garuḍa said:
O sinless one, you have stated that even a king [is subject] up to the first rite;
by whom and for whom was that first [rite] performed by a king in the past?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Suparṇa, listen; I shall tell you how the rite was performed by the king.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king of the Vaṅga people named Babhruvāhana.
O Lord of Birds, that sovereign of the earth, as a protector of the earth bounded by the four oceans according to dharma,
enjoys the entire earth divided into four quarters.
While he was ruling that kingdom, there was no one who committed evil;
O Tārkṣya, there was neither fear of thieves nor indeed any fear of the base.
There was no fear of disease even when he was the lord of that realm;
they delighted in their own duty, and he was like the sun in his splendor.
In his imperturbability he was like Mount Meru, and in his endurance he was like the earth;
that mighty-armed one, possessing abundant forces and vehicles, at one time— ||| GarP_2,9.6 |||
Surrounded by hundreds of horses, he went into the dense forest amidst the lion-roars of the warriors and the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
As that king proceeded, there was a sound of joyful acclaim,
while he was being praised on all sides by the foremost of brahmins at every turn.
He went forth with great joy to the forest, desiring to hunt deer;
as he was going, the wise one beheld a grove resembling the Nandana garden.
It was strewn with bilva, arka, and khadira trees, joined by the kapittha as its banner,
and surrounded on all sides by rugged mountains.
It was devoid of water and devoid of humans, extending for many yojanas,
and filled with extremely terrible deer, lions, and other forest-dwelling creatures.
O tiger among men, he, together with his servants, forces, and vehicles,
sportively agitated that forest while slaughtering various wild animals.
Then the king pierced the belly of a certain deer;
following that deer, the monarch entered the forest.
Alone, his strength stolen away and afflicted by hunger and thirst,
he reached the edge of the forest and entered a vast wilderness.
Overcome by intense thirst, he searched for water here and there;
from afar, he saw a lake resounding with the cries of swans and cranes.
Having arrived at the lake as indicated, he plunged in together with his horse,
amidst the pollen of lotuses and the dust of blue water-lilies.
Having drunk water that was fragrant, pure, and cool, he emerged from the lake pavilion on its bank, exhausted by the fatigue of the journey.
Having seen a banyan tree, he quickly tied his horse to its roots;
having spread out a mat there and placed his shield as a pillow, he lay down.
Then, for a moment, he slept there, fanned by the wind;
while the king was sleeping there for a moment, the preta indeed appeared upon his preta-vehicle.
Then someone arrived there, accompanied by a hundred pretas,
his body consisting of nothing but bones, skin, and sinews, wandering about in distress.
Seeking food and drink, he could find no stability anywhere;
seeing this unprecedented being, the king fixed an arrow upon his bow.
Having seen the king, he too stood before him for a long time like a pillar;
observing him standing there, the king was filled with curiosity.
And he asked him, "Who are you, or why have you come to such a transformation?
The preta replied: "I have abandoned my state as a preta; I have attained a supreme destination."
"O mighty-armed one, through union with you, there is no one more fortunate than I.
Babhruvāhana said:
"What is this [you have done] in this terrible forest, so exceedingly fearsome in every respect?"
O Koṇapa, as it was being violently shaken by the wind in the form of a whirlwind, there were moths, mosquitoes, small insects, headless trunks, and heads. (GarP 2.9.25)
Fish, tortoises, lizards, scorpions, bees, and snakes—
with their heads downward and feet upward— were crying out most piteously.
The winds blow harshly, and lightning-fires blaze;
like a mass of grass being driven here and there by the wind, all things seem to whirl about.
Various living beings, serpents, and swarms of locusts are seen;
their cries are heard in many ways, yet they are not seen here or there.
"Seeing all this transformed, my heart trembles. He replied to him:
"Those for whom there is neither the consecration with fire, nor the *śrāddha* rite, nor the water-offering (*udakakriyā*)."
There are six funeral cakes and ten bodily parts, but there is no sapindikarana for those who are betrayers of trust, drinkers of liquor, and stealers of gold.

Those who have died by an untimely death, those people who are devoted to malice, those who are devoid of expiatory rites, and those who delight in approaching women who should not be approached; // GarP_2,9.31 //
Driven here by their own past actions,
those living beings are seen to be severely tormented, finding food and drink difficult to obtain.
O King, out of compassion for these, perform their funeral rites—
for those who have no mother, no father, no son, and no kinsmen.
The king himself should perform their duties, since he is the ruler;
however, he must also perform auspicious deeds for his own sake pertaining to the world beyond.

Liberated from all sufferings, by which one may cross over the miserable states—whose brothers are they, whose sons, and even whose wives, when they are experts only in their own self-interest? (GarP 2.9.35)
You should place no trust in them, because one must enjoy the fruits of one's own actions;
for wealth remains behind in the house, and kinsmen likewise at the cremation ground.
The body takes on wood [as fuel], while both sin and merit go along with it;
therefore, you who desire the true welfare of yourself should act quickly and correctly.
"One must perform the rites for the hereafter with this unstable body.
The King said:
"You appear like a ghost—emaciated in form and with terrifying eyes."
"O King of the Pretas, out of affection for me, tell me the truth exactly as it is.
Thus questioned by the king, he indeed related his entire story.
The preta said:
"O best of kings, I shall tell you everything from the very beginning;
having heard the cause of my state as a preta, you ought to show compassion here."
There was a city named Vaidiśa, which brought all prosperity and happiness;
it was crowded with people from various regions and filled with diverse jewels.
O King, I lived there, which was filled with various flowering groves and inhabited by various meritorious people, always devoted to the worship of the gods.
"I am Sudeva by name, of the Vaiśya caste; let this be known to you.
By me the gods have been gratified with sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors with ancestral oblations (kavya)."
The Brahmins were thoroughly gratified by me through various modes of giving;
indeed, both their food and their recreation were well-provided for by me.
That which was given by me in many ways to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished—
all that has become fruitless for me due to destiny having overtaken me.
"I have no lineage, my dear, nor friends nor kinsmen; nor do I have a well-wishing friend who might perform the funeral rites for me. (GarP 2.9.46)
"O best of kings, because of that, my state as a preta became firmly established;
[the rites for] the eleventh day, the three fortnights, the six months, and the annual anniversary [were neglected]. (GarP 2.9.47)
O King, there are indeed these other monthly *śrāddhas*, making sixteen in total;
for him to whom these *preta-śrāddhas* are not offered, [the ancestors remain as departed spirits].
"Her state as a preta remains firmly fixed even by hundreds of funeral offerings (śrāddha).
Knowing this, O Great King, deliver me from the condition of a preta. (GarP 2.9.49)
"O King, you are said here to be the kinsman of all the social classes;
therefore, O Indra among kings, save me, and I shall give this precious gem to you."
O best of excellent kings,
O lord of the earth, O Lord, having shown compassion toward me, you should act in such a way that I may attain auspiciousness.
"Because the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) was not performed for me by my sapindas or my gotra-kinsmen during the winter, I have consequently attained this wretched state of being a preta."
With my body overcome by hunger and thirst, I do not obtain food or drink;
therefore, this transformation indeed occurs, such as emaciation and the loss of flesh. (GarP 2.9.53)
I experience again and again the great suffering born of hunger and thirst;
indeed, the wretched state of a preta is brought about by failing to perform the rite of releasing a bull.
"Therefore, O King, ocean of compassion, I pray before you.
The King said:
"How is it to be known by men that a *preta* exists within my family?"
"Therefore, tell me this: how indeed is one released from the state of a *preta*?
The *preta* said: "A *preta* is always to be inferred by men through his physical signs and suffering. (GarP 2.9.56)
I shall describe those afflictions on earth caused by ghosts among the royalty:
when women's seasons become fruitless and the lineage does not increase. (GarP 2.9.57)
Those of tender age die, and that suffering arises from the realm of the departed;
there is the sudden loss of livelihood and indeed a lack of standing among people.
There may be a sudden fire in the house, that suffering arising from the spirits of the departed;
there will be constant quarreling in one's own home, as well as false accusations.
The occurrence of elephantiasis and similar ailments, as well as suffering arising from spirits of the departed (pretas),
occurs even when one has personally released wealth with great effort onto the path of the needy.
That suffering arising from the state of a preta would not even be found;
yet, despite good rains, there would be loss of crops, and from trade, the destruction of one's livelihood. (GarP 2.9.61)
The wife may become hostile, and that suffering arises from the spirits of the departed;
thus, O King, through such suffering, men obtain knowledge of the deceased.
If the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) is performed, one is then liberated from the state of a preta;
therefore, O Lord of Waters, you too should likewise perform the release of a bull.
Out of great compassion for this king, even though he was my enemy, I took upon myself the responsibility;
therefore, I have secured a certain prince who has been slain.
O King, having taken that [bull] from me, perform with its wealth a bull-sacrifice festival (vṛṣotsava) on the full moon of Kārttika, or during the month of Āśvayuja.
On a day joined with the constellation Revatī, you should perform my bull festival;
having summoned meritorious brahmins and established the sacred fire according to the prescribed rite.
O King, gold should likewise be prepared with six mantras according to the prescribed rite;
you should feed many Brahmins with wealth obtained from those jewels.
When this has been done, O protector of the earth, my liberation will come to pass.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"So be it," and then, O bird, the king accepted the jewel.
The right to perform the rites belongs only to him who takes the inheritance;
such is the conversation between those two—the deceased king and [the heir]—as they carry out their affairs.
Then, amidst the clanging of bells and the booming of kettledrums,
the fourfold royal army fell upon them.
As soon as she had arrived there, the preta vanished from sight;
having departed from that forest, the king also returned to the city.
On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika,
he performed the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) in honor of the deceased, according to the prescribed rules, using the wealth obtained from that jewel.

Even though he was a ghost, having instantly obtained a body of gold, he prostrated before the king, saying, "O King, this is your majesty's power. Praising him thus, that grateful being went to heaven as Garuḍa, by the king who recognized his debt of gratitude.
All this has been related to you, how he was indeed raised by the king from the state of a ghost; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second part, the section on Dharma (*dharmakāṇḍa*), within the *Pretakalpa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, the ninth chapter titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Release of a Bull Performed by Kings.
Śrī Garuḍa said:
Upon the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite and the annual anniversary (*ābdika*),
men attain the state of a god, a human, or a bird through their own actions.
How can a śrāddha offering truly bring satisfaction to those who have diverse diets, whether it is eaten by other twice-born ones or offered into the fire? (GarP 2.10.2)
How can that which is given by a deceased person, consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, be consumed?
Furthermore, the necessity of performing the *śrāddha* on the new moon day and other such occasions is heard in the scriptures. (GarP 2.10.3)
The Blessed One said: "O Lord of Birds, hear how the śrāddha rite grants satisfaction to the departed spirits (pretas),
even though this god has become a human being through the application of karma."
His food, having become nectar, follows him even in the state of divinity;
in the state of a gandharva, it takes the form of enjoyments, and in the state of a beast, it becomes grass.
For the ancestral offering (śrāddha) follows [the recipient] even when they have become a serpent in the form of wind;
it becomes fruit when they are a bird, and likewise, meat when they are among the Rākṣasas.
Likewise, in the state of a Dānava there is flesh; in the state of a Preta, blood;
in the state of a human, food, drink, and so forth; and in childhood, there is the flavor of sensual enjoyment.
Garuḍa said:
How do the *kavyas* and *havyas* offered here by people reach the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), and who is said to be the one who conveys them there?
If the *śrāddha* ceremony were to provide nourishment even for deceased beings,
it would be like adding oil to the flame of an extinguished lamp to make it grow taller.
And when men have died, O Lord, as they enter the destination produced by their own karma,
who could bring about the welfare of their son, and in what manner?
The Blessed One said:
"O Tārkṣya, the authority of direct perception is stronger than that of scripture;
yet, for an object revealed by scripture, its nature as nectar and so forth [is established]."
The name and lineage of the ancestors indeed bring [the offerings] of the *havya* and *kavya*;
likewise, the mantras of the *śrāddha* bring them through devotion. (GarP 2.10.12)
"How can these insentient things bring about attainment?"—this is not to be understood as a fault; I shall tell you another means of attainment. (GarP 2.10.13)

Agniṣvātta and the others are established as their presiding lords over that [offering] which is bestowed according to the rule, at the proper time, upon a worthy recipient, and acquired through righteous means.
These lead the food to wherever the living being resides;
their name, clan, and mantras lead the food that has been given.
Even when they have reached hundreds of wombs, satisfaction attends them as they dwell in other worlds under various names and lineages.
Three pindas, indeed, are offered upon darbha grass on the ground with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
they go to and satisfy the ancestors residing in the state of the departed (preta). Thus it is said. (GarP 2.10.17)
Those who have not reached the places of torment are the best among those born on earth in five ways;
they are those who have taken various forms within the species of animal births and the like.
Whatever food these ancestors have in their respective wombs,
that same food remains present in the *śrāddha* offerings.
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have wandered away,
so does food lead the Brahmin to the place where the living being resides.
The Pitṛs are the recipients of the Śrāddha, always together with the Viśvedevas;
having always consumed this Śrāddha, they in turn satisfy the ancestors.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when they are gratified in the śrāddhas, they satisfy the ancestors of human beings.
Just as a pregnant woman satisfies both herself and her fetus through the fulfillment of her longings,
so too do the gods satisfy themselves and the ancestral fathers of men through the śrāddha offerings.
Upon hearing that the time for the śrāddha has arrived, the ancestors rejoice;
having meditated upon one another in their minds, they descend with the speed of thought.
For the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space eat together with the Brahmins;
having become like the wind, they remain there, and after eating, they go to the supreme goal.
O Bird, those Brahmins who have been invited on the day preceding the Śrāddha—having entered as their ancestors and partaken of the meal—depart for their own abode. (GarP 2.10.26)
If, however, only one Brahmin has been invited by the performer of the *śrāddha*,
his father resides in his stomach, and his grandfather on his left side.
The great-grandfather stands to the south, and behind him is the consumer of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
At the time of the Śrāddha, Yama [releases] the pretas and the ancestors from the abode of Yama.
O Kāśyapa, he causes those dwelling in hell to be released from their human state,
as they cry out, tormented by hunger, while confessing the evil deeds they themselves have committed.
They desire milk-rice mixed with honey for their sons and grandsons;
therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the ritual rule with that very milk-rice.
Garuḍa said: "O twice-born one, O giver of honor, have your ancestors been seen by anyone as they have come from that world,
arriving on this earth to eat?"
The Blessed One said:
"O Garuḍa, listen; I shall tell you how Sītā beheld her ancestors within the body of the Brahmin, namely her three fathers-in-law and others, at one time."
Having indeed received his father’s command, Rāma departed for the forest;
thereafter, Rāma set out with Sītā for the purpose of the Puṣkara pilgrimage.
Having arrived at the sacred ford, he began the śrāddha ceremony;
meanwhile, Jānakī prepared ripe fruit and offered it to Rāma.
Having bathed because of the words spoken by her beloved,
she protected him when the sun had reached the middle of the sky and the Kutapa hour had arrived.
All the sages who had been invited by Rāma arrived;
seeing those munis come, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, [was filled with joy].
Having taken the food by Rāma’s command, she approached to serve it; then she stepped back to a distance and stood among the brahmins.
Then, having concealed herself by covering herself with shrubs, she remained hidden;
and at that time, the joy of the Raghus, knowing Sītā to be in a secluded spot, [approached].
Having reflected for a very long time on what this might be, that virtuous woman quickly went a little way off for the sake of modesty.
"Or rather, why should I not seek out that woman while feeding the Brahmins?
Reflecting thus, he himself proceeded to feed the Brahmins.
When the foremost of the twice-born had departed, Rāma said this to his beloved:
"How was it that you remained hidden behind your palms upon seeing the lords of the sages arrive?"

"O slender-limbed one, tell me the reason for all this; do not delay. Thus addressed by her husband, Sītā stood with her face cast down, shedding a flood of tears, and spoke these words to Rāghava: GarP_2,10.42 //
Sītā said:
"Listen, O Lord, to what kind of wonder has been seen by me here."
"O Rāghava, your father was seen by me in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas,
adorned with all his ornaments, along with two others who were likewise adorned."
Having seen your father, O Lord, I departed from your presence;
clad in bark and deerskin, how could I stand before the king?
"O slayer of enemy heroes, this which has been spoken is the truth:
how could food be given by me with my own hand to the king? (GarP 2.10.46)
How indeed could we possibly give food to him in a grass bowl, he who is even the servant of servants and never enjoys anything for himself? (GarP 2.10.47)
"How shall I go before the king, I who was formerly seen by the monarch adorned with all ornaments, now with my limbs smeared with sweat and filth?
O descendant of Raghu, I have been cast aside by him out of shame."
The Blessed One said:
Having heard these words of his beloved, Rāma was struck with wonder in his mind.
Realizing that it was a marvel, she then returned to her own abode;
she has already reported to you how Sītā beheld her ancestors.
Furthermore, listen briefly to something more regarding the greatness of the śrāddha:
when the day of the new moon has arrived, [the ancestors] stand waiting at the door of the house.
Becoming like the wind, the hosts of ancestors of men long for the ancestral offering until the setting of the sun, being distressed by hunger and thirst.
Then, when the sun had set, hopeless and filled with sorrow,
they departed after sighing deeply for a long time and reproaching their own lineage.
Therefore, one ought to perform the śrāddha with great effort on the new moon day (amāvāsyā);
if his kinsmen, such as sons and others, perform the śrāddha [on that day], [the ancestors attain satisfaction]. (GarP 2.10.54)
Those who have been uplifted by the *gayāśrāddha* share in the world of Brahmā;
for them, hunger or thirst never arises anywhere.
Therefore, a wise person should perform the *śrāddha* rite with great effort and correctly;
therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* with devotion according to the rules, even if only with vegetables.
One should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) at the proper time; in such a family, no one shall suffer.
[It bestows] long life, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, and prosperity.
Through the worship of the ancestors, one obtains cattle, wealth, and grain;
indeed, the rite for the ancestors always takes precedence over the rite for the gods.
For the nourishment of the ancestors is auspiciously preceded by that of the deities;
those who worship the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and the sacrificial fire [attain this]. (GarP 2.10.59)
For they worship me alone, the inner self of all beings,
having performed the śrāddha according to the Smārta rite in accordance with their own means.
Whatever scattering of food is performed by humans upon the earth, that man gratifies the entire world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass. (GarP 2.10.61)

O sky-walker, even those who have attained the state of a piśāca attain satisfaction through that [offering], as well as by the water that falls upon the ground from their bathing garments. (GarP 2.10.62)
By that, satisfaction arises for those who have attained the state of crossing over,
as the fragrant waters fall upon the surface of the earth.
By that [offering], nourishment is provided for those who have attained the state of gods,
as well as for those who are excluded from their own lineage, who are unfit for ritual acts, and who remain unconsecrated.

But those who have failed [in their duties] eat the scattered food, the sweepings, and the water; they consume the water used for rinsing after a meal, as well as the water that has been used during the day. (GarP 2.10.65)
Likewise, others who have attained the state of Piśācas or even the state of worms and insects find satisfaction through that same [offering] to the Brāhmaṇas. (GarP 2.10.66)
When the morsels of food have been lifted up, those who on earth desire food—
by them alone is the nourishment provided for those who have attained human birth.
While those twice-born ones were performing their rites in this manner,
some scattering of water or food occurred, whether pure or even defiled by remnants.
Through that food, when the śrāddha has been properly performed, there occurs nourishment for those in their families who have indeed passed into another birth.
The *śrāddha* that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means—by that, the Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas and others rejoice in their respective wombs. (GarP 2.10.70)
Thus it is obtained, O bird: that which is given here by kinsmen performing the śrāddha—through food, water, and vegetables—indeed brings about satisfaction.
All this that you have asked me has been explained:
the immediate attainment of another body upon the surface of the earth without delay.
I shall explain that to you in brief, as you have asked:
regarding both the immediate and the delayed [destruction] of the body. (GarP 2.10.73)
Hear from me how a mortal attains that distinction:
thereafter, he becomes a person the size of a thumb, like smokeless light.
He immediately attains a single body made of air, just as a water-louse, when about to die, withdraws its hind leg.
When the stability of the supreme foot has become firm,
then the embodied being completely casts off that former body.
At first, for the sake of enjoyment, a body composed of air (vāyavīya) appears,
just as the sense organ of one who is dying perceives its objects.
That [self] is devoid of activity; it moves through the body by means of the vital air alone.
Whatever body it attains, that too it departs from by itself.
Having grasped its own [nature], the individual soul departs like an embryo from its womb;
whether it is departing, stationary, or engaged in enjoyment, it remains endowed with the qualities (guṇas).
Those who are utterly deluded do not perceive it; those with the eye of knowledge do perceive it.
For they say that the *ātivāhika* body is indeed composed of air.
Thus they indeed speak of the bodies of the Yātudhānas; such is the body of men born from a physical aggregate, which is called Suparṇa.
If the ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) pertaining to the ten-day period are offered by sons and others,
then the one born of wind shall attain unity with the body produced from the funeral cakes.

If one born from a physical body were not subject to suffering, then one born from air would deserve it; O Lord of Birds, understand that just as this embodied being experiences childhood, youth, and old age within this very body, so too is there the attainment of another body. (GarP 2.10.83)
Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes others that are new,
so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones.
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (GarP 2.10.85)
It has already been told to you that one attains a body of wind immediately;
now hear from me indeed about that body which is attained after a delay.
Sometimes, while lingering, he may obtain a body born from a physical aggregate;
or else, he goes to the world of Yama in accordance with his own karma.
By the word of Citragupta, he experiences the hells;
having undergone the torments, he then assumes the body of a beast, a bird, or the like.
That which a person grasps becomes a locus of "mine-ness" through delusion;
having experienced the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious karma, the human being is liberated.
Garuḍa said:
"O ocean of compassion, tell me how even one burdened with many sins might reach you after having crossed the ocean of the existence of suffering."
O Lord of Ramā, tell me— who am listening and asking— as to how a person may no longer have contact with further suffering.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
A person who is devoted to his own respective duty attains perfection.
Listen to how one who is intent on his own duty finds success.
With the impurity of his past actions shaken off by constant meditation on Vāsudeva, he is endowed with a purified intellect and, having restrained himself through fortitude; GarP_2,10.93.

Having abandoned the objects of the senses such as sound and the like, and having cast aside passion and hatred, he should serve those who are dispassionate, eat only what is obtained by chance, and restrain his speech, body, and mind.
Constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and firmly established in detachment,
he [abandoned] egoism, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated, free from the sense of "mine," and tranquil, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Beyond this, O son of Kaśyapa, there is no further duty for human beings.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Satisfaction-bestowing Nature of Śrāddha," in the second section on the Pretakalpa within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 11.
Garuḍa said:
Why does one obtain human birth, and how does one meet death?
O best of gods, who is it that dies, having resorted to a body somewhere?
Whence do the sense faculties go? How can he be untouchable?
Where are the actions performed here, and how does he experience them as he moves along?
"Be gracious to me; you ought to sever my delusion entirely.
O best of gods, I am Kāśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā.
How do human beings go to the realm of Yama and to the realm of Viṣṇu?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, [one falls].
In a desolate forest region, he is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*;
he is reborn into a low caste as one who steals precious gems.
Whatever desire one contemplates, one is born with that as one's characteristic mark.
Weapons do not cut him; fire does not burn him.
Neither do the waters moisten it, nor does the wind dry it;
[therein are] the mouth, eyes, nose, ears, anus, and the passage for urine.
These apertures of all creatures, such as those born from eggs and so forth, extend everywhere from the navel up to the head; indeed, there are eight apertures directed upwards.
O Bird, virtuous mortals who have attained peace indeed depart through the aperture at the crown of the head, following the prescribed ritual from the day of death until the annual anniversary.
Indeed, even a man who is destitute can perform all actions;
for wherever a living being dwells within the body, there he experiences the results of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
O Lord of Birds, he thus consumes the defects born of mind, speech, and body;
when dead, he attains happiness and is not bound by the snares of illusion.
But that man who is bound by snares and devoted to improper action— *Garuda Purāṇa*, 2.11.11.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Gateways of Departure Indicating the Upward and Downward Courses. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Thus, O Tārkṣya, has this exposition on the nature of life been told to you for the benefit of human beings, in order to bring about their liberation from the state of a preta.
There are eighty-four lakhs of living beings, divided into four classes:
those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and those born from a womb.
Twenty-one lakhs are proclaimed as those born from eggs;
likewise, those born from sweat and those born from sprouts are stated in sequence.
Likewise, others such as humans and so forth are said to be born from a womb;
indeed, among all living beings, the human state is difficult to attain.
The state of possessing the treasure of the five faculties is attained through great merits by Brahmins,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of other castes.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla— these seven are indeed remembered as the lowest-born (antyaja).
Through the distinctions of Mlecchas and Tumbas, there are indeed numerous divisions of castes;
for all living beings, there are thousands of such caste-divisions.
Indeed, for all living beings, there are thousands of varieties;
yet their food, sexual intercourse, sleep, fear, and likewise anger are the same.
For all living beings, supreme discernment is exceedingly difficult to attain;
indeed, there are manifold distinctions of bodies, such as those with one leg and so forth.
Where the black-spotted deer roams, that place is called Dharmadaśa;
there all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, reside in every way.
Among beings, those endowed with breath are the best; among those who possess breath, those who live by their intelligence are superior;
among the intelligent, human beings are the best; and among humans, Brahmins are traditionally held to be the most excellent.
Having attained human birth, which is the sole means for achieving heaven—
if one does not accomplish either of these two goals, then by that act one has certainly deceived oneself.

One who possesses a hundred desires a thousand; one who possesses a thousand strives to acquire a hundred thousand; a lord of a hundred thousand seeks a kingdom; and even a king desires to obtain the entire earth.

Even as a wheel-bearer he attained the state of a god; in his divine state, he sought to become the sovereign lord of all gods; and as the lord of gods, he desired the higher realms—yet even so, craving does not turn back.
But one who is overcome by craving falls into hell;
however, those who are liberated from craving attain residence in heaven.
In this world, a person who is independent of the self certainly becomes happy;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are its qualities.
And so, one who is dependent on sense objects certainly becomes miserable.
The deer, the elephant, the moth, the bee, and the fish—these five are destroyed by the five [senses] alone.
How is it that the one who is heedless, who indulges in all five with the five, is not himself destroyed?
In childhood, a fool consists of his father and mother; in youth, he consists of his beloved; and in old age, he consists of his sons and grandsons; at no time does he consist of the Self.
A man bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released;
but one bound by the fetters consisting of son and wife is never released.
One person commits the evils, while the multitude enjoys the fruit;
those who enjoy the fruit are separated from the act, yet the doer is smeared with the fault.
No one—whether a child, an old man, or even a youth—conquers death;
likewise, pleasure, pain, and the rest come again and go away.
While everyone looks on, the deceased abandons everything;
a living being is born alone, and alone indeed does it perish.
Even alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone that of evil deeds;
having cast off the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, they depart.
Relatives turn away and depart, but Dharma follows him;
wealth remains in the house, while friends and kinsmen turn back at the cemetery.
The fire consumes the body, while one departs with both good and evil deeds;
though the body is burnt by the fire, merit and sin remain together.
Whether it be auspicious or evil, a human being experiences the consequences everywhere, for wealth was not given to those in need while the sun had not yet set. (GarP 2.12.27)
I do not know whose wealth that will belong to tomorrow morning;
his riches cry out, "Who shall be my master? (GarP 2.12.28)
Nor was anything given to the foremost of the twice-born for the sake of helping others;
whatever was obtained—whether much or little—was due to merit performed in a previous birth.
Having understood this, wealth is bestowed for the sake of the Dharma;
by means of that wealth, purified by a mind of faith, the Dharma is sustained.
Dharma devoid of faith yields no fruit either in this world or the next;
for from dharma arises wealth, and from dharma desire also arises.
Dharma alone leads to liberation; therefore, one should practice dharma.
Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by vast accumulations of wealth.

For the sages, possessing nothing yet endowed with faith, have gone to heaven. O bird, whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith is said to be "non-existent"; it yields no fruit either in this world or after death.

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, in the second part, in the *Dharmakāṇḍa Pretakalpa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the twelfth chapter titled "The Description of the Deceased Following Only Dharma.
[Chapter 13 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Garuḍa said:
"By what action, O Lord of Gods, does the state of being a preta never arise for any living being on earth? Tell me that, O Supreme Lord. (GarP 2.13.1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall briefly describe the funeral rites for the anniversary of death (kṣayāha),
which must be performed by men desiring liberation using only their left hand.
Especially for women, when a child has passed five years of age,
there is no rite on this earth other than the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) for the sake of ending the state of being a ghost (*pretatva*). (GarP 2.13.3)
Whether living or dead, he who performs the rite of releasing a bull shall not undergo the state of a preta, even without other gifts, sacrifices, or vows.
Garuḍa said: O best among the foremost of gods, O Madhusūdana, tell me at what time—one who is living or even one who is dead—should perform the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga). GarP_2,13.5.
But what fruit would there be in the end from the sixteen śrāddhas performed?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
But if one performs the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍapātana) without having performed the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga), that spiritual merit does not accrue to the giver;
it is fruitless for the deceased.
If for a deceased person the bull is not released on the eleventh day,
his state as a preta remains firmly established, even by the performance of hundreds of śrāddhas.
Garuḍa said:
For those whose death has been brought about by a serpent, no funeral rites such as cremation with fire are performed;
the same applies if one dies by water, by a horned animal, or by weapons and the like.
"And how can there be purification for those who have died an unnatural death, O Lord?
O God, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A Brāhmaṇa becomes purified in six months; a Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) in seven and a half months; a Vaiśya in seven and a half months; and a Śūdra is purified in one month.
If, having given all kinds of gifts at a sacred ford,
one dies while remaining pure and observant of celibacy, such a person does not go to an evil rebirth in this world.
Having performed the rite of releasing a bull and other such acts, he should practice the dharma of an ascetic;
if he meets his death while in the state of an ascetic, he shall go to the eternal abode of Brahman.
He who performs improper acts and is devoid of the conduct of the virtuous,
even after performing the rite of releasing a bull and other such deeds, shall not go to the domain of Yama.
Whether it be a son, a brother, a grandson, or likewise a kinsman,
a member of the same lineage, or a co-heir, one should perform the Vṛṣotsarga festival upon the death [of the deceased].
