In the absence of sons, the wife, the daughter's son, or even the daughter herself shall perform the rite;
while sons are present, one should not have the *vṛṣotsarga* performed by anyone else.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of the Gods, those men and women who have no sons—
O God, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There is no destination for one who is sonless, nor indeed is there heaven;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son.
Whatever gifts have been personally given by men,
all of those indeed stand before him.
Whatever various condiments, foods,
and edibles are given with one's own hand, at the end of life, the fruit thereof is inexhaustible.
Cows, land, gold, garments, food, and footwear—
wherever a living being dwells, these things attend him there.
As long as the body is healthy, one should practice dharma;
for when one is unwell and driven by others, one is unable to accomplish anything.
Even while living, for one who is as good as dead in this world, no funeral rites are performed;
having become like the wind and overcome by hunger, he wanders day and night.
He is born again as a worm, an insect, or a moth, and dies once more;
he may even enter an inauspicious womb, and having been born, perishes immediately.

As long as this body is healthy and free from disease, as long as old age is far off, as long as the power of the senses is unimpaired, and as long as there is no exhaustion of life—during that very time, a wise person should exert great effort toward their own spiritual welfare. For when the house is already ablaze, what kind of endeavor is it to dig a well?

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Release of a Bull, the Gift of Dharma, Sons, and Others. Śrī Garuḍa said:
O Lord, tell me the fruit of that which is given by one who is afflicted or dying;
or of that which is given by one in a healthy state, or even if it is given in violation of the prescribed rules.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: A single cow given by one whose mind is composed is equal to a hundred cows given by one who is ill, and a thousand cows given by one who is dying; yet these are all devoid of true wealth.
Even for one who has died, a hundred thousand [cows] purified by ritual are equal to that;
through the conjunction of a sacred ford and a worthy recipient, a single cow bestows the merit of a hundred thousand.
O best of birds, when given in a worthy vessel, the gift of a donor increases day by day for the sake of freedom from evil; likewise, the acceptance of gifts by the wise leads to the same result.
The fire of mantras, which removes poison and cold, is it ever a vessel for faults?
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions.
A wise person desiring their own welfare should never give anything to an unworthy recipient;
for a cow given to an unworthy recipient may lead the donor to hell.
It shall cause the downfall of the recipient along with twenty-one generations of their lineage;
for whatever has been done with one's own hand, its fruit is obtained after reaching another body.
Just as wealth placed in the ground with one's own hand, so indeed does one obtain the fruit; this I tell you, O Lord of Birds.
Even one who is childless,
and especially one who desires liberation, as well as one who is destitute, should particularly perform the funeral rites for his ancestors.
For whatever is performed with even a small amount of wealth by one's own hand becomes inexhaustible, just as clarified butter poured into the sacrificial fire.
A single milch cow should be given as a wedding gift for one son;
if she is sold, she burns the family down to the seventh generation.
Therefore, one should perform everything while life remains so fickle;
having taken the provisions of generosity, one travels happily upon the great journey.
"Otherwise, a living being suffers on the road like one who is without provisions for the journey;
knowing this, O best of birds, one should perform the sacrifice of the bull."
He who dies without having performed [the rite] and without a son does not possess liberation;
yet even one without a son who performs it goes happily upon the Great Path.
One does not attain through sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, nor even through various kinds of gifts, that destination which is reached by the rite of releasing a bull.
And among all sacrifices, the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayajña) is likewise the most excellent;
therefore, one should perform the bull-sacrifice with every effort.
Garuḍa said:
"Out of favor, please tell me about the anniversary of death (kṣayāha) and the funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika).
At what time, on which lunar day (tithi), and by what procedure should that be performed?"
"What fruit does one obtain by performing this? Tell me that now, O Govinda; by your grace, a human being becomes liberated."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: During the months beginning with Kārttika, when the sun has moved toward the southern solstice, in the bright fortnight, on auspicious lunar days such as the twelfth (dvādaśī) and others.
At an auspicious moment or during a favorable *lagna*, being composed in a pure place,
he should summon a Brāhmaṇa who is knowledgeable in the ritual rules and possesses auspicious characteristics.
One should perform the purification of the house through recitations, burnt offerings, and gifts;
on an auspicious day under the constellation Abhijit, one should worship the planets and the gods.
One should perform the fire sacrifice according to one's ability with various mantras;
O Lord of Birds, one should first perform the installation of the planetary deities.
The worship of the Mothers should be performed, and one should cause the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) to fall;
having established the fire right there, one should indeed perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having established a Śālagrāma stone, one should perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha;
and having worshipped a bull right there with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should first consecrate four yearling heifers;
then one should perform a circumambulation, and at the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), the ritual dismissal (visarjana) should take place.
Having recited this mantra, standing facing north:
"O Dharma, you were created in the form of a bull by Brahmā in ancient times."
By the power of your renunciation, deliver me from the ocean of existence,
having consecrated me with auspicious and purifying mantras according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform the ritual release of the bull with the *tanakrīḍanti* mantra;
then, one should consecrate Nīla with the water from the Rudra-pitcher.
Having established that water at the base of the navel, one should place it upon the head;
then one should perform the *ātma-śrāddha* and give gifts to the most excellent of the twice-born.
If one must travel upon water, one should offer water there; and whatever was dear to the person while they were alive, that one should give according to one's own ability.
When the rite of releasing a bull has been performed, what is deficient attains completeness;
one who dies while well-satisfied on a difficult path goes [to heaven], of this there is no doubt. (GarP 2.14.31)
Men who are always delighted in giving do not see the world of Yama,
provided that the *śrāddha* offering for the eleventh day is given to the deceased being.
Whether given by oneself or given by another, [the merit] does not remain here or in the hereafter;
rather, it lasts for thirteen, seven, five, and three [generations] respectively.
Endowed with faith and devotion, one should perform the gifts of land;
one should prepare seven or five vessels of sesame seeds in due order.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins and cause a single cow to be given away;
then, according to the Vedic injunction, one should offer a bull with the mantra "śanno devīḥ."
One should perform the marriage ceremony with four heifers;
likewise, a discus should be placed on the left side and a trident on the right.
The wise man should give the price for the bull and release that bull, performing the rite according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure with the utterance of *svāhā*.
One should diligently perform the rites on the eleventh and twelfth days;
prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should cause gifts of footprints to be given;
having placed Acyuta upon a cotton cloth within a copper vessel.
Having covered the vessel situated there with a cloth, one should offer the *arghya* with auspicious fruits;
having fashioned a boat made of sugarcane, one should wrap it with silk thread.
Having placed clarified butter in a bell-metal vessel for the sake of the Vaitaraṇī river,
one should perform the ritual of boarding a boat and worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
And that gift, according to one's own capacity,
is infinite for those submerged in the ocean of existence and afflicted by grief, heat, pain, and suffering.
For those who are destitute of the boat of Dharma, Janārdana is indeed their savior;
likewise, sesame, iron, gold, cotton, and salt— GarP_2,14.43.
The seven grains, land, and cows—each one of these is remembered as purifying;
one should prepare vessels of sesame seeds and cause the gift of a bed to be bestowed.
One should give gifts according to one's ability to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished;
he who does this, O Tārkṣya, whether he has sons or is sonless, [attains the same merit].
He attains success just like those celibate students;
a person should perform the obligatory and occasional rites as long as he lives.
Whatever dharma is performed, its fruit shall be inexhaustible;
for the śrāddha of the year [performed] for pilgrimages, vows, and so forth, indeed [yields such a result].
O bird, merit should be diligently bestowed upon the deities, the gurus, and likewise upon one's mother and father; it increases day by day.
For whatever abundant gift anyone bestows at this sacrifice,
all of that becomes inexhaustible for them, just as it is said to be on the sacrificial altar.
Just as ascetics who observe the vow of celibacy are most worthy of honor in the world,
so too are they always honored by everyone in the world.
I am always the granter of boons to him, as are the four-faced Brahmā and Hara;
they go to the supreme worlds—this is my true word.
Wherever the bull, having been released, drinks water from a reservoir, or constantly digs at the earth with his horns, being ever full of joy; GarP_2,14.52 //
Abundant food and drink for the ancestors will be present;
on the full moon or the new moon day, one should cause offerings of vessels of sesame seeds to be given.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving gifts during thousands of solar transits and hundreds of solar festivals, that indeed is obtained in the rite of releasing the blue bull.
Young heifers and footprints [of the deity] should be given to the Brahmins,
and vessels of sesame seeds should be offered to those twice-born who are devotees of Śiva.
And having clothed Umāmaheśvara alone, one should cause him to be given [offerings],
[visualizing him] resembling an *atasī* flower, clad in yellow garments, and imperishable.
For those who pay homage to Govinda, no fear exists;
those who, desiring liberation from the state of a preta, shall perform acts of veneration [will likewise be freed].
"They shall go to the higher worlds—this is my truthful word. All this, including the funeral rites for the deceased, has been explained by me to you. (GarP 2.14.58)
Having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Having heard of the incomparable majesty, Garuḍa was filled with joy and, for the benefit of human beings, questioned Keśava once again.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of Cows, the Release of Bulls, the Ten Gifts, the Abundant Gifts, and Other Rituals," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 15]
Garuḍa said:
"O Blessed One, tell me everything regarding the determination of the world of Yama—
the majesty and the detailed extent of the path, beginning from the moment a living being departs."
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O Tārkṣya, I shall declare the determination of the path of Yama— namely,
all the points of departure and the sixteen cities.
It measures eighty-six thousand yojanas in extent,
situated between the realm of Yama and that of humans.
O bird, when some disease arises due to the application of karma after one has experienced in this world the results of ill-deeds or evil deeds acquired as they were earned; GarP_2,15.4 //
For all beings, there is merely a sign according to their performed karma;
whoever has death ordained for them will certainly encounter it.
When the embodied soul, through the yoga of action, abandons its own body here,
one should then prepare the ground by smearing it with cow dung.
Then, having scattered sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, one should place gold in the mouth;
likewise, one should place a *tulasī* plant and a *śālagrāma* stone in close proximity.
Likewise, through the *Sāmādisūkta* mantras, death [occurring] at a bridge bestows liberation;
as does death in the houses of living beings [who perform] the scattering of golden needles upon heated [iron].
One [drop] should be applied to the mouth, and likewise again to the pair of nostrils;
two each should be applied in due order to the eyes and the ears.
Then, one should likewise place one [leaf] on the linga and one within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
one should also cause a tulasī leaf to be offered upon both hands and the neck.
A pair of garments should be given, and one should worship with unbroken grains of saffron;
one should provide it with a flower garland and lead it out through another door.
The son, together with his kinsmen, and the Brahmin, together with the city-dwellers, [prepared for the funeral];
the son himself, having placed the deceased father upon his shoulder along with his kinsmen...
Having gone to a cremation ground, facing either east or north,
one should construct the funeral pyre right there on ground that has not been burned before.
When the collection of impaired senses has become inert within consciousness, [he should offer] fuel consisting of sandalwood, tulasī wood, and palāśa twigs.
Then the vital breaths move forth, drawn near by the messengers of Yama;
one perceives the world as a single unity, and the divine vision arises.
A certain person exhibits a loathsome and dreadful form; with vital breaths clinging to the throat, he emits foam, and his mouth becomes covered in saliva.
The evil-minded are beaten there by the servants with bonds of nooses,
while the virtuous are led away with ease by the leaders of heaven.
The sinners go with suffering along the difficult path of Yama;
and Yama, having become four-armed, holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and other weapons.
One should properly behave toward those who delight in meritorious deeds and are virtuous as if they were friends;
having summoned all evildoers, Yama should subdue them with punishment.
Resounding like the thunder of the clouds at the end of an aeon, with a luster equal to a mountain of collyrium,
mounted upon a buffalo, difficult to propitiate, and possessing a brilliance like the flash of lightning.
With a body three *yojanas* in width, he is fierce and extremely terrifying;
holding an iron staff, the formidable one has a noose in his hand and a hideous form.
With crooked eyes and inspiring extreme terror, a person the size of a thumb emerges from the corpse of the sinners, crying out "Alas! Alas! (hā hā).
At that very moment, his own body— motionless, devoid of life-breaths, and loathsome— is led away by the messengers of Yama while he gazes upon it from his home.
It quickly becomes untouchable, foul-smelling, and despised by all;
for the body indeed passes through three stages, designated as worm-infested, excrement, and ashes. (GarP 2.15.24)
O Tārkṣya, what pride should be felt by men who perish in an instant?
For from wealth comes charity, from speech come truth and eloquence, and likewise from life come fame and merit.
The assistance rendered to others has been extracted as the essence from this worthless body;
yet, as it is being led away in this manner, the messengers indeed threaten it.
Displaying intense terror again and again for the sake of hell, [the messengers say]:
"O evil-souled one, move quickly! You have gone to the abode of Yama."
"We shall lead you without delay to the hells such as Kumbhīpāka and others.
Hearing these words of his kinsmen, as well as their lamentations, at that time—
Lamenting "Alas! Alas! loudly, he is led away by the servants of Yama;
therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* rite at the proper time and likewise on the eleventh day.
O Tārkṣya, at the time of the deceased's departure, one should offer six lumps of food in due order:
at the place of death, at the door, and at the crossroads for the sake of the cause.

In the resting place, in the piling of wood, and likewise in the gathering [of materials], there are six; hear the reason for that, O Tārkṣya, as well as in the preparation of the six funeral cakes (piṇḍas). GarP_2,15.31 //
In the place of the deceased, that which is called a "corpse" (śava) is offered by that name;
by that offering, the presiding deities of the house and the site are satisfied.
By that [offering], the ground becomes satisfied, as does its presiding deity;
furthermore, at the gate, a ball of food (piṇḍa) should be given, having addressed it by the name "Wayfarer" (pāntha).
With that which has been given, the household deities stationed at the doorway are gratified;
one should cause it to be offered with reference to the deity named Khecara at the crossroads.
Furthermore, beings and other divine classes do not cause harm;
therefore, one should have this known as a "resting for beings" performed there during the rest.
The piśācas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and whoever else dwells in the various directions,
none of them shall cause any unfitness for his body that is to be offered as an oblation.
"Pretahood arises from the funeral pyre, the funeral mound, and so forth;
some say that the 'accomplisher' (sādhaka) resides in the funeral pyre, O Lord of Birds."
Some wise ones who know the kalpas call him a preta;
from that time onward, he is offered [oblations] under the name of "preta" in various places.
Thus, by means of these five lumps, the corpse becomes fit for the oblation;
otherwise, those previously mentioned [impurities] indeed result in its defilement.
One should offer the first ball of rice at the time of departure, likewise at the half-way point, and the third on the funeral pyre; thus three balls of rice are prescribed.
In the first *piṇḍa* is Vidhātṛ; in the second, Garuḍadhvaja; and in the third, the messengers of Yama—thus the ritual application is proclaimed. (GarP 2.15.41)
When this third funeral ball (piṇḍa) is given, one is liberated from the defects of the body;
and the soul, having become the substratum, should cause the funeral pyre to blaze with flames.
Having swept and smeared [the ground], and having scraped and removed [the debris] from the altar,
he should sprinkle it with water and kindle the fire there according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda with flowers and unbroken rice grains:
"O Creator of beings, O Source of the world! You are the protector of the worlds. (GarP 2.15.44)
"Therefore, O gatherer, lead this deceased one to heaven.
Having thus honored the flesh-eater, one should perform the oblation of the body.
When the body has been thus half-burnt, one should then offer an oblation of clarified butter;
with the mantra "To the body hairs, svāhā," one should perform the homa according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed that deceased person upon the funeral pyre, one should then offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya) to Yama,
to Antaka, to Mṛtyu, and likewise to Brahmā.
One [oblation] should be offered into the mouth of Jātavedas, and likewise one into the mouth of the deceased;
thereafter, one should ignite the fire on the eastern side of the funeral pyre again.
"From this you were born; from you may he be born again.
For that world of heaven, Svāhā! The purifier blazes. (GarP 2.15.49)
Having thus offered an oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by mantras, the cremation must then certainly be performed by the son. (GarP 2.15.50)
Then one should weep intensely; in this way, he will find happiness there after the cremation, once the rite of piling the funeral pyre has been performed.
O Bird, one should offer a rice-ball for the deceased, which pacifies the pain of cremation;
for as long as that, the spirits wait for that deceased one who seeks his kinsmen.
Immediately after the cremation, the sons must perform a bath along with their clothes;
thereafter, they should offer water with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage [of the deceased], saying, "May it remain."
Then all the people of the countryside should clap their hands and cry out, "Viṣṇu! Viṣṇu! and they should extol the deceased by means of his virtues.
All the people, having come from every direction to his house,
[placed] cow dung and white mustard seeds on the southern side of the door.
Having placed the god Varuṇa within his own house and hidden him away, one should eat neem leaves; then, having consumed clarified butter, one may go home. GarP_2.15.56.
O Lord of Birds, some sprinkle the cremation site with milk;
one should not shed tears, but should offer handfuls of water to him.
Since the deceased helplessly consumes the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should indeed not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
O Tārkṣya, one should offer milk and water in an earthen vessel for three days,
once the sun has set, either at Valabhī or at a crossroads.
Bound and with a deluded heart, desiring his body and followed by his past deeds, he is led away by the messengers of Yama while looking back at the cremation ground, the crossroads, and his home.
For ten days, funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered day after day into the pit,
and handfuls of water should be constantly presented, dedicated to the deceased.
The increase [of the offerings] should be performed until the tenth-day funeral cake (piṇḍa) is reached;
for the rite must be performed by the son, and in his absence, by the wife.
In his absence, it should be done by the disciple; in his absence, by a uterine brother.
He should cause water and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered at the cremation ground or at another sacred site.
Whatever one gives on the first day— be it boiled rice, parched grain flour, or vegetables, roots, fruits, and so forth— one should give that same thing on the following day.
For ten days in this world, sons and others offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas);
these are divided into four portions every day, O Lord of Birds.
Two parts are for the sake of the body, providing pleasure to the five elements;
the third belongs to the messengers of Yama, and the fourth is that upon which others subsist.
Within nine days and nights, the deceased attains completion;
for the being whose body is now formed, intense hunger arises on the tenth day.
There is no ritual procedure, nor even a mantra, nor the invocation with *svadhā*, nor benedictions;
whatever is given after reciting the name and lineage, that pertains to the ten-day period.
O bird, when the body has been burnt, a body is produced once again in this manner:
on the first day, the head is generated from that primary mass.
In the second [recitation] the neck and shoulders; in the third, the heart;
in the fourth, the back; and in the fifth, the navel.

On the seventh day, the six [limbs]—the hips, the private parts, and the thighs—are formed; likewise on the eighth day, the palate and the two feet; and on the ninth day, hunger arises. On the tenth day, hunger occurs.
Having obtained a body and overcome by hunger, he stands at the door of the house;
on the tenth day, one should offer him that funeral ball (piṇḍa) together with meat.
Since the preta, once a body has arisen, is possessed by extreme hunger,
therefore his hunger is not extinguished by anything other than flesh.
On the eleventh day and the twelfth day, the deceased enjoys [the offerings] for two days;
one should apply the term "preta" (deceased) to both women and men.
Whatever substance is given— be it a lamp, food, water, clothing, or anything else—
it should be offered with the word "preta," for it bestows the joy of satisfaction upon the deceased.
On the thirteenth day, that preta is led along the great path;
relying upon a body born of funeral offerings, he remains hungry by day and by night.
The path of cold, heat, spikes, flesh-eaters, and fire belongs to the sinners;
whereas for those of purified self, everything is gentle, consisting only of hunger and thirst.
And on the path filled with forests of sword-leaves, these sufferings exist:
he is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and tormented by the servants of Yama.
Day after day, indeed, the deceased travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas in a single day and night.
Bound by the nooses of Yama and crying out "Alas!
Alas!", he abandons his own home and proceeds toward the city of Yama.
That preta proceeds gradually toward the city of Yama, experiencing various excellent cities along the way according to his good and evil deeds.
The region of Yama, the city of Saturn, the abode of the Lord of Mountains, the arrival at the Gandharva mountain,
Krauñca, the city of Cruelty, and the abode of Wonders— all these bring many calamities and bestow suffering.
Before him were the city of Nānākranda, the birthplace of Suta, the fierce Payovarṣaṇa, the cool Śītāḍhya, and the city of Yama, where many fear the Dharma.
On the thirteenth day, that preta was seized by the servants of Yama;
as he traveled along that path, he was like a captured monkey.
Likewise, as he travels along the road, crying out "Son! Son! and constantly wailing "Alas! Alas!", he says: "What kind of deed have I committed? (GarP 2.15.85)
"Why is human birth obtained? he asks as it spreads forth. "Human birth is obtained through the application of great merit. (GarP 2.15.86)
Having obtained that [wealth], he does not indeed give his own riches to beggars; rather, with a faltering voice, he says, "That has become dependent on others. (He laments. 2.15.87.
He is tormented excessively by the servants [of Yama] and remembers his former existence.
There is no giver of pleasure or pain; the notion that another gives them is a false understanding.
One always experiences the karma created in the past; O embodied one, atone in some way for what you have done.
I have given no gift, nor offered oblations into the fire; I have performed no austerity in the caves of the snowy mountains;
nor have I ever resorted to the great waters of the Ganges. O embodied being, cross over somehow that which has been done by you!
No constant charity was given, no daily gift of cows was made, no gift of the Vedas nor of scriptural books;
never before has such a path been seen, nor has it ever been traveled—O embodied one, cross over that which you have done!
Indeed, no reservoir was ever constructed for the sake of humans in this waterless land, nor for the sake of beasts and birds;
nor was a pasture made for the satisfaction of cattle—what you have done, O Dehin, has been done nowhere at all.

I have not enjoyed the pleasure of my husband's company, nor did I enter the fire when he died; while he was dead, I maintained that vow. O embodied one, deliver me from whatever [karmic debt] you have incurred.

This female body, a vessel for manifold sufferings, has been obtained by me through misdeeds committed in the past; it was not dried away by month-long fasts, nor by *cāndrāyaṇa* observances, nor by the combined performance of restraints.
I have spoken what was to be said regarding men; therefore, O bird, listen attentively.
Having obtained a female body, the embodied soul declares the deeds performed in the past.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, in the Dharmadṛpta-kalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Extent of the Realm of Yama, its Greatness, and the Journey Therein.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa 16]. The Blessed Lord said:
O Lord of Birds, as that preta was thus lamenting,
crying out intensely while being tormented by the henchmen, [Garuda spoke].
For seventeen days he is dragged along the path of the wind;
on the eighteenth day and night, he first proceeds to the city of Yama.
In that delightful, excellent city, there was a great multitude of pretas;
there also was the river Puṣpabhadrā and a banyan tree of pleasing appearance.
There he is brought to rest by the servants of Yama;
there, being deeply afflicted, he will remember the happiness of his wife, children, and others.
Afflicted by thirst and oppressed by exhaustion, he weeps with piteous words for his own wealth,
his wives, his home, his sons, and his pleasures.
Then he indeed grieves for his servants, friends, and everything else;
and while he is afflicted by hunger in that city, it is said to him by his servants:
The servants said:
"Where is wealth? Where are sons and wife? Where is the home? Where are you, such as you are?
Enjoy what has been earned by your own karma; go quickly upon the great path."
You know that provisions are the strength of travelers; yet, O traveler to the next world, you do not prepare your provisions.
You must certainly go by that path where there is neither buying nor selling for you.
"O bird, you have not heard the words uttered by the messengers of Yama.
Thus addressed, he was then struck by all of them with mallets.
If a monthly funeral cake (piṇḍa) is offered here by sons to a worthy recipient out of affection or compassion, he partakes of it and thereafter proceeds to the city of Sauri.
There, indeed, was a king named Jaṅgama, who bore the form of Death itself;
seeing him, [the people] became terrified with fear and resolved to take rest.
Having gone to that city, he eats water mixed with food;
then, having passed through that city, he proceeds to where that which was given at the three-fortnightly rite is located.
In the beautiful city of Nagendra, the deceased wanders day and night;
as he goes through the terrifying forests, he cries out there upon seeing them.
Afflicted by terrifying [beings], he weeps again and again;
then, at the end of two months, he passes beyond that city.
Having eaten food and drunk water here, or whatever has been given by kinsmen,
one who is then tormented by bonds is led away by the servants of Yama.
When the third month has arrived, having enjoyed the auspicious city of the Gandharvas for that third month, he goes forward there.
In the fourth month, he indeed reaches the city of Śailāgama;
there, stones rain down upon the one who has come to stand before the preta.
If one partakes in the śrāddha on the fourth month, one shall become happy therein.
Then, in the fifth month, the deceased goes to the city of Krūra;
staying in that city, the deceased indeed enjoys what was given here by his sons.
Thereafter, in the sixth month, the deceased goes to the city named Krauñca.
There, nourished by the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the ancestral offering (śrāddha) given previously,
he rested for half a muhūrta, trembling and deeply distressed.
Having passed beyond that city while being threatened by the servants of Yama,
he proceeds to the City of Citra, where King Vicitra resides.
Indeed, where the son of the Sun (Sauri) rules as king, he is the younger brother of Yama;
five and a half months constitute what is known as the six-month period.
Struck by the messengers of Yama, he eats there for less than six months;
moreover, on that path, hunger afflicts him excessively again and again.
"Is there anyone among my sons or kinsmen who remains alive, who might bring me joy as I am falling into an ocean of grief? GarP_2,16.24 //
While he was thus lamenting on the path and being restrained by the servants,
thousands of fishermen arrived there before him.
We [are here] for you who desire to cross the great Vaitaraṇī river,
which is a hundred yojanas wide and filled with pus and blood.
"Filled with various fish and surrounded by flocks of various birds, we shall carry you across in comfort," they said. (GarP 2.16.27)
"O traveler, grant me passage; if you have much desire for it," he said.
Thereupon, the cow was given by him, and by her the boat moved forward.
It is remembered that giving a gift for the benefit of humanity at the end [of life] is the Vaitaraṇī.
It burns away all the sins of others and leads them to the world of Viṣṇu;
O best of birds, if it is not given, one suffers by encountering it.
While the body is in a state of health, one should observe the Vaitaraṇī vow;
and by one desiring to cross that river, a cow should be given to a learned man.
But as he was being crushed, he reproached himself, saying:
"I did not give anything to a twice-born man for the sake of provisions for my journey."
"Nothing was given, nothing offered in sacrifice, nothing chanted, no ritual bath taken, and no praise performed;
O fool, experience the fruit of exactly the kind of action you have committed. (GarP 2.16.32)
At that very moment, utterly bewildered in his heart and struck by the soldiers, he speaks;
on the far bank of the Vaitaraṇī, he consumes the water-pot and other offerings given to him.
Having eaten at a śrāddha performed within six months [of death], one goes ahead;
therefore, O Tārkṣya, one should especially feed auspicious twice-born brahmins there.
Tārkṣya, though exhausted by day and night, travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas every single day.
When the seventh month has arrived, one should go to a city full of many calamities;
there, having eaten the śrāddha offered for the seventh month, [one is purified].
When the eighth month has arrived, one goes to the city of Nānākranda;
seeing the hosts of Nānākranda wailing most piteously.
And though his own heart is empty, he cries out in suffering;
yet, having partaken of that monthly *śrāddha* offering, he becomes happy there.
Leaving that city, the deceased goes toward Taptapura;
having reached Sutaptanagara, in the ninth month he enjoys the food for Brahmins, the offering of funeral cakes, and the Śrāddha performed by his son. (GarP 2.16.39)
When the tenth month has arrived, he goes to the realm of Rudra;
having consumed what was given during that tenth month, he departs.
Having eaten for ten months and one day, they encounter a rain of water;
there, the clouds pour down rain that brings suffering to the pretas.
Then the ship set sail, its occupants afflicted by great hunger and thirst;
in the twelfth month, he eats the śrāddha offering there, suffering intensely from cold.
When the year is somewhat less than that, or when it is eleven and a half years,
he goes to Śītapura, where the cold is exceedingly painful.
Then, afflicted by cold and hungry, he gazes toward the ten directions, wondering:
"Is there any kinsman who might remain and dispel my suffering?"
The servants speak thus to him: "Where indeed is such merit of yours?
Having heard their words, he exclaims, "Alas, fate! (GarP 2.16.45).
"For destiny is indeed one's prior merit, and that has not been accumulated by me.
Having reflected thus many times, he again takes recourse in fortitude.
Then, extending for forty-four yojanas,
lies the delightful city of Dharmarāja, teeming with gandharvas and apsarases.
It is presided over by eighty-four hundred thousand [beings] in both embodied and unembodied forms;
thirteen gatekeepers reside in the city of Dharmarāja.
Having repeatedly deliberated upon what is auspicious and inauspicious karma,
as well as the conduct of humans, the sons of Brahmā, Śravaṇas,
then speak of it in the world, being honored themselves by those who honor [them].
Whatever was spoken and whatever was done by men who were satisfied and well-nourished—
all that they reported to Citragupta and Yama.
Possessing the power of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar,
these eight, who move through the sky, the earth, and the netherworld (pātāla), perform such deeds.
Their wives were likewise formidable, each having a distinct name;
such was their power that they held authority over mortals.
Whatever human being worships me here through vows, gifts, and ascetic practices,
gentle planets are born for him, bestowing a peaceful death.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Procession for the Departed and Other Rites," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Glorious *Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: Chapter Seventeen.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, a single doubt oppresses my heart:
Whose sons are these ascetics, and how is it that they reside in the city of Yama?"
O Lord, why do they know the actions performed by human beings? How do they hear everything, and from where has this knowledge come to them? (GarP 2.17.2)
"O Lord of Gods, tell me by your grace where they eat.
Having heard the words of the king of birds, the Blessed One spoke these words: [GarP_2,17.3]
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to these true words that bestow happiness upon all;
I shall relate to you the conduct of those who listen.
When the entire world, both mobile and immobile, had become one, while I, the Lord of the World, was formerly asleep in the Ocean of Milk; GarP_2,17.5 //
Seated at his navel, he performed austerities for very many years;
the fourfold collection of beings was created as a single, unified world.
It was first created by Brahmā and then protected by Viṣṇu;
thereafter, Rudra, whose form is that of dissolution, was created by Brahmā.
Vāyu was created, all-pervading; then the Sun, possessing an increase of splendor, was created;
thereafter Dharmarāja was created together with Citragupta.
Having created all this and more, the Lotus-born one performed austerities;
many years passed while he remained in the lotus-navel of Brahmā.
Whosoever was previously manifested as a creator, he performed those respective deeds at a certain time there, accompanied by Brahmā and the world.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and likewise Dharma govern the earth;
we do not know anything—let that which is to be done here in this world be told.
Thus all the gods, intent on reflection, deliberated at that time;
then, having considered the counsel of Brahmā, he was urged by the deities.
Taking up flowers and leaves, he emitted twelve sons at the word of Brahmā; they were masses of splendor with large eyes.
Whatever one speaks in this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
they quickly bring it to the range of Brahmā’s hearing.
The cognition of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar—
because all birds hear [the Dharma] with that very [faculty], they are considered "hearers" (śravana).
Having remained thus in space and having understood whatever activity of living beings occurs, they speak at the time of death in the presence of the King of Dharma.
They discourse upon Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa;
for there is indeed one path of Dharma and a second path of Artha.
There is another path of desire and the fourth is the path of liberation;
indeed, O Vainateya, they proceed by means of the lower and the higher paths.
The giver of wealth travels by means of celestial chariots; the giver of desired objects travels by means of horses;
and he who longs for liberation moves about in celestial chariots yoked with swans.
But the other goes on foot through forests of sword-leaves,
afflicted by stones and thorns, and indeed proceeds while bound by nooses.
Whoever in this world of men should worship the earthenware vessels here with a water-pot filled with cooked food; ||| GarP_2,17.21 |||
O Lord of Birds, one should worship the ears there along with me;
I shall grant him that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having devoutly fed eleven auspicious and pure Brahmins,
one should honor the twelfth, together with his wife, for my pleasure.
Having been honored by all the gods, they go to heaven out of a desire for happiness;
when they have been thus honored, the King of Dharma, Citragupta, is well-pleased.
When they are satisfied, those people who are devoted to dharma go to my city;
[I shall describe] the greatness of the Śravaṇas, their origin, and their auspicious deeds.
O tiger among birds, he who hears this is not defiled by sins;
having enjoyed happiness in this world, he is glorified in the heavenly realm.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Śravaṇa" within the Pretakalpa of the Dharmakāṇḍa, in the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard the words of the Śravaṇas and having meditated for a moment upon them,
[he considered] whatever merit or sin had been performed by men day and night.
Having fully understood all of that, Citragupta shall report it;
then Citragupta tells him everything regarding his past actions.
Whatever action has been performed through speech, whatever has been performed through the body,
and likewise whatever mental action has been performed— one experiences its fruit, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, the determination of the path of the departed has been told to you;
now all the places where rest is found have been described to you.
Intending him as the recipient, one gives food; he travels happily on the great path.
By day or by night, one should be a giver of lamps in that place, intending him as the recipient. (GarP 2.18.5)
And those men by whom a lamp has been given travel upon a path that is terrifyingly dark, filled with dogs, devoid of landmarks, and ablaze.
The offering of lamps on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika indeed leads to happiness.
Now, I shall briefly describe the expiation for the path of Yama.
By the merit of the rite of releasing a bull, he goes to the world of the ancestors;
thereafter, by means of the rice-ball offering on the eleventh day, his body becomes purified.
By the gift of a water-pot, the servants shall obtain satisfaction.
By the gift of a bed, a person dwells in celestial palaces and goes to the heavens;
on that very day all [gifts] are given, especially on the twelfth day.
In the thirteenth [chapter], those who, while still alive, give here on earth the "footsteps"—the most excellent of all things—for the sake of the deceased for their own benefit; GarP_2,18.11.
Relying upon that, O Vainateya, he travels on the great path;
O Lord of Birds, there is only one conventional designation everywhere.
There shall be the attraction of those who are superior, inferior, or middling;
according to one's fortune, so much will be exceeded on the path.
Whatever is given by oneself with one's own hand, that alone empowers him there;
having relied upon what is given by kinsmen after death, he shall become happy.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of Gods, why are thirteen steps to be given, and of what nature are they? To whom are they given? Tell me that exactly as it is."
The Blessed One said:
An umbrella, sandals, garments, a seal-ring, a water-pot,
a seat, and a vessel— these are remembered as the sevenfold insignia.
The fierce heat that exists there, by which a human being is scorched,
becomes a beautiful shade through the gift of an umbrella, providing satisfaction to the departed spirits.
He who gives a pair of sandals certainly crosses over the terrible Forest of Sword-leaves, where those mounted on horses go.
If a seat, a welcome, and food are given to that twice-born one,
that preta eats with ease while traveling slowly along the path.
In a place crowded with many beings, free from wind and devoid of water,
one certainly becomes happy by the gift of a water-pot.
Whoever should offer a copper water-vessel intended for the deceased certainly enjoys the fruit of a thousand gifts of drinking-water stations.
The messengers of Yama, though exceedingly fierce, terrifying, and dark-brown in hue,
do not cause suffering out of courtesy because of the gift of clothing and ornaments.
And those messengers of Yama, though running with their weapons, do not come within the range of sight on the path due to the giving of the seal-ring.
By the gift of vessels and seats, by the offering of raw grain and cooked food,
and by the offering of clarified butter and the sacred thread, one shall attain the state of perfection.
Thus, while traveling on the road, one who is afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue will certainly become happy through the gift of a buffalo-cow and its milk.
Garuḍa said:
O Lord, whatever is given in one's own home for the sake of the deceased, that person travels upon the great path; by whom is that which was given received?
The Blessed One said:
Varuṇa accepts the gift; he delivers it into my hand;
and I, in turn, present it to the god Bhāskara; through Bhāskara, he enjoys happiness.
Due to the power of their improper actions, when their lineage is severed here on earth,
they all go to hell until the exhaustion of their sin.
At a certain time, when [the period] was complete, the righteous one, seated upon his buffalo throne,
beheld the hells filled with various cries of lamentation.
He is the lord of eighty-four hundred thousand hells;
among them, the most excellent and terrible are those twenty-one.
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāraurava, Śālmalī,
Raurava, Kuḍmala, Kālasūtraka, and Pūtimṛttika.
The Crushing Hell, the Iron Goad, the Poisonous, and the Heating Hell;
the Great Hell is a turbulent ocean, a great highway for those being revived.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka;
Asipatravana and Patana—these constitute twenty-one [hells].
But those who have indeed spent many years in the terrible hell for which there is no succession [of births], they go [after death] to the state of being messengers.
Sent indeed by Yama for the sake of a deceased human,
they seize day after day the food, drink, and other offerings that have been given.
Hungry, they indeed plunder the preta right there in the middle of the path;
at the end of the month, some people offer a ball of food (*piṇḍa*) as a meal for them there.
They all attain satisfaction every day for an entire year;
through such meritorious deeds as these, one shall gradually proceed to the city of Sauri.
Then, at the end of a year when the abode of Yama is drawing near,
a preta that causes great terror shall emit a hand-sized flame.
Seeing that body born in ten days from ten lumps of food, his splendor spread forth like that of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Relying upon a body born of karma, one should cast off the previous body;
then the vital breath, the size of a thumb, ascends to the leaf of a *śamī* tree.
Just as one who walks stands with only one foot while moving with the other,
so too the embodied being, driven by karma and lacking autonomy, moves like a caterpillar upon a blade of grass.
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out clothes, takes up others that are new,
so the embodied soul, having cast off worn-out bodies, enters into other, new ones.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Various Gifts through the Release of a Bull, the Journey to the World of Yama, and the Attainment of a Body Born of Karma," in the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the vision of the righteous and the departed spirits.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 19.
The Blessed One said:
Having become like the wind and overcome by hunger, he takes recourse in a body born of karma;
having reached that body, he goes together with Yama.
The city of Citragupta is there, measuring twenty yojanas;
the scribes (kāyasthas) residing there behold all sins and merits in their entirety.
When great gifts have been bestowed, one who has gone there shall become happy;
the auspicious city of Vaivasvata extends for twenty-four yojanas.
Those men by whom iron, salt, cotton, and vessels of sesame have been given—
by that very act, the attendants of Yama are satisfied.
Having gone there, they all spoke to the doorkeeper:
"The doorkeeper Dharmadhvaja always stands there."
By the gift of the seven grains, one becomes Dharmadhvaja;
having gone there, the gatekeeper announces his auspicious and inauspicious [karma].
The virtuous and meritorious people behold the form of Dharmarāja as it truly is, whereas the evil-minded perceive the terrifying form of Yama.
Seeing him, people cry out "Alas! Alas! in terror;
yet for those mortals who have practiced giving, there is no fear anywhere.
Seeing that virtuous man who had attained [the goal], the son of the Sun moved from his place, thinking:
"This one shall pierce my mandala and proceed to the world of Brahmā."
Through generosity, the Dharma is easily attained; the path of Yama brings happiness.
This path is vast, yet it is not followed by anyone here.
Without the merit of giving, my child, one cannot go to the palace of Dharma.
On that fierce path, indeed, one thousand terrifying servants of Yama stand before each individual city.
Having seized the sinner, the agents of torment cook him in water;
they seize him month after month until only a quarter of him remains.
"O Kāśyapa, those by whom funeral offerings have not been given go with great suffering; therefore, they should be given according to one's ability.
Without having given them, they go like cattle, seized by various bonds."
By performing such deeds, that man shall experience his destiny through his past actions—
whether it be a divine, ancestral, human, or even hellish rebirth.
Or, by the word of the King of Dharma, liberation may arise from that;
having truly attained human birth, that son shall attain the state of being a true son.
In whatever manner a person has performed an action, he shall go to that very womb; experiencing the results exactly as they were done, he wanders throughout all the worlds.
Having fully understood that all things are impermanent, one should practice the Dharma while human existence prevails— that which is the supreme happiness transcending the entire world.
The nature of bodies is always either worms, ashes, or excrement;
one might indeed fall into a vast and terrible blind well while holding a lamp in one's hand.
Through the power of great merit, a human birth is obtained;
he who, having attained it, practices the Dharma, shall go to the supreme destination.
Even knowing [this], one undergoes and departs from suffering in vain through the pursuit of dharma.
"O Bird, it is said that one obtains human status after a hundred births; even there, O twice-born one, the state of being a Brahmin is more difficult to attain.
For him who observes and cherishes the vows therein, immortality comes into his very hands by grace."

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Entering the Abode of Yama and the Attainment of Another Body, such as that of a Human, by Obtaining His Permission," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Chapter 20 of the *Śrī-Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*]
Garuḍa said:
"Where do those who exist in the form of *preta*s find their dwelling? Once liberated from the world of *preta*s, how and where do they go?"
It was attended by eighty-four million hells,
guarded there by Yama and by thousands of spirits.
Having heard what was uttered by Garuḍa— “How do they roam in the world, having emerged from hell?”— the Lord of Lakṣmī spoke this.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O King of Birds, listen to where the pretas indeed roam; [it is] because of taking another's wife for one's own purpose... (ba)
From the injury [caused] by the night-stalkers.
In that very same way, those most sinful beings, wandering about bodiless while intent on searching for their own offspring, were severely afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Released from the prison where living beings perish,
those hungry ghosts (pretas) nevertheless devise means for the slaughter of their kinsmen.
They block the doors to the ancestors and likewise cut off their path;
they seize the ancestral shares like thieves from travelers. (GarP 2.20.7)
Having returned again to their own abode, they enter the place of Mitra;
staying there, they behold the bonds of disease, sorrow, and the like.
They afflict [the patient] by turning into fevers, specifically under the guise of quotidian fever,
or as tertian fevers, causing suffering through cold, wind, and other such symptoms.
Furthermore, those who remain in places such as where food scraps are discarded constantly contemplate various other diseases, including headaches and cholera.
Deceived by their own sons, they drink water mixed with the leftovers of food, while the worlds are protected by hosts of elemental beings.
Thus do the pretas come into being, performing various wrong actions due to their manifold faults.
Garuḍa said:
How do those pretas act? In what form? Whose [are they], and what [is their nature]?
By what method are they known? Do they speak or do they not speak?
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, cut away this delusion of the mind;
for in this age of strife, the state of a preta arises frequently."
The illustrious Viṣṇu said:
A ghost torments his own family and torments others by seeking their vulnerabilities;
while alive he appears affectionate, but once dead, he attains a state of wickedness.
One who recites the Rudra-mantra, is devoted to dharma, honors deities and guests,
speaks the truth, and utters pleasant words— such a person is indeed not tormented by pretas.
One who has fallen away from all ritual duties, an atheist, a reviler of the Dharma,
and a man devoted to speaking untruths is tormented by pretas;
in the Kali age, one who is intent on impure actions becomes a preta, O Tārkṣya.
In the Kṛta age and up to the end of the Dvāpara age, there is neither a preta nor any affliction;
among many born of a single family, only one enjoys happiness.
One has performed evil deeds, while another possesses a virtuous lineage;
one is tormented by spirits, while another is endowed with sons and wealth.
One may suffer the loss of a son, while another may have a daughter;
there will be conflict with kinsmen due to the fault of a deceased ancestor, O Kāśyapa.
A continuity is not seen at all; what has arisen perishes.
The destruction of livestock and wealth, as well as that suffering arising from the state of a preta, [is observed].
There may be a reversal of one's natural state and enmity with kinsmen;
the sudden onset of calamities—that is the suffering arising from the Pretas. (GarP 2.20.22)
Atheism, the loss of livelihood, as well as great greed,
and constant quarreling— such is the suffering arising from the state of a preta.
A killer of father or mother, and a reviler of gods and Brahmins—such are the faults one incurs; that suffering arises from being a *preta*. (GarP 2.20.24)
One who is abandoned by obligatory duties, devoid of recitation and burnt offerings,
and a thief of others' property— that suffering arises from the state of a preta.
Even with good rain, there is loss of crops and commerce perishes;
in the world, it causes strife, and that suffering arises from the pretas. (GarP 2.20.26)
If a whirlwind should afflict him while he is walking on the road, that should be known as the affliction of a preta; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of Birds.
Connection with those of low birth, performing base actions,
and constantly delighting in unrighteousness— that is the suffering born of the state of a preta.
Through calamities there shall be loss of wealth, and what has been undertaken perishes;
there is ruin from thieves, fire, and kings—such is the suffering arising from the deceased.
The occurrence of a great disease, the affliction of children, and whatever suffering the wife undergoes—that pain arises from a preta. (GarP 2.20.30)
When there is an absence of righteousness arising from the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras,
that suffering arises from the state of being a preta.
That man who reviles deities, sacred fords, or twice-born brahmins—
whether in their presence or in their absence— suffers that pain arising from the state of a preta.
The seizure of one's own livelihood, as well as the destruction of one's own standing and the extinction of one's lineage— these would not be seen otherwise than through the fault of a *preta*.
Where there is destruction of the fetus in women, where menses are not seen,
and where there is death among children, that affliction arises from a preta.
If, due to impurity of disposition, one does not perform the annual *śrāddha* and other rites,
and does not perform them oneself, that suffering arises from the state of being a *preta*.
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), one who is attached to others abandons his own duty;
that lack of success in religious acts is the suffering arising from the state of a preta.
Quarreling between husband and wife, anger during meals, and a mind intent on harming others—such suffering arises from the influence of a preta. (GarP 2.20.37)
Where neither flower nor fruit is seen,
and where there is separation from one's wife— that is the suffering born of the realm of the departed spirits.
For those men for whom a sign indeed arises that is constantly intent on eradication, their own vital energy becomes fruitless in its own field; that suffering originates from a *preta*.
Indeed, one who destroys their own kin slays their own offspring as if they were an enemy;
there is neither joy nor happiness in that suffering born of the state of a preta.
He does not obey the words of his father, nor does he serve his own wife; always cruel-minded and agitated—that is the suffering arising from a preta. (GarP 2.20.41)
Likewise,
one is born as a *preta* due to improper rites and from contact with the wicked at that time, except in the case of the ritual release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Or even due to the power of attachment to what has been seen, O Tārkṣya, the state of a preta arises for those whose bodies have not been consumed by fire; by this, living beings are tormented.
Knowing this, O best of birds, one should perform the rite for the liberation of the deceased;
for he who does not acknowledge the existence of pretas shall himself become a preta after death.
In the family where there is the fault of a *preta*, happiness is not found;
intellect, joy, delight, wisdom, and fortune—these five are destroyed. (GarP 2.20.45)
In the third or fifth generation, the lineage will indeed be cut off;
moreover, he shall be poor, destitute, and a performer of evil deeds in birth after birth.

Whosoever among the forms of *pretas* have distorted faces and fierce appearances, or are terrifying and hideous, they do not recognize their own kin—sons, daughters, fathers, brothers, wives, or daughters-in-law.

Having assumed a desirable form, yet deprived of a happy state, they speak as they please; alas, what misery! Desiring food while fallen under the power of fate, they remember their own past misdeeds.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the Prata-kalpa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the twentieth chapter titled "Description of the Abode of Pretas and the Manner of Their Afflictions.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa 21] Garuḍa said:
I am eager to ask how the hungry ghosts (pretas) attain liberation, and why,
once liberated, no further suffering arises for human beings.
"O Lord, you have described these symptoms as being caused by affliction from a *preta*.
When will their liberation occur, and how may they no longer remain in the state of a *preta*?"
What is the authoritative proof regarding the state of being a preta, and for how many years in number does one remain in that state?
Having fallen into the condition of a preta for so long, how may one attain liberation?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Those spirits attain liberation; I shall tell you how that occurs:
as soon as a human being realizes, "This suffering has been caused by me," [they are liberated].
One who desires one's own welfare should report to the Vajrācārya the meaning of what was seen in a dream: "A beautiful tree, laden with fruit—such as a mango or a campaka—was seen. (GarP 2.21.5)
If a brahmin, a bull, or a deity is seen wandering while visiting sacred fords, or if such a dream is seen when some deceased kinsman of one's own lineage appears; GarP_2,21.6 //
Having fully understood the truth regarding dreams through the power of hungry ghosts (preta), wondrous things are seen; these are certainly due to the defects of hungry ghosts.
As long as the mind is intent on bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) while the heart remains devoted to dharma,
yet it brings about the decline of dharma, then the affliction of a preta shall descend.
Then, she causes a breakdown of his mind there for the sake of his destruction;
for auspicious things are beset by many obstacles at every step. (GarP 2.21.9)
O Bird, they repeatedly incite one toward what is not beneficial, as well as expulsion, cruelty, and everything else wrought by the *preta*s. (GarP 2.21.10)
He who, having abandoned all obstacles, practices the means to liberation,
his karmic fruit is excellent and his state as a preta becomes eternal.
He shall be liberated by that; what is given is supremely auspicious.
O bird, he himself is satisfied when that which is given is offered for his sake.

Listen, O Tārkṣya, to this truth: he who gives and he who enjoys [the gift] shall unite himself with spiritual welfare, and as a deceased being, he shall attain long-lasting satisfaction. (GarP 2.21.13)
Being satisfied, they always desire the welfare of their own kinsmen;
however, those wicked strangers who are unknown cause suffering to those born of their own lineage.
Once satisfied, they protect those who are being born out of compassion for them;
later, when the time has come, they attain liberation through their own sons.
O Lord of Birds, they always bestow prosperity and success upon their kinsmen.
That fool-souled person who, through seeing, speaking, gestures, or by causing harm,
does not lead [the deceased] to their destination, becomes tainted by the curses of the departed spirits.
He shall be childless, without cattle, poor, afflicted by disease,
destitute of livelihood, and lowly in birth after birth.
Thus do those pretas speak, depending upon whom they have taken refuge;
for those staying there, liberation shall occur when their own time comes and their karma is exhausted.
Garuḍa said:
"Neither the name nor the lineage is seen, and no recognition whatsoever arises;
yet some astrologers speak of affliction arising from a preta."
There is no dreaming, no activity, and never even a vision;
O best of gods, tell me for certain what must be done in that state.
The Blessed One said:
Whether they speak the truth or even what is untrue, the gods of the earth say this;
having reflected upon it in one's heart, this which has been uttered by the twice-born is the truth.
Placing devotion to his parents foremost,
he who is devoted to filial piety should perform the *kṛṣṇabali* offering preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
O Lord of Birds, one should perform the purification of the body through recitation, fire-offerings, and gifts;
by doing so, all obstacles are destroyed.
If he is afflicted by ghosts, spirits, or piśācas, or by others,
he should then perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali offering dedicated to the ancestors;
he shall be liberated from all afflictions— this is my truthful word.
Where there is suffering for one's ancestors that cannot be relieved by other rites,
therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the service of the ancestors.
In the ninth or tenth year, a man,
for the sake of destroying the Piśācas, should mutter ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number.
Having first performed the *kṛṣṇabali* sacrifice, one should carry out the rites such as the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Thus freed from all calamities, one shall obtain every happiness,
attain the highest world, and achieve preeminence among one's kinsmen.
In this world, there is no other supreme deity equal to one's father and mother;
therefore, one should always worship them with every possible effort.
For the father who instructs one in what is beneficial is a manifest deity;
whatever other deities exist in the world, they do not originate from the body.
The very body of living beings is the sole means for attaining heaven and liberation;
since he has bestowed such a body, who else could be more worthy of worship than him?
Having reflected thus in his heart, whatever the bird now offers, he eats all of that himself; those who know the Vedas understand this as a gift.
Because a son protects his father from the hell named Punnāma and other such realms,
he is therefore called "puttra" both in this world and in the next.
O Bird, if the parents of anyone should die of an untimely death,
one should abandon the performance of vows, pilgrimages, marriages, and ancestral rites (śrāddha) for a year.
Whoever reads or even hears this chapter on dreams, which indicates the signs of a deceased person, shall not see the marks of one who has passed away.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dreams," in the second part (Dharmakāṇḍa), within the Pretakalpa of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 22.
Garuḍa said:
How do the pretas come into being, and by what means is their destiny determined? What would their form be like, O Lord, and what would be their food?
O Lord of the Gods, how are those hungry ghosts (pretas) so well-pleased, and where do they dwell? O God, being gracious out of compassion, please explain this question to me.
The Blessed One said:
"Those who are indeed devoted to evil deeds and follow the influence of their past karma, they are born as *preta*s after death; listen to them as I speak."
He established step-wells, wells, and tanks, as well as groves, temples of the gods,
water-stations, dwellings, excellent trees, and likewise dining halls.
He who sells the dharma inherited from his father and grandfather incurs sin;
upon death, he attains the state of a preta for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
Those who, out of greed, encroach upon pasture lands, village boundaries, ponds, gardens, or forest thickets, indeed become pretas.
Death for those who have committed evil deeds comes from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning-fire, or from fanged beasts.
Those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons, those who committed suicide, and likewise those killed by cholera and other such diseases; // GarP_2,22.8 //
Those who have died from great diseases, those from malignant diseases or by bandits, those who have passed away without funeral rites, and those who have abandoned prescribed conduct; 22.9 //

He for whom a Śūdra performs the fire-rituals—such as the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and others—and for whom the monthly rice-balls (piṇḍas) are omitted, is one who has his sacred fires carried by a Śūdra. He [is thus defiled].

Those who die from the falling of mountains or the collapse of walls, those who die due to defects such as menstruation, and those who have died upon the ground—[these do not attain the fruit]. (GarP 2.22.11)

Those who died in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) devoid of the remembrance of Viṣṇu, and those here on earth who exist in the state of a ghost (pretabhāva) due to birth-impurities or contact with dogs and other such things; [all these attain liberation].
Those who have fallen under the power of such and other untimely deaths all dwell in the realm of hungry ghosts, wandering through the desert wastes.
He who abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law,
or daughter when no fault has been seen in them, certainly becomes a preta after death.
O Tārkṣya, one who betrays his brother, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed,
or a stealer of gold and silk— such a person indeed attains the state of a preta.
One who steals deposits, betrays friends, is devoted to the wives of others,
violates trust, and is cruel— such a person will certainly be born as a preta.
Having abandoned the traditions of his own family and likewise delighting in the dharma of others, and being devoid of both learning and virtuous conduct, he will certainly be born as a preta.
In this very context, O observer of noble vows, they cite this ancient history— the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīṣma—
which I shall relate to you, by hearing which one may attain happiness. (GarP 2.22.18)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what ripening of karma does the state of a preta arise? Or by what is one released from it? Tell me that, O Grandfather."
Having heard which, O observer of noble vows, I shall never again fall into such delusion.
Bhīṣma said:
By that very same [action] by which one becomes a ghost (preta), and by that very same [action] by which one is liberated,
one reaches a terrible hell difficult to cross even for the gods.
By the constant hearing of this, and by its meritorious recitation and glorification,
men who have fallen into the wombs of pretas are completely liberated.
For it is heard, O child, that in ancient times there was a brahmin of celebrated vows,
known by the name Santaptaka, who had retired to the forest for the sake of asceticism.
One who is devoted to the private recitation of sacred texts, engaged in fire-offerings, intent on sacrifice, and endowed with compassion—
performing all sacrifices through proper method and passing his time accordingly.
Devoted to the holy life, engaged in austerity and gentleness,
possessed of fear regarding the next world, and stainless through truth and purity.
For he is disciplined by the words of his guru, disciplined in the honoring of guests,
ever-exerted in the yoga of the self, and free from all dualities.

Always engaged in the practice of yoga with the desire to conquer cyclic existence, one who is thus disposed, of virtuous conduct, longing for liberation, and having conquered the senses; // GarP_2,22.26 //
Many years indeed passed for him in the lonely forest;
then, a thought arose in him regarding the visiting of sacred fords.
"I shall wither this body with the meritorious waters of sacred fords.
Having bathed quickly at that sacred ford at sunrise, the ascetic,
having performed his recitations and prostrations, set out upon the road.
One day, while traveling on the road, a brahmin of great asceticism lost his way and beheld five most dreadful pretas upon the path.
In a lonely forest region, in a narrow place devoid of trees,
having seen these five beings of distorted form and terrifying appearance,
his heart slightly trembling with fear, he stood with his eyes wide open.
Then, summoning his courage and casting fear far away, he who spoke with sweet words asked: "Who are you, you whose faces are so deformed?"
What impure karma was performed by which you have reached this transformation? Or how did you set out together in one direction, and where is it certain that you will end up?
The King of the Pretas said:
"O best of the twice-born, this state of being a preta has indeed been attained by each of us through our own respective actions;
we were all devoted to harming others and have fallen under the power of a sinful death."
Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, they have attained the state of hungry ghosts (preta);
their speech is lost, their splendor is destroyed, their consciousness is ruined, and they are devoid of reason.
"O Father, we do not know the direction or the intermediate points, being exceedingly distressed;
where indeed shall we go, we who are deluded Piśācas born of our own karma? (GarP 2.22.35)
"Neither mother nor father are ours; we have suddenly fallen into the state of pretas through our own actions, overwhelmed by the agitation of arisen suffering. (GarP 2.22.36)
O Brahmin, by the sight of you we have been gladdened and refreshed;
stay for a moment while I shall relate the entire account from the beginning.
I am named Paryuṣita, and this one is Sūcīmukha; Śīghraga and Raudhaka are likewise remembered as the fifth scribe.
"In this way, we have all indeed attained the state of a preta by these names.
The Brahmin asked:
"How does the occurrence of names come about for pretas born of their own karma?"
On account of some cause, you should speak of those who bear your own name.
The King of the Pretas said:
"O twice-born one, I have always eaten what was delicious, while I have been given what was stale."
"Because I was indeed requested by a hungry brahmin who was traveling quickly, for this reason my name is 'Paryuṣita' (the one who has stayed overnight). GarP_2,22.41 //
"O best of the twice-born, he travels swiftly because he was indeed entreated by a hungry brahmin; it is for this reason that he is called Śīghraga."
"O Brahmins, many were indicated by him out of a desire for food;
with this as the cause, he is remembered as Sūcimukha (the Needle-mouthed)."
He who always eats delicacies alone, neglecting those whom he ought to support,
is called a *rodhaka* (obstructor) by reason of his lack of devotion toward the Brahmins.
In the past, having observed silence, he drew lines on the ground when requested;
by the ripening of that karma, he is called a scribe (lekhaka).
O twice-born one, they attained the state of a preta through the power of their karma; these were their names:
Meṣānana, Lekhaka, Rodhaka, and Parvatānana.
Moving swiftly with a face like that of a beast, the informer has a needle-like mouth;
look at this reversal of form, O Lord, for they are exceedingly miserable.
Having assumed forms created by magic, we roam upon the surface of the earth;
all of us with deformed appearances, with hanging lips and distorted faces.
"Those with massive bodies and fierce forms were born by their own very actions.
All this, which is the cause of their state as a preta, has been explained to you by me."
"Through the sight of you, we have all become wise;
ask whatever you have faith in hearing, and I shall tell it to you."
The Brahmin said:
"All living beings who live upon this earth are rooted in food;
I wish to hear from you, moreover, the truth regarding your own food."
The pretas said:
"O best of the twice-born, O illustrious one, if you have faith to hear about our foods, then listen with a well-composed mind."
The Brahmin said:
"May the great pretas each describe their food individually.
Thus addressed by the Brahmin, the pretas spoke as follows, one by one.
The pretas said:
"Listen to our food, which is despised by all beings;
having heard it, O Brahmin, you will despise it again and again."
The food of the pretas consists of phlegm, urine, and excrement, along with the impurities of bodies, as well as other kinds of leftovers.
Indeed, the hungry ghosts (pretas) feast there in houses that are impure, with household utensils strewn about, soiled, and where a birth has occurred.
In that house where there is no truth, no purity, and no self-restraint,
and where there is association with outcasts and thieves, the hungry ghosts indeed consume the food.
Those offerings which are devoid of the bali-mantras, those which lack the fire-oblation (homa),
and those which are deficient in Vedic study and vows— indeed, the pretas consume them there.
When a householder there is conquered by women, there is neither shame nor moral restraint;
where the elders are not honored, the ancestors truly do not eat there.
Where there is greed as well as anger, sleep, sorrow, fear, and pride;
where there is constant indolence and quarreling—there indeed the pretas feast.
And when a woman deprived of her husband resorts to the seed of another,
the *pretas* indeed consume that seed, which is mixed with urine and excrement.
O dear one, shame arises in me as I speak of my own food;
for that which is the menstrual blood from the womb, the hungry ghosts (pretas) indeed consume it. (GarP 2.22.62)
"Disgusted with this state of being a preta, I ask you, O one of firm vows:
tell me, O rich in asceticism, how I may not become a preta again. Constant death is better for a living being than to ever become a preta. (GarP 2.22.63)
The Brahmin said:
A man who is constantly devoted to fasting, intent upon the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances,
and purified by various vows, does not become a *preta*.
A man who observes the vow on the eleventh day, accompanied by a night vigil and purified by other meritorious deeds, is neither a *preta* nor is he born as a *preta*.

That man who, having indeed performed sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha and others, bestows gifts, and who is the builder of parks, gardens, ponds, and the like, as well as of water-stations (prapās); GarP_2,22.66 //
He who, according to his ability, marries off a maiden to Brahmins,
and who bestows knowledge and fearlessness, is not born as a preta.
A man who dies while the food of a Śūdra remains undigested in his stomach,
or one who dies by an unnatural death, is reborn as a preta.
A man who performs sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, who abandons those worthy to sacrifice,
and who is constantly devoted to craftsmen, is born as a preta.
Having associated with those who drink liquor, having consorted with women who drink liquor,
and eating meat out of ignorance, that man is born as a preta.
He who gives away the property of the gods, the property of Brahmins, or likewise the property of his guru,
and who gives a maiden for a bride-price, that man is born as a preta.
He abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law, and likewise his daughter—
though they have committed no visible offense— that hungry ghost is as dull-witted as a fool.
One who steals deposits, betrays friends, is constantly devoted to the wives of others, is treacherous, and is deceitful— he is destined for that [hell].
One who betrays his brother, a slayer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, one who violates the teacher’s bed,
one who abandons the family path, one who is always devoted to speaking falsehoods,
and a stealer of gold and land— he shall see that [vision].
Bhīṣma said: While the brahmin was speaking thus, the sound of a drum arose in the sky,
and a rain of flowers released by the gods fell upon the twice-born one.
Five celestial palaces belonging to the pretas indeed arrived;
having gone to heaven in those divine palaces, they questioned that sage.
Through conversation with a Brahmin and by the proclamation of meritorious deeds,
the deceased are liberated from their sins and attain the supreme state.
Sūta said:
Having heard this narrative, Garuḍa trembled like a leaf of the holy fig tree; for the benefit of human beings, he questioned him once again.
