Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Five Pretas Concerning the Origin of the State of a Preta and Liberation Therefrom," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
(Chapter 23 of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*).
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of the Gods, what indeed do the *pretas* do when they are situated in the state of *piśācas*, or do they ever speak? Tell me that."
The Blessed One said:
I shall describe their true nature, their signs, and their dreams exactly as they are.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they indeed enter their own homes.
O Lord of Birds, the signs bestow stability upon the bodies of the Vāyus, and they cause those born of their own lineage who lie there to see [the truth]. GarP_2,23.3 //
There he goes with his own sons, his own wives, and his own kinsmen;
horses, elephants, bulls, and mortals are seen there with distorted faces.
But he who, having risen, perceives himself lying down in a distorted state and sees his own self as inverted— that one should know to be a creation of the *preta*.
For if in a dream two men are bound in various ways with fetters, and the deceased elder brother, appearing in disheveled attire, begs for food in the dream; GarP_2,23.6 //
In a dream, one whose food is being eaten may see someone—whether oneself or another—seize that food and flee; or, afflicted by thirst, one may drink water. (GarP 2.23.7)
In a dream, he mounts a bull and travels together with bulls;
he leaps up and goes into the sky, and he goes to a sacred ford while afflicted by hunger.
He who speaks with his own voice regarding a bull, a brahmin, a horse, a phallus, an elephant, a deity, a spirit, a ghost, or a night-stalker; ||| GarP_2,23.9 |||
Furthermore, O Lord of Birds, in the midst of a dream, one will certainly see various signs of a *preta* due to the affliction of a *preta*:
one's own wife, kinsman, son, or powerful husband, whether they are currently living or deceased. (GarP 2.23.10)
He who, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, begs from another even in a dream,
shall undoubtedly burn funeral cakes at a sacred ford (tīrtha) to purify himself from the defects of the deceased.
Or else, in a dream, one sees a son, a child, or an animal departing from the house; likewise, one sees a father, a brother, or a wife as if afflicted by the defects of the deceased.
O Lord of Birds, upon seeing these signs, one should announce the expiation;
having performed a bath at home or at a sacred ford, one should offer libations with water at the Śrīvṛkṣa tree.
One should offer black grains and worship to a master of the Vedas;
the wise person should perform the fire-oblation according to his ability and have the scriptures recited in their entirety.
For whoever, with faith, recites or even hears this description of the signs of a preta, the marks of a preta shall perish.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the State of the Preta, its Causes, its Signs, and the Means of Liberation Therefrom," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
*Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 24.
Garuḍa said:
"No one dies before their time; such is the teaching of the Vedas.
Why then does death come upon a king or even a learned Vedic scholar?"
That which was previously stated by the Brahmins as false is indeed seen to be so;
however, the statement spoken in the Vedas that "a human lives for a hundred years" [is true].
In the human world, within the region known as Bhārata-khaṇḍa, all castes— both the twice-born and those born of the lowest orders or among the Mlecchas— subsist.
That is not seen in the Kali age; why is that, O Lord? Please instruct us.
From the moment of conception, whether a child, an old man, or a youth, one meets with death.
Whether possessing wealth or destitute, delicate or handsome, unlearned or learned— a Brahmin or any other person— [is equal].
The man who is devoted to austerity, whose nature is yoga, who possesses great knowledge,
who delights in all forms of wisdom, who is illustrious, whose soul is dharma, and whose valor is incomparable—
all this arises without exception upon the surface of the earth.
Why does death come upon either a king or even a learned brahmin?
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Since you are my devotee and dear to me, listen to these secret words which destroy various lands."
Death, ordained by the Creator, departs swiftly taking [the life] with it;
therefore, O Lord of Birds, son of Kaśyapa of great splendor, I shall speak further.
It was declared by the Veda in ancient times that a human being lives for a hundred years;
yet, through the power of improper action, one perishes even quickly.
By the mere study of the Vedas, one does not follow the family tradition; through laziness, there is abandonment of duties and constant devotion to what is forbidden. (GarP 2.24.11)
Eating at various houses, as well as delighting in the fields of others—
through these and other such great faults, the exhaustion of one's lifespan occurs.
A Brahmin who lacks faith, is impure, is an atheist, has abandoned auspicious rites, and delights in malice toward others and falsehood— [one should avoid] his abode.
A king who does not protect, who is constantly devoid of dharma,
cruel, addicted to vices, foolish, and excluded from the teachings of the Vedas—
a king who oppresses his subjects is subject to the command of Yama.
They bring [the person] under the power of death, and thereafter he undergoes torment,
having abandoned his own actions as well as those which were his primary occupations.
He who is constantly devoted to the work of others, and a Śūdra who performs any service whatsoever without serving the twice-born, goes to the realm of Yama.
Whether among the highest, the lowest, or the middling, he is cooked in the world of Yama;
bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, study of scripture, and worship of the gods [are of no avail].
That day of men on which these are not practiced is wasted;
for the body is impermanent, unstable, without support, and born of the vital fluids.
In this body composed of food and water, I shall describe these qualities:
the food that is prepared in the morning certainly perishes by evening.
O Lord of Birds, what permanence can there be in a body nourished by such flavors, once one realizes that half of the body has already departed due to its own past actions?
A person should take the supreme medicine for the destruction of evil: is the body more [belonging] to the one who provides food, or rather to the mother who provided the seed? 24.21.
Whether it be for both [the gods and ancestors], or for the Lord, or even for a child, a fire, or a dog—
what supreme sacrifice can there be in that which is designated as worms, excrement, and ashes?
One must exert the supreme effort toward the destruction of sin;
for the sin accumulated over many births is indeed threefold.
When he attains human birth, then he suffers for everything;
remembering all his previous births, his mind becomes despondent.
Having observed the dwellings in the womb and likewise the destinies born of karma,
if one then dwells within a human belly, one becomes a sinner.
Among the beings born from eggs and the other modes of birth, wherever they may move,
there arise mental afflictions, physical diseases, the defilements, old age, and the transformation of form.
O best of birds, though liberated from dwelling in the womb, one who is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and has resorted to childhood does not know [the truth].
He who, even in youth, perceives while blinded by darkness is a partaker of liberation;
whether a child, an old man, or a youth, he meets death through the [karmic] deposit.
Whether possessing wealth or being destitute, whether delicate or ill-favored,
whether unlearned or learned— O Brahmins, such is the case for all other people as well.
The man who is devoted to austerity, whose nature is yoga, who possesses great wisdom,
who delights in great generosity, who is illustrious, whose soul is dharma, and whose prowess is incomparable—
he experiences neither pleasure nor pain without a human body.
Through the bonds of natural karma, a human being encounters death;
for five years after conception, one undergoes ripening through very slight sins.
Having exceeded five years [of age], one ripens through great sins;
because one fills the womb, even after death one comes and goes.
"By the power of that gift, though dead, he shall live as a mortal on earth for a long time.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Garuḍa spoke these words. *Garuḍa Purāṇa* 2.24.33.
Garuḍa said:
How should one perform the rites such as the offering of rice balls (piṇḍadāna) when a child has died,
or when those who have perished in the womb, up until the rite of tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa) for the infant?
"How, what, and by whom should it be given? What rite is prescribed at the end of life?
Having heard these words spoken by Garuḍa, Viṣṇu then replied.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
If the fetus of a woman miscarries or is lost,
the period of impurity lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained.
One who desires his own welfare should not do anything for him thereafter;
even when he has died, [the duty continues] until the tonsure ceremony of the child.
Milk food is to be given to children according to their capacity;
however, until the age of five, at which time the tonsure ceremony is performed, the cremation of the body is prescribed.
Milk should be offered as the auspicious food for children;
for one who has died at more than five years of age, however, the rites prescribed for their own caste should be performed.
O best of birds, one should perform all the rites, beginning with the water-pitcher and ending with the milk-rice offering; for he is indeed bound by the debt.
"For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
O tiger among birds, [this cycle] must indeed continue until the destruction of the body."
If one does not give to him what he desires, even though he belongs to a destitute family,
that person will become short-lived and impoverished, devoid of pleasure and devotion.
A mortal may undergo rebirth; therefore, [the gift] should not be given except for a child.
This verse is sung in the Purāṇa, and it appears clearly to me in every respect. (GarP 2.24.43)
Sweet food should be given as an offering, for the capacity to give is difficult to find;
likewise, the capacity to enjoy the meal is found in the case of excellent women, who possess the power of delight.
The power to give arises from spiritual excellence; it is not the fruit of meager austerity.
Through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through serving sacred fords one obtains happiness.
He who dies after speaking well is a wise man, the best among those who know the Dharma.
From taking what is not given one becomes poor; from the state of poverty one commits evil deeds;
through the power of evil one goes to hell, becoming poor once more and again an evildoer.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of Short Life and Death and the Last Rites for Children," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
— *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: 25.1.24.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Hereafter I shall declare the determination regarding men and women,
whether they be living or dead, or even those more than five years of age.
But when the fifth year is complete, the male child becomes firmly established;
he perceives all the sense faculties as well as the distinctions between form and formlessness.
Through the ripening of past karma, the killing and binding of living beings—
whether they be Brahmins and others or even those of the lowest castes— is certainly a sin that leads to death.
When the embryo is lost, no ritual is required; when the infant has died, milk should be given.
Furthermore, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and milk due to the calamity of its weakness.
On the eleventh or twelfth day, one should prescribe the rites for a boy, even without the bull sacrifice or the ritual for the bull,
and without the great gift-offering.
Food for princes and children, clothing, and ornaments—
for the child, the youth, or the old man, when he has died, there is indeed a funeral jar.
One should cast a child less than two months old, or one up to two years of age, upon the ground;
beyond that age, O best of birds, cremation of the body is prescribed.

According to all the scriptures, one is called an infant (*śiśu*) from birth until the eruption of teeth; a boy (*bāla*) until the tonsure ceremony (*āśikha*); and a youth (*kumāra*) from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjibandhana*).

How should one act regarding Śūdras and others? Since they are excluded from the investiture with the girdle (mauñjī), there is doubt; having omitted the ninth month from conception, [the period for initiation] lasts until the sixteenth year for a child.
Furthermore, the child is to be known as "para" (the other) until twenty-seven months;
until five years of age he is "kaumāra" (youth), and until nine years he is "paugaṇḍa."
A youth shall be sixteen years old; beyond that, one should designate him as being in his prime.
Even if he dies in the fifth year, whether he has been initiated or not, [he is considered a child].
One who desires the ten-piṇḍa rite should perform exactly what was previously described;
for due to the engagement in very little action and the bondage of very few sense objects, [this is sufficient].
As long as a living being is subject to accumulation and remains entangled in sense objects, he desires even the slightest activity regarding his body and clothing. (GarP 2.25.13)
Whatever may be the means of subsistence for someone, that very thing one desires to give here;
such are the sons born from the seed of Brahmā, who are beloved by the divine sages.
O bird, they are certainly punished by Yama and the messengers of Yama;
whether a child, an old man, or a youth, all embodied beings desire a jar [of water].
The embodied soul, being omnipresent here, always experiences pleasure and pain;
yet it eventually abandons that body, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
The person, though only the size of a thumb, is sustained by vital breath and possessed by hunger;
therefore, it is certain that gifts should be given when a child has died.
If a child who has not been consecrated with sacraments dies within five years of birth, one enjoys for five years the merit of whatever was given on his behalf;
however, if the death of the child occurs after five years have passed, [the fruit is lost].
Rites such as the release of a bull, excluding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,
and the sixteen *śrāddhas* should be performed when the twelfth day has arrived.
One should offer rice-balls with milk-rice and jaggery in due order,
as well as the offering of a water-pot and whatever other supplementary gifts there may be.
One should give food to a twice-born man, as well as great gifts and so forth according to one's ability;
and whatever gifts such as lamps may be given, this should always be done for one who is more than five years old.
O best of birds, before the vow, everything must be performed for the satisfaction of the deceased;
if it is not all done, he attains the state of a Mudgala.
Indeed, before the vow itself, one should first offer to the assembly of ancestors;
one should perform the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites with the utterance of *svāhā*.

With straight darbha grass and white sesame seeds, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīti), and performing the rite with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (apasavya), those who have performed [the rite] certainly attain the supreme goal.
Furthermore, having become long-lived, they are surely born again into their own family;
such a son bestows all happiness and increases the joy of his parents.
Just as space is indeed one, and just as the moon and sun appear as one [in the sky],
so too see all forms within jars and other objects as being distinct, yet equal to that [space].
In the same way, the Self should always behave toward all sons according to the nature each possessed previously at the union of the semen and the blood.
Through that application of his being, he takes on the form of a father and is born as the son of someone whose sons perform those same actions.
"From his father's side, he is someone exceptionally rich in beauty, a connoisseur of virtue, and devoted to charity;
there has never been anyone like him in this world, nor will there ever be."
The blind do not produce the blind, nor are the mute born from the mute;
the deaf do not come from the deaf, nor indeed does the learned come from the learned. Those who are worthy [of this] are not seen; listen to my words. (GarP 2.25.30)
Garuḍa said:

"The ten kinds of sons, beginning with the legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son born of the field (kṣetraja), are recorded in tradition; what then is the status of a son who is merely taken in, or the son of a female slave?"
Having fallen under the power of birth and death, what destiny does he attain who has neither a daughter,
nor a grandson, nor a son?
"How should his *śrāddha* rite be performed, and by what procedure should it be done?
The Blessed One said:
"By beholding the face of a son, one is released from the debt to the ancestors."
By the sight of a grandson, a person is liberated from the three debts;
through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, one attains endless worlds and reaches heaven.
A son who has been born in another family and provides only worldly enjoyment—
such a son should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules for his ancestors.
Other sons perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, not the *pārvaṇa*.
One born of a Brāhma-marriage elevates [the deceased], whereas one who has been "taken" (an adopted son) leads him downward.
Indeed, by performing the annual śrāddha, he is born into hell.
O bird, indeed all gifts should be given, except for the gift of food;
a son who has been formally adopted should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, not the *pārvaṇa*.
By offering the annual *śrāddha* to his father and mother, he is not defiled;
however, if he abandons the *ekoddiṣṭa* and performs the *pārvaṇa* instead, [he incurs fault].
He who has been seized, as well as those such as the sons of female slaves and others, shall lead both himself and his ancestors to the abode of Yama.
At a sacred ford, they should perform the ancestral śrāddha rite and give gifts to a twice-born man;
likewise, he who, having taken up a son, provides cooked food [for him].
A twice-born man should know that a *śrāddha* performed with the food of a Śūdra is in vain;
that *śrāddha* does not gratify the ancestors, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā). Knowing this, O best of those who go to heaven, one should abandon sons of low birth.
One born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Brāhmaṇa is considered the lowest, like a Caṇḍāla;
likewise, so is he who is born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a renunciant or from a Śūdra.
Know these two to be outcastes (caṇḍālas), O Lord of Birds: he who is born of a woman of the same lineage, and the son who, having fathered a child by a woman permitted for heaven, [is born of her].
Happiness is to be attained through good conduct; one of bad conduct goes to hell.
Even those born of low birth prosper in happiness if they possess good conduct.
Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, honored by hosts of Siddhas, and fanned by celestial nymphs with chowries of immortality,
he alone shall rescue even his hundred ancestors, as well as his kinsmen, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, who have been submerged in hell.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Funeral Rites for a Deceased Child and the Funeral Rites Performed by Sons— Whether Legitimate or Adopted," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharma-kāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa— 26]
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, best of gods, show compassion toward me and speak the truth:
at what time should the *sapiṇḍana* rite be performed for deceased living beings?"
From where do they go when there is sapinda-relationship, and what is the destination when there is no sapinda-relationship?
By what means is there sapinda-relationship between a man and a woman? You should explain this to me.
How do a woman and a man attain supreme oneness together?
While her husband lives, how can there be a *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for women? (GarP 2.26.3)

O Lord of the Gods, how do women go to the world of their husbands or to the heavenly world? How is the funeral rite (śrāddha) performed for one who ascends the funeral pyre, and how does the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) take place?
O Lord, for the benefit of the worlds, please graciously explain how the offering of the water-pot (ghaṭadāna) should be performed once the sapindikarana has been completed.
The Blessed One said: "O bird, I shall explain to you exactly how the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is performed;
O best of birds, I shall describe what a human being practices for the duration of a year."
Once the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed, he goes to the world of the ancestors;
therefore, the son must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father.
When the year is complete, one should perform the introduction of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-praveśana);
by the rule for the introduction of the rice-balls, his annual death-day rite (mṛtāhnika) becomes perpetual.
O tiger among birds, it is certain that at the end of the year there shall be a reunion of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Once the offering of the cake together with [the ancestors] has been performed, the deceased then attains the supreme goal;
having completely relinquished that name, he thereafter becomes part of the host of the ancestors.
Or one may reunite with one's great-grandfathers after three fortnights or six months,
having ascertained the auspicious occasions such as births and marriages, as well as those rites prescribed for one’s own lineage.
One should not perform a marriage while the householder is deceased;
nor should a mendicant accept alms until the sapindikarana rite has been performed.
Even within one's own lineage, one remains impure as long as the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) has not been offered;
O Lord of Birds, through that offering, the designation "preta" (ghost) ceases.
Because family customs are endless, because the lifespan of men is subject to exhaustion,
and because the body is unstable, the twelve-day period is commended.
Whether he is without the sacred fires or possesses them, one should perform the sapindikarana rite on the twelfth day.
The sages who perceive reality have declared that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed on the twelfth day, or after three fortnights, or six months, or even a year.
For one who has a son, an ekoddiṣṭa rite should never be performed;
rather, after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, it should be offered wherever [the rites] are prescribed.
In each of those cases, the triad [of rites] must be performed; otherwise, one becomes a killer of one's ancestors.
One who is incapable may perform the three with the *pārvaṇa* rite, as taught by the Sage.
Therefore, one should perform it day by day from the mouth of Pitāmaha;
because [the specific days and months] might be unknown, the pārvaṇa rite is thus prescribed.
For one whose body has not yet arisen, there is no giving together with the ancestors;
by these sixteen śrāddhas, the deceased is liberated and reborn.
One should not perform the sapinda-rite for one who has no son, nor even for women; and as long as she remains a devoted wife, one should never perform the sapinda-rite together with her.
In marriages such as the Brāhma and others, whatever woman has been consecrated here,
the rites of offering rice-balls and water for her must be performed by means of her husband’s lineage.
In marriages such as the Āsura and others, whatever maiden may have been wedded,
one should perform the rites of the rice-balls and the water-libation for her according to the *gotra* of her father.
The son must always perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father;
in the absence of a son, it shall be the wife, and in the absence of a wife, a uterine brother.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the nāndīmukha rite.
O Bird, for a man who is childless, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed by his younger brother, his son, or his wife, specifically for the sake of the eldest.
Manu has declared that among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son alone.
In the case of all those who are childless, the wife shall perform the sapindikarana rite;
or she may have it performed by the officiating priest (rtvij) or even by the family priest (purohita).
Having had his tonsure and initiation performed, he should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for his father;
he may utter the word *svadhā*, but he must not recite the syllables of the Veda.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a woman must be performed by three [relatives]: her husband and the others;
or by her paternal uncle, her brother’s son, or her younger uterine brother.
Whether before a year has passed, at the juncture [of the year], or when a full year has elapsed—
for those deceased ancestors who have been made *sapiṇḍa*, there shall be no separate ritual performance.
O child, once the sapindikarana has been performed, separate status is indeed censured;
he who offers a separate funeral cake (pinda) becomes a slayer of his father.
Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, separate status is no longer possible;
if a separate *piṇḍa* has been offered, one must perform the *sapiṇḍana* again.
He who performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite after having already performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* shall lead both himself and the deceased to the realm of Yama.
For a year, the offering of barley-gruel (yāvaka) should be performed by the wise [son] according to the name and lineage;
the water-pot and other items, as well as the daily meals and the various gifts,
should be offered to only one [deceased ancestor] once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has been completed.
O bird, having calculated the annual [oblation], food together with water should be given to a Brahmin, as well as a jar filled with water and other such items.
At the conclusion of that single alms-offering, his entire livelihood for the year is provided according to his own capacity;
possessing a divine body and seated in a celestial chariot, he goes happily to the abode of Yama.
While the father is still living, there is no sapindikarana for the son;
likewise, for women, there is no sapindikarana while the husband is alive. (Garuda Purāṇa 2.26.37)
On the fourth day, the devoted wife who has ascended the funeral pyre must perform on her husband's anniversary the rites such as the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) and other ceremonies.
Before the birth of a son, the daughter shall belong to the family of her husband;
after the birth of a son, she shall again go to the family of her father.
When the two wives ascend the funeral pyre together, their unity is eternal;
however, on the day known as the anniversary of his death, the son must perform the śrāddha for each separately.

If two childless persons should die on the same day, one should perform their separate śrāddhas on a single funeral pyre; however, the sapindikarana rite for the wife should be performed together with that of her husband.
Whether individually, as a collective unit, or as a couple together with the husband, one is not stained by great evils; this is my truthful word.
If a husband and wife have both met their death by ascending the same funeral pyre,
one should perform a single offering of cooked food, but offer the rice-balls separately.

In the eleventh month, one should perform the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), the sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased, the gift of water-pots and other items, and whatever great gifts (*mahādāna*) there may be; these should be performed separately for a year, whereby the deceased shall attain long-lasting satisfaction.
But for those who have died within the same lineage, whether they be women or men,
one should prepare a single sacrificial mound, yet perform the fire-oblation separately for each.

On the eleventh day, the śrāddha rite, the separate offering of rice balls (piṇḍas), and the feeding [of Brahmins] should be performed with a single cooking; it is censured for husbands and wives to have separate rites or for others to do so.
A son may perform the Śrāddha rites with a single cooking;
he should offer only one scattering of food (vikiro), yet he may offer many funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
This may be done at a sacred ford (tīrtha), during the dark fortnight, or even during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
When a woman, having approached her husband who is like a corpse, burns him,
the fire consumes his limbs but does not afflict her own self.
Just as the impurity of metallic ores is consumed when they are being smelted,
so too does a woman consume the body in a fire that is like nectar.
In the divine [state] and others, the person, possessing a divine body, becomes pure;
he is not burned at all by heated oil, iron, or fire.
Likewise, she who is united with her husband is never burned;
even when he has died, the inner self (antarātman) has attained oneness with him, though it too has perished.
If she dies elsewhere after abandoning union with her husband,
she does not go to the world of her husband until the dissolution of all beings.
Having abandoned even her mother and father, who were endowed with wealth and fortune,
she prospers in happiness for a long time by following after her deceased husband.
For a duration measured by three and a half million divine years,
he shall dwell forever in heaven together with the stars.
At the end of that [life], she moves through the world and is born into a family of wealthy people;
for that devoted wife, having attained great joy, dwells together with her husband.
A woman who does not thus unite with her husband in accordance with dharma will,
in birth after birth, be afflicted by suffering, ill-behaved, and unpleasant in speech.
A female mongoose, a house-lizard, or a two-headed lizard, having abandoned her own husband, becomes a follower of another man. (GarP 2.26.57)
Therefore, with every effort, a woman should serve her own husband—
whether he be dead or living— with her mind, her actions, and her speech.
Whether he is alive or even dead, she who commits a transgression against him shall become unfortunate and attain widowhood in birth after birth.
Whatever is offered with faith to the gods and to the ancestors, that fruit is obtained from the worship of one's husband; therefore, one should perform the honoring of the husband.
When this has been done, O best of birds, one shall dwell in the world of the ancestors for a long time;
as long as the sun and moon endure, so long shall one remain in heaven like a god.
Furthermore, having become long-lived, they are born into a noble family;
just as a woman devoted to her husband does not experience the suffering caused by her husband.
All of this has indeed been told by me to you, O Lord of Birds;
I shall now describe the specific [rite] that bestows happiness upon the deceased.
Everything performed on the twelfth day must be repeated until the *sapiṇḍana* ceremony;
one should always and constantly perform the monthly offerings of water-pots and food.
O bird, there is no performing of what has already been done, except for funeral rites;
if any man performs such [a rite], his previous merit perishes.
One should perform [the rite] again for the deceased; thus the departed spirit shall attain inexhaustible merit.
Every month, jars filled with water and accompanied by cooked rice should be offered.
O Tārkṣya, even if a son performs the *sapiṇḍana* rite before the completion of a year and before the offering of the *karaṇa* water,
he must nevertheless offer one ball of rice (*piṇḍa*) and a jar of water every month for a year.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Sapiṇḍana," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, within the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*. Tārkṣya said:

How do the pretas dwell here, and what is their appearance? O Lord, by which various fruits of karma do the great pretas and the piśācas exist? For the sake of compassion for all beings, tell me this, O Madhusūdana. (GarP 2.27.1)
"O Lord of Gods, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, tell me that gift by which one is released from the state of a preta, O auspicious one."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Well asked by you, O Tārkṣya, for the benefit of mankind indeed!
Listen attentively as I describe the characteristics of the departed."
For this is most secret of secrets and must not be told to just anyone;
yet, O mighty-armed one, because you are devoted, I shall tell it to you.
Long ago in the Tretā Yuga, O dear one, there was a king named Babhruvāhana in the beautiful city of Mahodaya; he was devoted to righteousness and possessed great strength.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, illustrious, devoted to the Brahmins, and esteemed by the virtuous;
he was endowed with good character, conduct, and virtues, and possessed of compassion and courtesy.
That king of great strength, ever devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, constantly protected his subjects like his own sons, meting out punishment to those who deserved it.
Once, that mighty-armed one, having gone out on a hunt with his army,
entered a dense forest filled with various kinds of trees.
Then, in the middle of the forest, the king saw from afar a deer in a place frequented by hundreds of tigers and resounded with the cries of various birds.
Pierced by that very firm arrow,
the deer took the shaft from him and vanished into the forest.
With that blood flowing from his armpit, the king followed him;
then, following the trail of the deer, he entered another forest.
With his throat parched by hunger, the king, fainting from exhaustion and heat,
reached a body of water and plunged into it along with his horse.
Having drunk that cool water, scented with the fragrance of lotuses,
Babhruvāhana then emerged from the pure water.
Having reached a banyan tree— cool-shaded, enchanting,
with great spreading branches, heart-pleasing, and resounded by flocks of birds— GarP_2,27.14.
Having reached that great tree, which stood like a raised banner for that entire forest, the lord of the earth sat down.
Then he saw a hungry ghost (preta), whose senses were agitated by hunger and thirst,
with hair standing on end, filthy, hunchbacked, emaciated, fleshless, and terrifying to behold.
With its feet consisting of bones bound together by sinews, it was running hither and thither,
surrounded on all sides by many other pretas.
Seeing that terrible and hideous sight, Babhruvāhana was struck with amazement;
and the preta, seeing the king who had arrived in that dreadful forest, was likewise amazed.
Then, becoming joyful in mind, he approached him;
at that time, O King, the Lord of the Pretas spoke these words to Tārkṣya.
I have abandoned the state of a preta and have attained the supreme goal;
through union with you, O mighty-armed one, there is no one more fortunate than I.
The king said:
"You are black-complexioned with a gaping mouth; you appear like a ghost (preta).
Out of affection for me, tell me truly how it is that you are thus."
Thus questioned by the king, he indeed related his entire story.
The preta said:
"O best of kings, I shall tell you everything from the beginning regarding the cause of my state as a preta; having heard it, you ought to show me compassion."
There was a city named Vaidiśa, endowed with every prosperity;
it was crowded with people from various regions, filled with diverse jewels,
possessed of manifold merits, and thick with various kinds of trees.
There I dwelt for a long time, always devoted to the worship of the gods;
know that I am a Vaiśya by birth, Sudeva by name.
The gods have been gratified by the oblation (havya), and likewise the ancestors by the ancestral offering (kavya);
and the Brahmins have been fully satisfied by me through various modes of giving.
I have indeed properly arranged marriages and alliances,
and I have bestowed gifts in many ways upon the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished.
All that, O dear one, has come upon me through fate and become fruitless;
I shall tell you how my meritorious deeds have likewise become useless.
"I have no lineage, dear father, nor friends, nor kinsmen;
indeed, I have no such friend who might perform my funeral rites."
"O best of kings, because of that, my state as a preta has become firmly established.
There are the eleventh-day rite, the three-fortnightly rite, the six-monthly rite, the annual rite, and other monthly rites; thus there are sixteen śrāddhas. (GarP 2.27.30)
O King, for him to whom these *śrāddha* offerings for the deceased are not given,
his state as a *preta* remains firmly established even if hundreds of other *śrāddhas* are performed.
Knowing this, O Great King, deliver me from the state of a preta;
for among all the social classes, the king is said here to be their kinsman.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, deliver me; I give this jewel-gem to you, so that, O best of excellent monarchs, there may be for me the attainment of auspiciousness.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, if you desire compassion for me,
quickly perform for yourself all the rites pertaining to the afterlife and this world.
The King said:
"How do beings here become *preta*s even when the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) have been performed?
And by what actions do they become *piśāca*s here? Tell me that."
The preta said:
"O best of kings, those who seize the property of the gods, the property of Brahmins, or the accumulated wealth of women and children, go to the womb of a preta."
Those who indeed consort with female ascetics, women of the same lineage, or those who are forbidden,
become great pretas who carry off lotuses.
Those who steal coral and diamonds, those who carry off garments,
as well as those who steal gold, when encountered face-to-face in battle— [they shall be destroyed].
Those men who are ungrateful, nihilistic, fierce, and likewise reckless; those who are devoid of the five sacrifices, yet devoted to great acts of giving; GarP_2,27.39 //
O King, those who commit treachery against their master, those who commit treachery against friends or Brahmins,
and those who commit sins at sacred fords, are born as pretas;
O Great King, it is through such acts that one is born into the preta realm.
The king said:
"How do you and they become liberated from this state of being a preta here?
And how should I perform the funeral rites for my own self?"
Tell me all of this: by what ritual procedure is that to be performed?
The preta said:
Listen, O Indra among kings, to the summary of the practice centered on Nārāyaṇa:
listening to the true scriptures, worship of Viṣṇu, and association with virtuous people. (GarP 2.27.42)
"I have heard that these lead to the destruction of the preta-rebirth;
therefore, I shall describe to you the worship of Viṣṇu, which destroys the state of being a preta."
O King, having procured two measures of gold, one should fashion an image of the divine Nārāyaṇa, adorned with all ornaments.

Covered with a pair of yellow garments and anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste, one should bathe her with various waters after performing the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), and then worship her.
In the east, one should worship the god Śrīdhara; in the south, Madhusūdana;
in the west, the god Vāmana; and in the north, Gadādhara.
Having worshipped Pitāmaha in the center, one should likewise worship the god Maheśvara separately according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, having circumambulated [the fire] and gratified the deities with ghee, curd, and milk in the fire, O King, he likewise [satisfied] the Viśvedevas.
Then, having bathed, with a disciplined mind and composed, the sacrificer performed his funeral rites for himself before Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rule.
One who has disciplined his self and is free from anger and greed should undertake all the *śrāddha* rites, as well as the ritual release of the bull.
To thirteen brahmins he gave garments, umbrellas,
sandals, rings, and pearls, along with vessels, seats, and food.
Water-pots containing both food and water should indeed be given for the benefit of the deceased;
furthermore, having given a gift of a bed, one should offer a water-pot for the deceased.
One should worship the name "Nārāyaṇa" enclosed within a *saṃpuṭa*;
by doing so according to the prescribed rite, one shall obtain the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions.
The King said:
How should one prepare the *pretaghaṭa* (the vessel for the departed), and by what ritual procedure should it be offered?
Speak for the sake of compassion for all, regarding this vessel that grants liberation from the state of a *preta*.
The preta said:
"Well asked, O Great King! I shall tell you; listen to me regarding that firm gift by which the state of being a preta may no longer exist."
The gift known as the "Vessel for the Pretas" destroys all that is inauspicious;
it is difficult for all the worlds to obtain, and it brings about the end of miserable rebirths.

Having fashioned a vessel made of refined gold, adorned with Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu along with the world-protectors, and containing a cavity filled with milk and clarified butter, bow down with devotion and give it to a Brahmin; what need have you for any other hundreds of gifts?
Brahmā is in the center, as well as Viṣṇu and the immutable Śaṅkara;
and upon his neck, one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) in order, starting from the east.
Having worshipped according to the rules, O King, with incense, flowers, and sandalwood,
one should then offer a golden pitcher containing milk and clarified butter.
This [offering] is superior to all other gifts and destroys great sins;
it should be performed with faith, O King, for the sake of averting the state of being a preta.
The Blessed One said:
While he, whose mind was thus restrained, was conversing with the deceased,
his army— crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots— arrived on his heels.
Then, when Bala had arrived, the preta gave the great jewel to the king,
and having paid homage and made his request once more, he vanished from sight.
Departing from that forest, the king also went to his own city;
having reached his city, he related all that had been spoken by the preta.
O bird, he performed the funeral rites and other ceremonies according to the rules;
by the gift of his merit, the deceased was liberated and went to heaven.
"Even a deceased ancestor attains a good rebirth through a funeral rite (śrāddha) offered by another;
how much more so, then, does a father go to a higher state when the rite is offered by his own son? This is truly marvelous! (GarP 2.27.65)
Whoever hears this meritorious history or causes others to hear it,
those two do not fall into the state of a preta, even if they are possessed of sinful conduct.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of the State of a Preta and the Means for its Cessation," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, specifically the dialogue between Babhruvāhana and the Preta.
— *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: 28.
Garuḍa said:
O Madhusūdana, for the sake of compassion toward all beings, tell me by what gift or meritorious deed one may be released from the state of a preta.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, for I shall proclaim the gift that quickly destroys all misfortunes.
Having fashioned a jar made of refined gold, one should endow it with Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava, together with the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Having prostrated with devotion before a Brahmin, give him a vessel filled with milk and clarified butter; what is the use of your hundreds of other gifts?
Garuḍa said: "O Lord, what has been told? Tell it to me in detail, O Lord:
the rites for the next world following the time of the soul's departure."
O Lord Janārdana, tell me, what is my duty in this saṃsāra? And how should men properly perform the rites pertaining to the afterlife?
O best of gods, how do the pretas come to have such massive bodies, fierce forms, and terrifying appearances? By what auspicious or inauspicious karmas do they become so?
"O Lord of Gods, by the fruit of what karma do piśācas come into being here? Tell me that, for I desire to know it."
Why is the fivefold jewel cast upon the ground, and from where does it come into the mouth?
Why are sesame seeds and *darbha* grass placed below, while the feet are positioned toward the south?
For what purpose is the mandala smeared on the ground with cow dung?
For what purpose is Viṣṇu remembered and the Viṣṇusūkta recited?
For what purpose do his sons and grandsons stand before him?
For what purpose is the offering of lamps, and for what purpose is the worship of Viṣṇu?
For what purpose does a sick person give gifts to the best of the twice-born?
And why does he ask forgiveness from his kinsmen, friends, and enemies?
For what reason are sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt, the seven grains, land, and cows given? (GarP 2.28.11)
And how does a living being die, and from where does one who has died go? And how does the *ativāha* body come to rest at that time?
The son should carry the Śaṃva on his shoulder, and the grandson is the giver of fire.
For what purpose, O God, Lord of Gods, is there an anointing with clarified butter? Why is it so? (GarP 2.28.13)
For what purpose should one recite the Yama-sūkta while carrying water toward the northern direction,
using a single garment and gazing at the solar disc?
One should place barley, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, and stones; one should chew nimba leaves;
and a man and a woman should exchange their garments, placing each other's above and below.
Having come to the house, food should be eaten together with those of the same lineage;
for what purpose should the son offer the nine rice-balls?
For what purpose is milk placed at a crossroads in a baked earthen vessel,
having tied three pieces of wood with a cord and positioned it at a four-way junction at night?
A lamp is offered every day throughout the year during the night;
for what purpose is the burning of water, and why is there conversation with one's own kinsmen?
O Blessed One, what occurs when nine balls of rice are offered during the *ativāha* rite?
How is the invocation of the gods and ancestors performed, and how is the *vāha* invoked?
O Lord, why is this performed, and for what reason should one cause the balls of rice to be given?
What is that which is given to him immediately after the offering of the funeral cakes?
And what is the purpose of the collection of the bones and the gift of the bed?

On the second day, how can there be a bath for a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires? On the fourth day, why should a ritual bath for removing impurity be performed by all people together on the tenth day?
Why should one bring shoulder-carriers home with oil and ointments?
They should also provide them with massages while they are resting on land or in water.
On the tenth day, one should offer that rice-ball (piṇḍa) with meat;
but why is there a rice-ball on the eleventh day, and how does the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) take place? || GarP_2,28.23 ||
Tell me, from where do these sixteen *śrāddhas* come that last for a year?
[They are] indeed three hundred and sixty, prompted by the offering of food and other such things.
And every day, food from a jar should be given for the satisfaction of the deceased;
for at the appointed time, O Lord, mortal man dies, being impermanent.
"I do not see any opening at all; how then did that living soul depart? Whither do the elements—earth, water, and likewise mind—go?"
"O Protector, tell me of fire, as well as wind and space;
and how do these five winds proceed toward attainment?"
Greed, delusion, and the other five, as well as thieves within the body—
thirst, desire, and egoism— whence do they depart, O Janārdana?
Whether it be merit or demerit, whatever good deed has been performed—
where do those various gifts go when the body has perished?
For what purpose is the *sapiṇḍana* performed, whether at the completion of a year or otherwise? With whom is the merging of the deceased joined, and what is the ritual procedure therein?
For those who have been cremated, those who have not been cremated, those men who have fallen upon the earth,
and whatever other beings there may be— what will become of them at the end?
Those who are sinful and of evil conduct, those who have attained the state of a Mudgala, the self-killer, the slayer of a Brahmin, the thief, and the betrayer of trust; GarP_2,28.32.
O Mādhava, what is the destiny of that Śūdra who drinks from a tawny cow, who recites a syllable of the Veda, or who wears the sacred thread? GarP_2,28.33 //

"When a Brahmin’s wife becomes possessed by a Brāhmaṇī, I am afraid of that sin; tell me about that, O Lord of the World. Since I have asked you all this, please speak for the benefit of the world. (GarP 2.28.34)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Questions Regarding the Fruits of Various Gifts and Rites Performed at the Time of Death and for the Benefit of the Deceased," in the *Pretakalpa* (Section on the Dead) of the *Dharmakāṇḍa* (Section on Dharma), within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* (Latter Section) of the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa— 29]
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Well asked by you, O blessed one, for the benefit of human beings indeed!
Listen with an attentive mind to everything concerning the rites for the deceased."
Free from the distinctions of desire, extracted from the Śruti and Smṛti,
that which has not been seen even by the gods led by Indra, nor by yogis who contemplate yoga.
"O child, this which is more secret than the secret has never been told to anyone anywhere;
for you are devoted, O illustrious one, so I shall tell it all to you."
"For one who has no son, there is no destination, nor indeed is there heaven;
by whatever means possible, the birth of a son must be accomplished."
A son may deliver [his ancestors] from hell if liberation is not found;
the cremation must be performed by the son, and the fire-offering must be given by the grandson.
With sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, the hut on the ground should indeed be made of clay;
and five jewels should be placed in the mouth, by which the life-force (*jīva*) flourishes.
One should smear the ground with cow dung and scatter sesame seeds and darbha grass upon it;
on that very spot, the afflicted person, being liberated, burns away all sin.
One who offers *darbha* roots leads [the deceased] to heaven; there is no doubt about this.
For those *darbha* blades on the ground that are joined with sesame seeds—of this there is no doubt.
Everywhere the earth is pure where no smear exists;
wherever a smear remains, it is purified by further smearing.
Yātudhānas, piśācas, and rākṣasas of cruel deeds—these enter the patient who is unstained [by sin] and liberated; of this there is no doubt.
The daily fire-sacrifice, as well as the ancestral rite and the washing of the feet of Brahmins—
these performed upon the ground without a mandala become fruitless.
On this earth, a sick person is never liberated without a maṇḍala;
for Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Hutāśana himself abide within the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
Whoever dies otherwise— whether a child, an old man, or even a youth—
he indeed goes to another womb and sports with the vital wind.
Just as iron mixed with copper undergoes a corresponding birth [as a hybrid],
so too for one who has become wind, there is neither the *śrāddha* rite nor the water-libation ceremony.
O Tārkṣya, these sesame seeds produced from my sweat are purifying;
through the gift of sesame, the Asuras, Dānavas, and Daityas are satisfied.
May white sesame seeds, black sesame seeds,
and sesame seeds resembling cow’s urine burn away the sins committed by me with my body.
A single drona of sesame seeds is equal to a drona of gold;
when given for the purpose of libations, gifts, or fire-offerings, it becomes inexhaustible.
Darbha grass is produced from the hair of Mallomā; sesame seeds arise from her sweat.
The deities are satisfied by gifts, and likewise the ancestors by the śrāddha rite.
Through the ritual application and by means of subsistence, Brahmā and the universe also [are sustained].
With the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (savya), Brahmā and the other deities attain satisfaction;
with it worn over the right shoulder (apasavya), the ancestors and the gods of the celestial realms are satisfied.
Brahmā is located at the base of the kuśa grass, Keśava in the middle of the darbha, and one should know Śaṅkara at the tip of the darbha; thus the three gods reside within the kuśa.
O Lord of Birds, Brahmins, mantras, kusha grass, fire, and tulasī do not become "worn-out offerings" (nirmālya), even when they are employed again and again.

The kusa grass in the funeral cakes, the floral remains from the gods, the Brahmins at a feast for the deceased, the mantras among Shudras, those who have fallen from their caste, and the fire upon the funeral pyre—[all these are impure]. // GarP_2,29.22 //
Tulasī, Brāhmaṇas, cows, Viṣṇu, and Ekādaśī, O Bird—
these five are indeed the vessels for the virtuous who are sinking in the ocean of worldly existence.
Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, the brāhmaṇa,
and the cow— this sixfold path bestows liberation in the boundless and difficult wilderness.
Sesame seeds, the three kinds of purifiers, darbha grass, and tulasī leaves—
these ward off the miserable state of one who is dying.
One should sprinkle the ground with water using *darbha* grass held in both hands;
at the time of death, one should place the *darbha* blades into the two hands of the afflicted person.
That man who is cast upon *darbha* grass while being encircled by *darbha* goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu, even if he is devoid of mantras.
He who dies on the ground at the root of *darbha* grass while holding *darbha* in his hand,
being purified by this expiation, [is freed] from the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
Standing upon a layer of darbha grass on ground smeared with cow dung,
one dispels all evil through the gift given there.
Salt is that divine essence which grants all desires to men;
for, without salt, all other food-flavors do not become intense.
And because this salt flavor has originated from the body of Viṣṇu, it is dear to the ancestors, auspicious, and therefore bestows heaven.
Yogins especially praise the gift of salt for Brahmins,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and the Śūdra class.
When the life-breaths of the afflicted depart upon the surface of the earth, salt should then be given; it is the opening of the door to heaven.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Necessity of Giving Sons, Darbha Grass, Sesame, Tulasi, Cows, Land, Cloth, Copper Vessels, and Other Items in the Rites for the Deceased," within the *Dharmakāṇḍa* of the *Pretakalpa*, in the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 30.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to the supreme secret, the most excellent gift among all gifts.
It is the supreme among all gifts, and the highest secret of the dwellers of heaven.
One great gift should be given, namely the most excellent of cotton cloths;
by giving which, the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar are pleased in their respective order.
All the deities, beginning with Brahmā, shall obtain satisfaction from this rite;
this great gift should be bestowed for the sake of the liberation of the deceased.
He shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra, and thereafter he shall become a king here on earth—
handsome, fortunate, eloquent, illustrious, and of incomparable valor.
Having conquered the realm of Yama, O Tārkṣya, he goes to heaven.
Whoever gives a cow, sesame seeds, land, or gold to a twice-born man,
his sin accumulated over lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Sesame seeds and cows are a great gift that destroys even the most heinous sins;
these two are to be given to a Brahmin, never to one of another caste.
A gift consisting of sesame seeds, cows, or land is given only to one's own kin;
never to others of different castes, nor to those who are to be supported.
Likewise, one should give unreserved gifts to those who must be supported and to women;
in the case of the afflicted or during an eclipse, a twofold gift is especially distinguished.
A gift given to the afflicted takes effect at that very moment.
But what is given again to one who is still living reaches him even if he has not been consecrated;
this is true, truly true, and again true: that which is given to one whose faculties are impaired.
And whatever the son rejoices in, that gift becomes infinite;
therefore, whether it be a son or anyone else, one should give for as long as he lives,
since by doing so the deceased attains a vehicle and likewise enjoys pleasures.
When one is unwell at the time of death, or when the body has fallen and remains upon the earth,
there shall be satisfaction for the soul through the subsequent offering of food.
When a gift is given to one who is lame, blind, or one-eyed, or even to one whose eyes are only half-opened,
and when *darbha* grass is spread over sesame seeds, that gift is said to be inexhaustible.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt,
as well as the seven grains, land, and cows— each one of these is traditionally held to be purifying.
The King of Dharma is pleased by the gift of iron and other metals; by the offering of sesame seeds, he is satisfied;
and when salt is given, there is no fear of Yama.
By the gift of cotton, there shall be no fear from living beings;
cows rescue a man from the three kinds of sins.
From the gift of gold one attains happiness in heaven; from the gift of land one becomes a king;
and by the gift of both gold and land, there shall be no suffering in hell.
All the messengers of Yama, who are as terrifying as Yama himself,
all go forth as bestowers of boons, gratified by the seven kinds of grain.
By the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, the supreme goal is attained.
All this has been told to you: the goal that is reached by mortals.
Therefore, they praise a son who, by his father’s command, gives [the earth] to him;
for seeing his father standing upon the ground with eyes only half-opened, he offers it.
At that time, whatever son causes all kinds of gifts to be given shall be distinguished by his performance of the *gayā-śrāddha*; such a son is the delighter of his lineage.
When he has fallen from his own station, his sons must then exert effort for the sake of their father who is lacking [in merit]; they are the ones who deliver their father.
What is the use of giving many gifts? One should perform the funeral rites for one's father; the great horse-sacrifice does not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
That righteous son is indeed highly honored even by the gods,
he who causes gifts to be given on behalf of his afflicted father on this earth.
One should give a gift of iron with the hand joined to the ground;
one will not encounter the terrible Yama, nor shall one go to his abode.
The axe, the pestle, the staff, the sword, and likewise the dagger—
these are seen in the hands of Yama for those who have committed evil deeds.
Therefore, one who is afflicted by illness should give iron to a Brāhmaṇa;
this gift is proclaimed for the satisfaction of Yama’s weapons.
Those who are in the womb, as well as infants, youths, and the elderly—
by these specific gifts, they may burn away their own sins.
The Churiṇas, Śyāma and Śabala, the Ṣaṇḍas and Mārka, the Udumbaras,
and the Śabalas and Śyāmadūtas— these are pleased by the gift of iron.
Sons, grandsons, kinsmen, those of the same lineage, and friends likewise do not give gifts for one who is afflicted by disease; for they are equal to slayers of Brahmins.
Listen now to the destiny of one who has attained the state of the five elements;
moreover, the *ativāha* preta shall obtain the merit [of his deeds] after a year.
The triad of fires, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three immortals,
the three times, the three junctions of the day, the three castes, and the three powers.
From the feet upward to the waist, Brahmā presides;
from the navel to the neck, Hari resides within the body of a human being.
Īśāna, the Great Lord, both manifest and unmanifest, resides in the head;
he is the single form whose three parts are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara.
I am the vital breath residing within the body in the fourfold collection of beings;
I bestow upon them righteousness and unrighteousness, intellect, pleasure and pain, and what is done and left undone.
Having established the growth of a living being as it was previously infused into its vital points (*marmans*),
I alone thus impel all living beings toward their actions; and so,
living beings certainly go to heaven, hell, or liberation.
Whether they reside in heaven or in hell, there shall be nourishment for them through the śrāddha;
therefore, a wise person should perform the three kinds of śrāddhas.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf,
Rāma [Dāśarathi], Rāma [Bhārgava], Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki— these ten names should always be remembered by the wise. (GarP 2.30.37)
Living beings go to heaven in happiness, and when they fall from heaven,
those humans who were endowed with compassion and courtesy, having obtained happiness and wealth,
shall live for a hundred autumns, enriched with sons, grandsons, and riches.
One should give gifts to the sick and cause the worship of Viṣṇu to be performed;
likewise, one should mutter the eight-syllabled mantra or the twelve-syllabled mantra.
One should worship with white flowers and food offerings cooked in ghee,
as well as with perfumes and incenses prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and Manu.
Viṣṇu is the mother, Viṣṇu is the father, and Viṣṇu is one's own kinsmen and relatives;
what use have I for that dwelling where I do not behold Viṣṇu?
Viṣṇu is in the water, Viṣṇu is on the land, and Viṣṇu is on the peak of the mountain;
even amidst the mass of flaming garlands, it is Viṣṇu—the entire world is permeated by Viṣṇu.
We are the waters, we are the earth, we are the darbha grass, we are the sesame seeds;
we are the cows, we are the king, we are the wind, and we are all living beings.
We are gold, we are grain, we are honey, we are clarified butter;
we are the Brahmins, we are the gods, and we are Śambhu, Bhūḥ, and Bhuvaḥ.
I am the giver, I am the receiver, I am the sacrificer, I am the sacrifice;
I am the taker, I am Dharma, for I am indeed the earth and the water.
O bird, one should apply the mind to righteousness and unrighteousness through auspicious and inauspicious actions;
whatever action is performed anywhere is acquired in a previous birth.
I shall bestow my mind upon Dharma, and likewise upon Adharma;
he too inflicts torment upon Dharma, yet I grant him liberation.
O Tārkṣya, at the end [of the journey], the Vaitaraṇī is said to exist for the benefit of human beings;
having crossed over that river, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu, leaving behind the flood of his sins.
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, in youth, and in old age— whatever sin was done in all stages of life, even in other births.
Whatever action was performed by deed, mind, or speech during the night, likewise at dawn, at midday and afternoon, or during the two twilights;
Having given even once a Kapila cow that fulfills all desires, one shall,
at the time of death, deliver oneself from the accumulation of sins.
May cows be before me, behind me, and likewise at my sides;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
That goddess Lakṣmī, who belongs to all beings and who resides within the gods— may she, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Gifts," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 31,
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Those men who are joined with evil go to the abode of Yama;
however, for men, that which is given in my presence shall yield infinite fruit.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for as many years as there are atoms in that land;
and those who give sandals go forth mounted upon horses.
Due to the merit of giving umbrellas, those hungry ghosts are never burned by the heat of the sun through the exertion of travel; indeed, they wander happily on the road.
For whomsoever one gives food, by that [act] he shall be nourished.
In darkness that is most terrible, formless, and devoid of any visible mark,
men proceed by means of illumination alone through the gift of a lamp.
The offering of a lamp should indeed be given for the sake of happiness during the months of Āśvina, Kārttika, or Māgha, on the anniversary of one's death, or on the fourteenth lunar day.
And men should offer [this] every day on a very difficult path,
even for as long as a year, out of a desire for the happiness of the deceased.
The pure-souled man shines within his family; he attains radiance.
That man who gives the gift of a lamp becomes composed of light and is worthy of worship.

In a temple, one should place a lamp facing east for a member of the twice-born caste, and facing south for a deceased ancestor; having consecrated it with water, one should ensure it remains very steady.
In this regard, there are thirteen verses accompanied by all ritual offerings;
whoever, while still living, gives them here for the sake of a deceased person or for his own sake,
he goes upon the Great Path, free from great suffering.
Whatever seat, vessel, and food is given to a twice-born man, if he does not eat it with pleasure, he will not proceed easily on the path because of that. (GarP 2.31.11)
By the gift of a water-pot, one who is thirsty drinks water.
A vessel, a gift of clothing, a flower, and a finger-ring—
these eleven things should be given for the sake of the liberation of the deceased from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Thirteen words such as these should be offered according to one's ability by one desiring the welfare of the deceased; thus that deceased person shall be gratified. (GarP 2.31.14)
By giving food, sesame seeds, thirteen water-pots, a finger-ring, and a pair of garments, she goes to the supreme goal. (GarP 2.31.15)
He who bestows a horse, a boat, or even an elephant upon a Brahmin enjoys the corresponding happiness in accordance with its greatness.
He who gives a buffalo wanders through various worlds;
the mother of Yamaputra, the buffalo, bestows a happy rebirth.
Betel and flowers should be offered to the servants of Yama to increase their joy;
being thus gratified, they all cause no suffering in that place.
They say that gifts of cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold should be given according to one's own capacity.
Whatever person should offer a water vessel made of clay for the sake of the deceased,
that human obtains the fruit of offering a thousand vessels of water.
The messengers of Yama— extremely fierce, terrifying, and dark-brown—
do not frighten him once the gift of clothing has been made.
Indeed, one who is traveling on a path, afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue,
will certainly become happy through the practice of giving water from a jar.
A bed provided with a southern-facing orientation, equipped with weapons and garments,
and accompanied by a golden image of the Lord of Fortune (Śrīpati), should be given to a Brahmin for his welfare;
thus, being liberated from the state of a preta, he rejoices together with the gods.
This, O Tārkṣya, has been told to you regarding the gift arising from the funeral rites;
now I shall describe another matter: the entry into another body.
For a living being born in the world of death, death is indeed certain;
O scorcher of foes, one who dies shall go according to one's own dharma.
O Lord of Birds, for living beings who have died in former times,
this wind, having become subtle, issues forth from the circle of the mouth.
Through the nine gates, the hairs, and the cavity of the palate of people,
the life-force certainly departs through the anus in the case of the most sinful.
And after the Lord of Maruts has departed, the body falls;
struck by the wind, it falls indeed like a tree that is without support.
Earth dissolves into earth, and likewise water into water;
fire dissolves into fire, and wind into wind;
and space dissolves into space within Śaṅkara, who is all-pervading.
In that regard, O Tārkṣya, desire, anger, and the five sense organs—
these are declared to be the thieves dwelling within the body.
For desire, anger, and egoism—of which the mind is the leader—are present right there;
and this Time, accompanied by merit and demerit, is the destroyer.
The very nature of the world is fashioned by one's own karma;
furthermore, a person goes to another body according to their good and evil deeds.
Endowed with the five sense faculties and together with all objects of perception,
he enters a new body, just as a householder enters a new house when his old one has been burnt down.
Those elements which reside within the body and give rise to all constituent parts—
this body consists of six sheaths, and its elements are derived from those of the mother and father.
O Tārkṣya, in that same way, all the bodily winds of living beings, as well as urine, feces, and whatever other diseases arise from their conjunction, would come into existence. (GarP 2.31.35)
Bone, semen, and likewise sinew are burned along with the body;
this, O Tārkṣya, has been described to you as the destruction of all embodied beings.
Furthermore, I shall describe to you how their body comes to be:
it has a single pillar, bound together by tendons, and supported by two columns.
The tiny body is endowed with the sense organs and possesses nine gates;
it is assailed by sensory objects and agitated by desire and anger.
The city known as the person is filled with passion and hatred, is extremely difficult to cross due to the fortress of craving, and is ensnared by the net of greed. (GarP 2.31.39)
Endowed with these qualities is the body of all embodied beings;
within it abide all the deities and the fourteen worlds.
Those men who do not know the self are considered to be like beasts;
thus have I explained to you this fourfold body.
In the past, eighty-four hundred thousand types of birth were manifested:
those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb.
O sinless one, all this that I was asked by you has been explained.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Fruits of Giving and Entering Another Body," in the Pretakalpa of the second part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—Chapter 32.
Tārkṣya said:
How is a living being produced within the fourfold collection of elements: skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, bone, and life? GarP_2,32.1 //
The feet, the hands, as well as the private parts, the tongue, the hair, the nails, the head,
the joints, the channels, and likewise many various kinds of lines.
Desire, anger, fear, shame, the mind, joy, pleasure, and pain—
[this body] is variegated, perforated, and enveloped by a manifold net.
I consider this world to be a magician’s trick within the ocean of essence-less saṃsāra;
who here, O Hṛṣīkeśa, is the creator in this saṃsāra so crowded with suffering?
The illustrious Viṣṇu said:
I shall declare the supreme, most secret determination of this treasury,
by the mere knowledge of which omniscience is attained.
Well asked by you, O Vainateya, regarding the cause of life in this world with compassion; listen now with a one-pointed mind.
And during the fertile period of women, the first four days should be avoided,
because in ancient times, within that period, the sin of killing a Brahmin arising from Vṛtra [was present].
Brahmā, having rescued him from Śakra, gave him a fourth part;
his face was not seen as long as his body remained [in that state].
On the first day she is a Cāṇḍālī; on the second, a Brahmin-slayer;
on the third, she is to be known as a washerwoman; on the fourth day, she becomes pure.
Within seven days of performing the worship, she becomes fit for the ancestors and the gods;
however, the embryo conceived within those seven days arises from impurity.
At the time of conception, whatever kind of mental conceptualization arises in the minds of the parents, such is the birth of the embryo that occurs; of this there is no doubt.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, avoiding the first seven nights, one should approach [one's wife] on the even nights.
It is commonly declared that women have sixteen nights of the season;
if the embryo remains within her during the fourteenth night, [it results in a male child].
There a virtuous son, a treasure-house of merit and fortune, shall be born;
that night, O Lord of Birds, cannot be obtained by ordinary people.
Generally, conception occurs here within eight days;
on the fifth day, women should be given sweet food to eat.
One should avoid from afar that field which is pungent, alkaline, sharp, and hot; for it is a vessel for medicinal herbs, yet its seed is like nectar.
Having sown [seeds] therein, a person who is their master shall obtain the fruit properly;
and one should avoid the sun's heat upon it, practicing only coolness.
Equipped with betel, flowers, and sandalwood paste, and wearing clean garments,
a man, having taken dharma to heart, should lie down upon a comfortable bed.
Whatever conceptualization of the mind a person has at the time of conception,
a being enters the womb with the arising of a nature corresponding to that.
From the union of semen and blood, the formation of a mass arises;
the living being grows within the womb like the lord of stars in the sky.
For consciousness, in the form of a seed, is eternally established within the semen;
when desire, the mind, and the semen attain a state of unity, [then conception occurs].
Then the man attains a state of liquefaction within the womb of the woman;
if there is an excess of blood, a female is born, and if there is an excess of semen, a male is born.
When the semen and blood are in equal proportion, the embryos attain the state of being eunuchs;
after a day and night it becomes a *kalala*, and after five days it becomes a *budbuda*.
On the fourteenth day, flesh arises, accompanied by the mixed elements;
on the twentieth day, the flesh becomes solid, and the embryo grows gradually.
On the twenty-fifth day, strength and nourishment arise;
likewise, when the month is complete, one should maintain the five principles.
When two months have passed, the skin and fat are produced;
marrow and bones in three months, and hair and fingernails in the fourth.
The ears, the nostrils, and the chest are formed in the fifth month;
the throat-passage and the abdomen in the sixth; and the private parts and so forth in the seventh month.
Then, after eight months, the embryo is complete with its major and minor limbs;
in the eighth month, the living soul moves repeatedly within the womb of the nurse.
When the ninth month has arrived, the vital energy of the one staying in the womb becomes firm.
Upon the exhaustion of that stay in the womb, medical treatment arises for him;
he is then born as either a woman, a man, or a neuter.
It possesses the three powers, has large eyes, is endowed with the six sheaths,
is equipped with the five sense organs, and is adorned with ten channels.
He who knows that which is endowed with the ten qualities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a knower of yoga:
marrow, bone, semen, flesh, hair, blood, and likewise strength. (GarP 2.32.31)
This physical aggregate of a living being consists of the six sheaths and is composed of the five elements;
in the ninth or tenth month, it is born as one composed of the five elements.
Drawn forth by the winds of birth, overwhelmed by agony,
and nourished by the *suṣumṇā* channel, he remains in the womb of the woman in great haste.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
afflicted by these elements and bound by the ligaments of sinews, [the soul remains].
These seven, situated within the channels (nāḍī), are declared to be the fundamental constituents:
skin, bone, channels, body hair, and flesh as the fifth.
"O Lord of Birds, O Kāśyapa, these five qualities of the earth have been described by me; now hear how water likewise possesses five qualities."
Saliva, urine, semen, marrow, and blood as the fifth—these are declared to be the five qualities of water; they should be understood with diligence.
Hunger, thirst, as well as sleep, laziness, and lust—
O Tārkṣya, these are declared by all yogis to be the five qualities of fire (tejas).
Passion and hatred, as well as shame, fear, and likewise delusion—
this, O Tārkṣya, is said to be the fivefold group born of wind.
Contraction, running, leaping, extension,
and the fifth, cessation— these are declared to be the five functions of the wind (vāyu).
Sound, thought, profundity, hearing, and the transition into truth—
these five qualities of space should be known with effort, O Tārkṣya.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose are the organs of cognition;
the two hands, the two feet, the anus, and the genitals are the organs of action.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Gajajihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Yasā.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
these ten principal channels are situated within the center of the body.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
Thus these ten vital airs (vāyu) have been described, which are well-established within bodies;
they alone provide nourishment for all embodied beings from the food that has been consumed.
The vital wind, the giver of life, leads [the breath] through all the joints in the body;
as soon as food is eaten, it is divided into two parts by the wind.
Having entered the cave properly, he placed the food and the water separately;
he placed the water above the fire and that food upon the water.
The vital breath itself is below the fire; one should gently blow upon that fire with the wind.
