Blown by the wind, the fire separates the waste from the essence.
Through the twelve impurities, the dross is separated from the body and becomes distinct:
the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, navel, skin, and anus.
For these nails are indeed a locus of impurities, as are feces and urine;
this body, arising from the union of semen and blood, is known as the sixfold sheath.
Likewise, there are thirty-two million hairs, together with an additional half-million;
his teeth are said to be thirty-two in number, O son of Vinatā, according to the general tradition.
There are seven hundred thousand hairs and twenty nails;
one thousand palas of flesh are generally situated within the body.
One hundred palas of blood, one hundred palas of *tārkṣya* (bile), and ten palas of fat were indeed known by the ancients; the skin is equal in measure to that [fat].
The marrow is twelve palas, the great blood is three palas;
the semen should be known as two kuḍavas, and the blood is recorded as one kuḍava.
Phlegm is six [parts], as are the feces and urine according to their respective measures;
indeed, the bones are said to exceed three hundred and sixty.
Thus has the *piṇḍa* been fully explained; now we shall describe its manifestation (*vaibhava*).
For happiness, suffering, fear, and security are indeed obtained through action alone.
The wind draws [the fetus] out from the womb with its face downward and feet upward;
having placed the palms of its hands against the sides of the knees, it grows.
The two thumbs are placed above, the fingers of the hands are at the knees,
the eyes are on the back of the knees, and the nose is between the knees.
In this way, the being situated within the woman's womb undergoes gradual growth;
the bones attain solidity, and it lives by means of what is eaten and drunk.
There, a channel named Vāpyāyanī is fixed at the navel;
in women, it becomes attached to the cavity of the intestines.
Thus, what has been eaten and drunk by women enters into the womb;
nourished by those [substances], that living being attains growth.
There, many memories arise in him regarding the various states of cyclic existence;
consequently, being tormented here and there, he comes to feel world-weariness.
"I shall never do this again; as soon as I have eaten here, I will strive in such a way that I may not conceive a womb."
Thus reflecting, the living being indeed recalled hundreds of births that had been previously experienced, whether as gods or as human beings.
Then, in the course of time, as the creature turns head-downwards,
it is born in the ninth or even the tenth month.
As he is emerging, he is tormented by the wind belonging to Prajāpati;
then, oppressed by suffering, he emerges while wailing.
Emerging from the belly, he experiences an unbearable fainting;
then, endowed with the pleasure of the touch of wind, he regains consciousness.
Then the deluding Māyā of Viṣṇu seizes him;
with his mind bewildered by that, he suffers a fall from knowledge.
Then, having lost its knowledge while in the state of a child,
the living being subsequently attains the stage of childhood, youth, and even old age.
Furthermore, in that same way, a human being undergoes death and birth;
consequently, he wanders in this wheel of saṃsāra like a waterwheel.
At times a man attains heaven, and at times he goes to hell;
he experiences both heaven and hell as the fruit of his own actions.

O best of the twice-born, when one has experienced [the fruits of] karma in heaven or in hell, one returns to the earth after that experience is nearly exhausted, having traveled there with little effort.
This is a great suffering in the hells, which even those dwelling in heaven perceive: that they do not rejoice here, being cast down by the denizens of hell.
Even in heaven there is incomparable suffering, for from the very moment of ascent, the thought dwells in the mind: "I shall fall."
Beholding even those who have gone to hell, one experiences great suffering;
thus, day and night, I am restless with the thought, "I too shall go to such a fate."
There is great suffering in dwelling in the womb; for one being born, there is the pain of passing through the birth canal; and once born, there is suffering indeed in both childhood and old age.
The connection with desire, envy, anger, and the like is difficult to endure even in youth;
old age is like a bad dream, and at death there is intense suffering.
And being dragged by the messengers of Yama, he goes downward even into hell;
furthermore, there shall be birth from a womb, and likewise death, which is difficult to overcome.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, living beings are whirled around like a water-wheel;
bound by their former fetters, they are pierced again and again.
O son of Vinatā, there is no happiness whatsoever for a bird in a realm crowded with hundreds of sufferings; therefore, men should strive for liberation.
All this has been explained regarding how the formation of the embryo occurs;
I shall now speak to your question concerning the sequence, for you have an interest in it.
Garuḍa said:
"I have received the answer to the two great questions posed in the middle;
let an answer also be provided for the third question."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
You have asked what must be done by one who is dying;
listen, I shall tell you the answer that has been spoken there in brief.
Having recognized that a person’s death is imminent, one should then bathe them with cow urine,
cow dung, good earth, water from sacred fords, and water infused with kuśa grass.
Then, having put on two clean, pure, and auspicious washed garments,
one should first spread out darbha grass and scatter it with the tips pointing toward the south.
One should place sesame seeds there upon ground smeared with cow dung.
Or else, O Lord of Birds, one should place gold in the mouth [of the image] with its head facing either east or north;
there, the Śālagrāma stone and the Tulasī plant should also be present.
Furthermore, one who is to be instructed should, in his presence, light a lamp of clarified butter and likewise perform the recitation: "Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva."
First, having uttered the *praṇava*, worship and the offering of gifts are prescribed;
then, one should duly honor Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship with prostrations, meritorious hymns of praise, meditation, and yoga,
and by giving gifts to Brahmins as well as to the poor and the helpless.
One should withdraw the sense of "mine" regarding sons, friends, wife, fields, grain, wealth, and so forth, while remembering the feet of Viṣṇu in one's heart.
If one is in a state of extreme distress, then his sons and others should recite the Puruṣasūkta aloud while he is dying.
All this has been told to you regarding what must be done when death is imminent;
I shall now tell you in brief the fruit of all this.
Through bathing, one attains purity, and from that, the removal of impurity;
thereafter comes the remembrance of Viṣṇu, and from the knowledge of Him, the bestowal of all fruits.
A bed of *darbha* grass leads the afflicted person to heaven, without a doubt;
and a bath performed with scattered sesame seeds and *darbha* grass becomes equivalent to a sacrificial rite.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and likewise Agni attend upon it in the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
O bird, if a man’s evil is slight, he goes to the highest world with his head turned toward the east or the north in this body.
When the five jewels are released into the mouth, knowledge sprouts within the living being:
Tulasī, Brahmins, cows, Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, and the bird (Garuḍa).
For men sinking in the ocean of worldly existence, there are these five very rafts:
Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, the Gītā, Tulasī, and brahmin-cows.
In this essence-less and difficult saṃsāra, the six-syllabled mantra that bestows devotion—
“Namo bhagavate vāsudevāya”— is what a person should mutter.
One shall attain union [with the Divine] preceded by the syllable Oṃ; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, through worship, one attains my world and proceeds from there to heaven.
In the absence of bondage, yet in the presence of the sense of "mine," knowledge arises from the Puruṣasūkta;
for whichever of these means is predominant, O Kāśyapa.
Understand that the respective fruits also become superior;
these should be given according to one's capacity, so that he may always be pleased.
All this fruit regarding bathing and other rites has been recounted by me to you;
whatever qualities exist in the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa), those are established within the body.
The netherworlds, the mountains, the worlds, as well as other continents and oceans,
and all the planets beginning with the Sun, are situated within the body.
One should know that the region below the feet is Tala, and likewise, the region above the feet is Vitala;
know that Sutala is at the knees, and Mahātala is in the region of the thighs.
Likewise, the wise one should perceive Talātala in the thighs, Rasātala in the region of the genitals, and Pātāla situated in the hips, starting from the feet.
One should know Bhūrloka in the middle of the navel, Bhuvarloka above that,
Svargaloka in the heart, and likewise Maharloka in the region of the throat.
One should place Janaloka in the region of the mouth, Tapoloka on the forehead, and Satyaloka in the great aperture; thus [are] the fourteen worlds.
Meru is situated in the triangle, Mandara in the lower corner;
Kailāsa is in the south, and Himācala is on the left side.
Niṣadha is in the upper portion, Gandhamādana is in the south,
and Malaya is on the left line; these seven are the principal mountain ranges.
Jambūdvīpa is situated in the place of the bones; Śākadvīpa is established in the marrow;
Kuśadvīpa is situated in the flesh; and Krauñcadvīpa is located in the veins.
Śālmalidvīpa is situated in the skin, Plakṣa in the collection of body hair, and Puṣkaradvīpa resides in the nails; following these are the oceans.

Likewise, the ocean of salt-water (Kṣāroda) resides in the urine; the ocean of milk (Kṣīroda) resides in the bile; the ocean of wine (Surodadhi) resides in the phlegm; and the ocean of clarified butter (Ghṛtasāgara) resides in the marrow.

One should know the ocean of taste (rasodadhi) to be in the sense of taste, and the ocean of curd (dadhisagara) in the blood; the sweet ocean (svādūda) is located in the region of the uvula, and the ocean of the womb (garbhoda) is situated in the semen.
The Sun is situated in the nāda-cakra, and the Moon in the bindu-cakra;
Mars is to be known as residing in the eyes, and Mercury is remembered to be in the heart.
One should know that Jupiter is situated in the place of Viṣṇu; Venus is established in [the place of] Śukra;
Saturn is stationed in the place of the navel; and Rāhu is always situated in the mouth.
The planet Ketu is situated in the region of the anus; thus the mandala of the planets within the body is declared to be distributed from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Those who are born in saṃsāra certainly die;
they suffer from fierce hunger and thirst, as well as from burning sensations and fainting.
Where these fierce afflictions arise, they are indeed born from the stings of scorpions;
and at the time of their fullness, the destruction of all embodied beings occurs.
For those who have gone to the world of Yama run on and on through the midst of heated sand and into the midst of blazing fire.
Seized by their hair and dragged away by the servants of Yama, O Tārkṣya,
are those most wicked and base ones who are utterly devoid of compassion and righteousness.
"These dwell in the world of Yama within a hut; no [new] birth occurs there.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, a living being is born in the mortal realm through its own karmas."
For those who are born in saṃsāra certainly die; there is no doubt regarding their lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death itself.
For these five are created while the embodied being is still in the womb;
by karma a creature is born, and by karma alone it perishes.
Happiness, suffering, fear, and security are encountered solely through one's own karma;
and the wind draws the fetus from the womb with its head downward and feet upward.
From birth, the Māyā of Viṣṇu swiftly deludes [beings];
a creature undergoes rebirth through a connection formed by its own karma.
From good deeds one becomes superior, possessing enjoyments and what is to be enjoyed, and is born into a noble family;
whereas according to the degree of evil deeds, one is born into a lowly family.
Poor, diseased, foolish, a doer of evil, and a vessel for suffering—
O Lord of Birds, what more than this need I tell you?

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of Living Beings, the Division of Their Constituent Elements, and the Division of the Worlds," in the second section (Uttarakhaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the vision of Dharma and the vision of the deceased. The Glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 33.
Garuḍa said:
"The origin and characteristics of living beings have been told to me, your son;
but how large is the realm of Yama within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile?"
Tell me that in detail; how long is the duration of that path said to be?
O Lord, by what evil deeds or by what auspicious action do human beings go there? Please tell me this in detail.
The Blessed One said:
"The distance between the world of humans and the realm of Yama is eighty-six thousand yojanas in measure."
Like heated, molten copper, the great path is a blazing fortress;
there, the most sinful men of deluded minds go.
There were indeed thorns of many kinds, extremely sharp and terrible to behold;
by them the ground was covered, and likewise the fire was fierce.
There is no shade of a tree where a man may rest,
for he is seized by the nooses of Time through the fierce deeds he has committed.
On that path there was no food by which one might nourish one's life,
nor was water seen there by which thirst might be quenched.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, he travels along the great path;
somewhere on the exceedingly difficult road of Yama, he trembles from the cold.
Whatever kind of evil belongs to a person, such is the path for him;
wretched, miserable, and deluded, they cross over it, overwhelmed by sufferings.
Some weep bitterly, and others utter cries of betrayal,
as they are repeatedly tormented by the faults produced by their own past actions.
O bird, such indeed is that path to be known as terrible;
those men in the world who are free from craving travel easily upon it. (GarP 2.33.11)
Whatever gifts have been given by men on earth, those very same gifts appear before them on the path in the world of Yama.
The sinful do not receive the funeral water-offering or the *śrāddha* rites;
those base evildoers wander about like the wind. (GarP 2.33.13)
Such is that terrible path described to you, O observer of noble vows;
I shall further describe the condition of the road of Yama.
Between the southern and southwestern directions lies the city of Vaivasvata;
it is entirely made of diamond, divine, and impenetrable even by gods and asuras.
It is square, with four gates and seven ramparts and archways;
Yama himself dwells therein, accompanied by his messengers.
It is said to be a thousand yojanas in measure;
it is divine, composed of all kinds of jewels, and possesses the brilliance of lightning-flames and the sun.
That cave of the King of Dharma was vast, with a golden luster,
and rose to a height of five hundred yojanas.
It was surrounded by thousands of pillars adorned with lapis lazuli gems,
featuring latticed windows of pearl nets and decorated with hundreds of banners.
It was always adorned with hundreds of archways rich with the resonance of a hundred bells,
and with other such ornaments as these.
There, the Blessed One sat upon a level and auspicious Dharma-seat,
ten *yojanas* in extent, resembling a dark blue cloud.
He knows the Dharma, is of virtuous character, and is endowed with righteousness; he is a beneficial Yama, a source of fear for those joined with evil, and a bestower of happiness upon the righteous.
Accompanied by gentle breezes, various festivals, diverse expositions, and the sounds of conch shells and musical instruments; GarP_2,33.23 //
Upon entering the center of the city, there is indeed the house of Citragupta,
extending twenty-five yojanas in width.
Ten stories high, it was a magnificent divine palace, encircled by an iron wall,
with hundreds of thoroughfares and adorned with hundreds of banners fluttering in the sky.
The house of Citragupta was crowded with hundreds of lamps and filled with the sound of singing, and it was adorned by those skilled in various paintings.
Seated upon a divine and most wonderful throne made of jewels and pearls,
he stationed there calculates the lifespan among humans and among other beings.
He is never deluded regarding either good or evil deeds;
whatever has been acquired by anyone, he knows that very thing exactly as it is.
He records the performed actions, free from the eighteen defects;
to the east of Citragupta’s abode lies the great house of Fever.
On the south [side] are those of the trident and the eruption of boils;
on the west are those of the noose of Time, as well as indigestion and loss of appetite.
In the north of the central seat, one should know there is likewise another, Viṣacikā;
in the northeast, indeed, is headache, and in the southeast, muteness.
Atisāra is in the southwest, and the one known as Dāha is in the northwest;
Citragupta always stands there, surrounded by these.
Whatever action anyone performs, O Tārkṣya, all of that is inscribed at the gate of the palace of Dharmarāja; likewise at night, messengers stand there with those of evil deeds,
the lowest of men, as they are being cooked in torment.
Beaten by the messengers of Yama with great nooses and mallets,
men are slaughtered for their various sins committed through their past actions.
And by various supreme weapons and likewise by various machines,
those of evil deeds are cut in two like pieces of wood with saws.
Others, intensely surrounded on all sides by blazing coals,
are scorched like lumps of iron due to the ripening of their past karma.
Others, having been cast upon the surface of the earth, were hacked with axes;
they were seen wailing due to the ripening of their past karma.
Some most wicked men are tormented intensely by the messengers of Yama with preparations of molasses, and others likewise with preparations of oil.
On that very day, I saw millions of others in the world of Yama begging, "Give! Give! while I was saying, "This is mine; it was eaten by you."

Thus, O Tārkṣya, the hells for sinners have been described many times through the numerous deeds proclaimed and spoken of in all the scriptures. Now I shall speak of the benefit of giving, so that there may be happiness therein.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Extensive Splendor of the Realm of Yama," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa, the second part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Prata-kalpa, during the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa—34.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to the characteristics of dharma and adharma according to the proper method:
the good and evil deeds of men run ahead of them as they run.
In the Kṛta age they praise austerity; in the Tretā age, the means of knowledge;
in the Dvāpara age, sacrifice and giving; but in the Kali age, giving alone.
The wise have declared this to be the supreme duty for householders:
there is no sin for those who perform sacrifices and works of public utility according to their own ability.
For one who has planted trees and [constructed] wells, pits, and reservoirs,
there will be great happiness as they travel along the path of Yama.
Those who provide fire and warmth to a twice-born man afflicted by the cold attain happiness,
being fully satisfied with all their desires.
Gold, gems, pearls, and the like, as well as garments and ornaments—
all this has been given by him who has given the earth.
Whatever gifts have been bestowed upon the earth by men,
those remain in close proximity to them on the path to the realm of Yama.
O son, whatever various condiments, foods, and edibles one gives according to the prescribed rite, that reaches the deceased.
The self indeed has the name "son"; a son is a savior in the abode of Yama.
Because he delivers his father from the terrible [realm], he is therefore called a "putra."
Therefore, the son must offer the śrāddha until the end of his own life;
for by that means, the deceased indeed obtains enjoyments during the period of transition.
When a funeral libation of water is offered by kinsmen for a deceased person who is being cremated, that libation takes the form of a ghost;
thus satisfied, it goes to the abode of Yama.
If milk is placed for three days in an unbaked earthen vessel,
one should bind three pieces of wood together with cords and place them at a crossroads at night for the sake of propitiating [the deity].
On the first day, the second, and likewise the third, O bird,
the deceased, assuming a body of wind, drinks milk situated in the sky.
On the fourth day, the collection [of bones] should be performed; or even on the fourth day for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*).
The gathering of the bones should be done, and thereafter one should offer handfuls of water (*āpāñjali*).
Neither in the forenoon, nor at midday, nor in the afternoon, nor during the twilights;
but when the first watch has passed, one should offer handfuls of water for the deceased.
When the funeral offering has been presented by the son, all those kinsmen and well-wishers—
both of his own caste and of other castes— should offer a handful of water into the river.
A Brahmin should not go quickly to offer the handful of water;
he should do so only when the women have returned, for that is the eternal custom of the world.
When a Śūdra has passed away and one who carries wood for his funeral pyre follows him,
that Brahmin shall remain impure for three nights.
Then, when three nights have passed, he should go to a river that flows to the ocean;
by performing one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.
A Śūdra may go everywhere; a Vaiśya, to three [classes]; and the one beyond him (the Kṣatriya), to two;
each may go among their own respective castes to offer handfuls of water when [a person] has died.
After offering the water libation, one should thereafter perform the cleansing of the teeth;
O Kāśyapa, all kinsmen of the same lineage abandon [the deceased] for nine days.
The best of the twice-born go to offer the funeral libation (jalāñjali) at that very place where one has died— whether on the road or in the house—
for the wise have ordained that there is no displacement from that location.
Women should walk in front, and the newly gathered provisions behind;
those standing upon stones should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should look at barley, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass in the full vessel;
one should consume neem leaves and perform a bath with oil.
One should not perform [the rite] with those of low caste, nor should one feed them from the house;
one should eat from an earthen vessel and avoid using one that is turned upside down.
One should grasp the virtues of the deceased and recite the verses of Yama;
one should contemplate the auspicious and inauspicious [deeds] accumulated through previous karma.
With that very body he has obtained, he experiences the fruits of his good and evil deeds;
becoming like the wind, he indeed wanders, and as wind, he goes upward.
A hut is certainly constructed through the performance of the ten-day rites;
indeed, by means of the sixteen *navaka-śrāddhas*, a person enters that hut.
The hut on the ground should indeed be made of earth with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass;
and five jewels should be placed in the mouth, by which the life-force (*jīva*) sprouts forth.
When the flower has indeed perished, then one should not conceive a fetus;
therefore, with care, one should scatter sesame seeds and darbha grass upon the ground.
Whether he is born in the state of an animal or as an immobile being, wherever that creature is produced, there the śrāddha offering reaches him.
Just as an arrow released by an archer toward a target reaches it,
so too does a śrāddha performed for a specific person accrue to that very person.
As long as the body has not been produced, there is no satisfaction for the ancestors through funeral offerings;
it was only after ten days that he, having fallen into the delusion of hunger, was satiated.
He for whom no offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) was made wanders in the sky;
dwelling in water for three days and also in fire for three days,
he dwells in the sky for three days and for one day in a dwelling.
When the body has been cremated and the fire itself satiated with water,
one should perform an oil-bath with water alone, and in the house, a bath with cakes and *kṛsara* porridge.
On the first day, the third, the fifth, or even the seventh,
as well as on the ninth and the eleventh, the Śrāddha is called "the ninefold" (navaka).
Whether at the door of one's house, in a cremation ground, at a sacred ford, or even in a temple—
wherever the first rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered, there one should complete all [the offerings].
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common;
bathing is prescribed for the sake of purification for all four castes.
Having performed the eleventh-day rite and having bathed again, he shall become pure;
he who gives a bed to a Brahmin as prescribed bestows liberation upon the deceased.
It would not come to pass when even another person of that lineage performs the rite, or when some man, being satisfied, acts for the sake of women. (GarP 2.34.40)
Whatever rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered on the first day according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform all subsequent śrāddhas with that very same food.
One should perform the funeral rites (śrāddha) for ten days without mantras, according to the name and lineage;
having discarded the garments in which the śrāddha was performed, one should enter the house.
Whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man,
whoever performs [the rite] on the first day shall complete it over ten days.
The body of the living being is certainly produced by ten lumps [of food],
just as the growth of the one dwelling in the womb occurs over ten months.
For as long as there is impurity for him, so long shall the rites of the rice-balls and water-libations be performed;
this very rule is prescribed for all four castes.
Where there is impurity for three nights, one should cause three [pindas] to be offered on the first day,
four on the second day, and likewise three on the third day.
One should offer milk and water separately in two bowls for one day;
indeed, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the fourth day.
By the rice-ball offered on the first day, the head is produced;
by the second day, the eyes, ears, and nose are produced.
On the third day, the cheeks, the face, and likewise the neck are produced;
on the fourth day, the heart, the flanks, and the belly arise in exactly the same manner.
On the fifth day, the hips, the back, and the anus are formed;
on the sixth, the two thighs are to be known as appearing; and on the seventh, the ankles arise.
When the eighth day arrives, O bird, the two shanks appear;
the feet are to be known [as manifesting] on the ninth, and on the tenth there is powerful hunger.
On the eleventh day, one should offer that rice-ball (piṇḍa) with meat;
cooked food should be given to him, as well as kṛśara, cakes, and milk.
Having washed the feet of the Brahmin, one should offer water for honor (arghya), incense, and a lamp.
There are twelve monthly śrāddhas, as well as one on the eleventh day;
there is also the three-fortnightly rite, and the two half-yearly rites—these constitute the sixteen śrāddhas.

Those who know the Vedas understand that the first month is to be known as that month in which the lunar day (tithi) on which death occurred falls; [the śrāddha] should be offered every month on that specific lunar day.
The śrāddha performed with the corpse in hand, at the place of death, or upon the seat of a twice-born—this indeed is the first śrāddha; it should take place on the eleventh day.
That lunar day on which a man died is the one to be observed for the monthly *śrāddha*;
however, one should certainly not observe that same lunar day when it falls on an empty (*rikta*) tithi or during the three-fortnight period (*tripakṣa*).
For one who dies on the full moon, the *conaka* occurs on the fourth day;
for one who dies on the fourth day, the *conaka* occurs on the ninth day.
He who dies on the ninth day, and for whom the fourteenth is a *riktā*—
these should be known as *riktā* days by one skilled in the funeral rites.
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is proclaimed as the "Navaka" (the ninth);
one should discard the food at a crossroads and perform a bath once again.
Beginning from the eleventh day, food accompanied by water for the jar should be given day after day to the best of the twice-born until the end of the year.
In the human body, there exists indeed a collection of bones;
in all bodies, their number is three hundred and sixty.
For those bones indeed become nourished by the water-pot;
therefore, the pot is offered, and satisfaction arises for the deceased.
On whichever day a living being dies, whether in a forest or on difficult terrain, at that very time there shall be cremation; the period of impurity (sūtaka) begins from the day of death.
A sesame vessel, as well as food, incense, perfumes, and so forth, should be given on the eleventh day; by that, the twice-born becomes purified.
A Kṣatriya becomes pure in twelve days, and likewise a Vaiśya in fifteen;
for a Śūdra, purification occurs after one month in the case of both birth and death.
For a period of three months, there shall be a three-night impurity; for six months, however, it is a "pakṣiṇī" (two days with the intervening night).
For a period less than a year, it is one day; when the year is complete, one becomes pure after offering water libations.
According to this very principle, purification shall apply to all castes.
Starting from the eleventh day, every year thereafter,
one should worship the Viśvedevas and offer a single rice-ball (piṇḍa).
Just as all the hosts of stars are eclipsed by the rays of the sun, so too is everything eclipsed; a preta never exists anywhere.
The best of the twice-born always praise the gift of a bed;
since life is transient, who indeed will provide one after death? (GarP 2.34.69)
A father is a kinsman only so long as he lives;
once a man has died, realizing "he is dead," affection ceases in an instant.
"Indeed, the self alone is the friend of the self"; having realized this again and again, and reflecting that "even while living," one should pursue one's own welfare. (GarP 2.34.71)
"Who among the deceased would have a son offer a bed for a brahmin with a cotton mattress?
Knowing all this to be so, one should cause [the gift] to be given by one's own hand. (GarP 2.34.72)
Therefore, having obtained a bed made of strong wood, firm,
beautiful with ivory and other ornaments, lovely, and adorned with bands of gold;
and having placed upon it an image of Hari made of gold, accompanied by Lakṣmī—
And one should fashion a pitcher filled with clarified butter;
it should be understood by the wise as the "sleep-pitcher" for the pleasure of Garuḍa.
Betel, saffron powder, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a seat, and a vessel.
One should place seven kinds of grain according to one's ability at the sides,
as well as whatever else may be useful for one who is lying on the bed.
Having prepared a bed equipped with a water-pitcher, a vessel, a mirror, and a five-colored canopy, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having worshipped her who bestows the happiness of the heavenly realm along with her husband,
and having honored her with most beautiful garments, one should cause her to put on a new cloth.
The house should be furnished with ornaments for the ears, neck, fingers, and arms, with various other decorations,
household utensils, and provided with a cow.
Then the *argha* offering should be presented with the five jewels, fruits, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Just as the couch of Kṛṣṇa is never empty of the daughter of the ocean,
so may my bed likewise be never empty in birth after birth.
Having thus provided a pure bed and asked for forgiveness, one should dismiss [the officiants];
this is the procedure proclaimed for the eleventh day as well.
For he who, when a kinsman has died, gives for the sake of dharma to that kinsman—hears now from me as I describe the specific distinction regarding this case. GarP_2,34.83 //
Whatever he previously possessed in his own home that was useful—
whatever clothing, vessels, or vehicles were attached to his body,
and whatever else was dear to him— all that he should provide.
The wise man should place a beautiful golden figure upon the bed;
having performed worship, the aforementioned bed for the deceased should be given away.
By the power of the gift of a bed, all comforts of a living being shall attend him in the abode of Purandara and likewise in the residence of the Son of the Sun.
The terrifying-faced messengers of Yama do not torment him;
that man is never afflicted by heat or cold.
By the power of the gift of a bed, even a hungry ghost (preta) is released from bondage;
though joined with evil, he goes to the heavenly world.
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and served by hosts of apsarases,
he shall remain there, freed from all sins, until the dissolution of all beings.
The woman who performs the *navaka*, the sixteenfold *śrāddha*, the *śayyā-śrāddha*, and likewise the annual *śrāddha* for her husband, gains indeed infinite merit.
For the benefit of her husband, she was thus alive and not dead;
as a virtuous and truthful woman, while living, she rescued her beloved.
For the woman, one should cause her to receive curd-rice, a bed, gold, saffron, collyrium, clothing, ornaments, and likewise a couch; indeed, all of this should be given.
Whatever here may be beneficial for women—be it an ornament clinging to the body or any object of enjoyment and the like—[is to be given]. (GarP 2.34.93)
Having gathered all of that together, one should assign it to its respective places;
one should worship the world-protectors, the planets, the Goddess, and Vināyaka.
Then, wearing white garments and holding a handful of flowers, the wise man should recite this mantra in the presence of the Brahmin: *GarP_2,34.95*
This is indeed an image of a preta, provided with all requisites and endowed with every kind of jewel; it has been offered to you by me, O Brahmin.
The Self is Śambhu; Śivā is Gaurī; and Śakra is with the hosts of gods.
Therefore, by the gift of this bed, may that very Self be propitiated.
It should be given to a teacher who is a Brahmin with a family; when it has been accepted, one should proclaim there, "Who gave this? GarP_2,34.98.
Then, having circumambulated and prostrated, O bird, one should dismiss [the recipient] by means of this rite; indeed, one should cause the gift of a single [cow] to be given.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many;
for these, when divided as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), cause the donor to fall.
O Tārkṣya, hear now what the fruit is for one who bestows it in this manner:
he is honored in the heavenly world for more than a hundred divine years.
Whatever merit is gained during a Vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day of Kārttika, or during the two solstices;
and whatever merit is gained at Dvārakā during an eclipse of the moon or the sun—[that merit is attained by this]. GarP_2,34.102 //
Whatever [merit] is gained at Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, or the Arbuda tīrtha, as well as at the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean; GarP_2,34.103 //
Whatever gift is given to them, this [gift] is even superior to that;
it does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a bed.
In whatever place that living being is born, there indeed he experiences the fruit [of his actions].
Upon the exhaustion of karma, the man of auspicious appearance returns to the earth.
Possessing great wealth, knowing the Dharma, and proficient in all the scriptures,
that bull among men, upon his death, goes again to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot and surrounded by apsarases,
oh, he rejoices together with the ancestors in the offerings made to gods and manes.

The śrāddha performed on the aṣṭakās, as well as on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), during the Maghā asterisms, and on whatever other festivals for the ancestors (pitṛ-parvan) there may be— on all those occasions [one should offer].
Listen, O Tārkṣya, according to the rule: if the ancestors remain in the state of a preta, the śrāddha offerings do not reach them unless the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has been performed.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed when the year is complete, without a doubt; having first performed the sixteenth *akṣayya-śrāddha* for the sake of purifying the corpse.
One should join the purification of the paternal row with fifty [bricks];
indeed, having reached prosperity, one may perform [the rite] for a Śūdra according to one's own will.
Now, the *sapiṇḍana* rite for one who maintains the sacred fires should be performed on the twelfth day;
as long as he does not perform it, he remains a *preta* even though he possesses the fire.
Therefore, the *sapiṇḍana* must be performed by the one with the sacred fires on the twelfth day.
One should not perform the *gayāśrāddha* or the fortnightly *śrāddha* within the year following the cremation of the bones, except for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
If there should be many co-wives, yet only one of them has a son,
all of them shall be considered as having sons by virtue of that single offspring.

A son who does not belong to the same *sapiṇḍa* lineage as his father and who does not maintain the sacred fire should not perform the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). By performing it, he would become a sinner and is even born as a slayer of his ancestors.
When her husband has died, if a woman likewise renounces her life,
one should perform the sapindikarana for her together with her husband alone.
Even for those who were not formally wedded— whether they be Vaiśyas or Kṣatriyas—
a son may perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for any of his father’s wives.
When a Śūdra woman is married by a Brāhmaṇa through negligence, that Ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha is performed for her by him alone; she is indeed united with him.
But as for the other ten sons born within the four castes,
they should always be joined with their respective mothers during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.

On the Anvaṣṭakā days, at the śrāddha performed for prosperity, and at the śrāddha for the father, the offering should be made separately; however, in the Sapiṇḍana rite, the pinda is offered to the woman [along with her husband].

O Tārkṣya, it is my opinion that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed for the mother together with her paternal grandmother, and for the father together with his paternal grandfathers. GarP_2,34.121 //
But when she has died without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite;
he should thus join her with the three [ancestors] beginning with his mother, in accordance with the Dharma.
O Tārkṣya, for women who have neither a son nor a husband,
the sapindikarana rite should be performed at the time of a prosperity-rite (vṛddhi) by their brothers, heirs, or brothers-in-law.
For those who are bereft of sons and grandsons, there is neither a kinsman nor a husband’s brother;
the offering should be given by others together with their brothers through the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
If the sapindikarana has not been performed due to ignorance or some obstacle,
one should then perform the nine-fold rites, the sixteen śrāddhas, and the annual anniversary rite.
If there is no burning, it should not be performed; if there is burning, the wise man should have it done.
Having fashioned an effigy of *darbha* grass, he should cause the corpse to be cremated with fire.
A son must perform [the rites] for his father, but a father should not perform them for his son;
out of excessive affection, one should not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a virtuous [son].
Even when there are many sons, one alone may perform the rites:
the *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the other sixteen *śrāddhas*. (GarP 2.34.128)
However, even among those whose wealth has not been divided, one alone may perform the funeral rites;
this has indeed been declared by the sages.
Once they have been divided, the annual rites and other such duties should be performed separately;
each son must perform them individually for himself.
For him to whom these sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased have not been offered,
his state as a *piśāca* remains fixed, even by hundreds of other *śrāddhas* performed.
O Lord of Birds, in the absence of a son, a brother, a brother’s son, a sapinda relative, or even a disciple should perform the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
For all those who are childless, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for the wife;
or else, one should have a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) or even a family chaplain (*purohita*) perform it.
If an eclipse should occur within the year after the father has died,
the sons must not perform the pārvaṇa śrāddha, nor the nāndīmukha śrāddha.
One should not perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the *gayā-śrāddha*, or any other ancestral *śrāddha* during the year following the death of a preceptor or a great teacher (*mahāguru*).
And during the Yamaka-śrāddha, on the Gajacchāyā day, and on other Yugādi days,
the pinda for the ancestors should not be offered except for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
Whatever gift is given to the Yajñapuruṣa, as well as that which is for the gods and others, should be performed even if the year is incomplete and even during its middle; so say some authorities.
For that which is given even to the ancestors, excluding the water-offering (argha) and the rice-ball (piṇḍa), all of that must indeed be performed; this is remembered as the prescribed rule.
The ancestors are gods to the gods, and likewise the sages are gods to the ancestors;
the gods are the ancestors of the sages; therefore, the Father indeed triumphs.
The Lord is the master of the sacrifice for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
whatever is given to the master of the sacrifice is given to all embodied beings.
If a son performs a Śrāddha within a year after his father has died, he is deprived of the merit earned over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
But those who have become pretas, their rites of rice-balls and water-liberation having been neglected,
all wander about driven by the wind, tormented by hunger and thirst.
When the father has passed away, the ancestral rites (*paitṛka-kriyā*) are suspended;
however, if the mother’s death should occur, the rites for the father are not suspended.
If the mother has died while the father remains alive, and the paternal grandmother is also living,
the sapindikarana must nevertheless be performed together with the paternal grandmother.
"Truth, truth, and again the truth—listen to my words:
for those men on earth whose funeral cakes have not been offered,"

One should certainly not attend to those for whom various kinds of offerings have been given by their sons; neither the *hantakāra* nor the *śrāddha* nor even a handful of water should be offered on their behalf.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Post-Mortem Rites and Other Duties," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
The glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 35.
Tārksya said:
Furthermore, O Janārdana, tell me of another doubt of mine:
whose person, it is said, has come to the state of the five elements?
The paternal grandmother lives, as does the great-grandmother, and likewise the great-great-grandmother; and similarly, the father is devoted to his mother.
O Lord, tell me this: by what means is the mother united with the maternal grandfather, as well as the great-grandfather and the great-great-grandfather? GarP_2,35.3 //
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O bird, I shall speak again regarding the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite;
one should certainly unite [the deceased] with Umā, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī.
Three are to be known as eaters of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), and three are remembered as those who abandon it;
three are those who smear the rice-balls, and the tenth is the one present at the row (paṅkti).
Thus these men are renowned within the families of their fathers and mothers;
by performing this sacrifice, the patron shall deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants.
He becomes a sapinda at the outset once the sapindikarana has been performed;
however, the most remote ancestor, the great-great-grandfather, should be known as the one who must be excluded.
The last should be known as the renouncer (*tyājaka*), while the first would be the smearer (*lepaka*);
and he who is the last smearer would be one who stays near the row (*paṅktisannidha*).
"The sacrificer shall be one; there are ten in the higher [lineage] and ten in the lower.
Thus these ancestors are to be known as numbering twenty-one.
He who performs the supreme śrāddha in this world according to the prescribed rule—there is no doubt that he is reborn here; hear now what the fruit of that is as well.
O bird, if one's lineage is severed, it is indeed the father who provides sons;
even he who is his great-grandfather may become the giver of the oblation.
When the śrāddha has been performed, these are indeed remembered as the benefits for the ancestors;
moreover, the great-grandfather, being aged, shall receive abundant food and other offerings.
O bird, that man whose lineage is indeed severed in this mortal world shall dwell in a terrible hell, like an elephant sunk in the mud.
He is born in other wombs where trees and reptiles dwell;
without [attaining] spiritual continuity (*saṃtati*), he is certainly not liberated from hell.
Whether it be his teacher or his disciple, even if he be far away, one who has a physical body should perform the Nārāyaṇabali out of devotion on his behalf.
Purified and freed from all sins, he will certainly dwell in the world of the gods, having escaped from hell; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā and ending with Revatī, this group of five constellations is always defiled and shall always be inauspicious.
No cremation (bali) should be performed there for Brahmins or any other castes;
no water should be offered there, for misfortune will certainly arise.
Even if one's own kin are afflicted by suffering, the funeral rites (lokayātrā) must not be carried out.
Everything else for him must be performed immediately after the *pañcaka*;
otherwise, suffering arises even for his sons and kinsmen.
In these constellations, there shall be loss for that person, and whoever dies under them—
or even if the cremation is performed during those constellations— [the same result follows].
For human beings, it is performed immediately for the sake of offering oblations;
the merit of making an immediate offering at a sacred ford is supreme even compared to cremation.
The brahmins must perform [the rite] according to the rules, accompanied by mantras and preceded by the prescribed ritual;
then, effigies are cast near the corpse.
Then, four brahmins made of darbha grass and consecrated with mantras should be used; by means of them, along with those effigies, the cremation must be performed.
Then, at the end of the period of birth-impurity, the son should perform the most excellent rite of pacification.
For that man who has died among the five [categories of the deceased] and does not attain a [favorable] rebirth,
one should offer sesame seeds, cows, gold, and clarified butter on his behalf.
A gift is given to the Brahmins, which destroys all calamities;
at the end of the period of impurity, that deceased person attains a [favorable] state through virtuous sons.
O Brahmin, a vessel, sandals, an umbrella, a golden seal, and two garments are given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which releases one from all sins. (GarP 2.35.27)
Indeed, for children, the elderly, and the sick who have died among the five [categories of persons],
if one does not perform the prescribed rite, an obstacle arises for him.
In a śrāddha for pretas, one should avoid these eighteen things:
blessings, double-folded darbha grass, the syllable Om, and the practice of offering a single piṇḍa.

One should not utter the word "svadhā," nor the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestors), in relation to the offering into the fire, the remnants of the śrāddha, the Vaiśvadeva portion, the scattered food (vikiro), or the ritual exclamation.
One should not utter the word "anu," nor perform the invocation, nor carry a firebrand;
one should not perform the circumambulation or the ritual dismissal beyond the boundary.
A twice-born man should not perform a sesame oblation (*tilahoma*) nor likewise a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
if he does not perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite, the performer goes to a low state.
The sixteen [rites] previously mentioned, known as the "impure śrāddhas," are likewise [performed] at the site,
at the gate, on the half-way path, at the funeral pyre, and when the corpse is in hand.
The fifth is for the spirits dwelling in the cremation ground;

the sixth is declared to be at the gathering [of the bones]. These ten rice-balls (piṇḍas) offered during the ten days, along with the sixteen-fold śrāddha, are proclaimed as the first [set of rites].
Furthermore, O Tārkṣya, hear from me the sixteenth [chapter], the second in the middle [section]:
here, according to the prescribed rule, eleven śrāddhas must indeed be performed.

Those who know the reality have declared that there are sixteen [shraddhas]: those dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and so forth, as well as another set of five shraddhas. Thus they speak of this group of sixteen.
There are twelve monthly *śrāddhas*, as well as one on the eleventh day; that which occurs every three fortnights, and two on the new and full moon days—these, O Bird, constitute the sixteen.

Having first performed the rite for the purification of the corpse, one should perform another consisting of three times sixteen [oblations] for the purification of the paternal lineage; however, one should not employ even half of a hundred [oblations].
He who is deprived of half of a hundred and is not included in the row [of diners] does not partake of it;
likewise, the forty-fold rite for the eight ancestors destroys the state of being a preta.
One who has fallen short of fifty by even a single unit may become a member of the assembly;
in truth, such a person should be admitted to the *śrāddha* rite through the mediation of those who possess exactly fifty.
(Now, the ritual for the corpse:
The binding of the hands and feet of the corpse upon the bier must be performed there;
if this procedure is not prescribed, it will result in the corpse being desecrated by piśācas.
If a corpse is expelled during the night, the kingdom becomes free from fear; yet if one does not release the corpse, or if it is released, there will be misfortune due to its foul touch.
If one eats at will when it is heard that a corpse is situated in the middle of the village, that food should be known as being like meat, and its water like blood. (GarP 2.35.43)
When a deceased person remains within the village, one should avoid betel, tooth-sticks, eating, and sexual intercourse; one should also avoid the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍapātana*).
[Furthermore, one should avoid] bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the worship of the gods.

When a deceased person remains in the midst of the village, the kinsmen must act according to the dharma for the sake of purification, O Lord of Birds; such is the practice among those related by kinship. By violating the duty toward kinsmen, one becomes defiled by the sin of the deceased.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sapiṇḍana and the Rite for the Corpse," in the second section on Pretas within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 36—
Tārkṣya said:
Why is fasting meritorious and bestowing an inexhaustible state? It is because one who, having abandoned their own home, dies indeed at a sacred ford (tīrtha). 36.1.
If one who has become a *kuṭīcara* dies at home or dies when death has arrived without having reached a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), what destination does he attain? 2.36.2.
If one undertakes renunciation either at a sacred ford or even at home,
how should it be performed for him, even if death has not yet arrived?
O God, if a restriction is established and the mind indeed becomes disturbed,
how could there be accomplishment for him— whether through that which was performed or that which was left unperformed?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"If anyone indeed meets death after practicing fasting,
having cast off the human body, he shines forth equal to me."
For as many days as one lives while observing a vow of total fasting,
those days are equal to sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees.
If one undergoes renunciation at a sacred ford or in one's home and then dies there,
he too obtains every day twice the previously mentioned fruit.
And when one has undertaken a fast upon the onset of a great disease, that disease shall not arise again; indeed, one shines like a god.
If a person, being afflicted by illness, takes up renunciation,
he is not born again on this earth in the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Day after day, food should be given to the Brahmins;
likewise, one should offer vessels of sesame seeds according to one's ability, give lamps, and worship the gods.
For one who conducts themselves in this manner, all various sins are consumed;
upon death, they attain liberation, just as all the great seers did.
Therefore, fasting grants men the state of Vaikuṇṭha;
thus, when one is healthy or in the final stage of life, one should accomplish that which is characterized by liberation.
For that man who, having renounced his sons, wealth, and other possessions, goes to a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha),
the deities beginning with Brahmā shall become bestowers of satisfaction and nourishment upon him.
If one who has set out facing a sacred ford (tīrtha) should die even in the interim while engaged in the vow of fasting, he shall dwell in the assembly of the ṛṣis.
Having undertaken the vow of fasting, even if one dies in one's own home,
one shall leave behind one's family and wander alone in heaven.
If a person renounces both food and likewise water, having drunk the water from my feet, he is not born again upon this earth.
The forest deities protect that person who has gone to that sacred ford and sits with his work completed;
specifically, the messengers of Yama do not remain by his side.
That man who frequents sacred fords (tīrtha) and is freed from all sins,
if he dies there or is cremated there, shall partake in the fruit of that sacred ford.
Even if one dies elsewhere while constantly practicing [this],
that wise person shall become a twice-born knower of the Vedas in an auspicious land and family.
O Tārkṣya, a man who, having fasted to death, returns to life again,
should summon the Brāhmaṇas and renounce all his possessions.
Having been permitted by those twice-born ones, he should perform the entire Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he should not speak untruth thereafter, but should practice only dharma.
And whoever, having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), returns home again,
being permitted by the Brahmins, should then perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).
Having given gifts of gold, cows, land, elephants, and horses,
he who reaches a sacred ford at the time of death is truly fortunate.
When death is imminent, one who has set out from home for a sacred ford (tīrtha) gains the merit of a gift of a cow at every step, provided that no violence occurs.
Whatever sin is committed in the home is purified by bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha);
however, if one commits a sin there [at the ford], it is indeed like an adamantine cement (vajralepa).
He shall suffer there for as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist; there is no doubt in this matter.
Furthermore, the gifts given there truly become inexhaustible.
When someone is afflicted by illness, even men who are destitute should give gifts:
cows, sesame seeds, gold, and especially the seven kinds of grain.
Seeing a man who is generous, all the inhabitants of heaven,
together with the ṛṣis, Dharma, and Citragupta, are always delighted.
As long as wealth remains under one's own control, one should bestow it upon a Brahmin;
once it has passed into the hands of another, who will compassionately give it all away after death?
The wealth that was placed in the hands of Brahmins by his sons on behalf of their father,
he made himself possessed of that wealth along with his sons and grandsons.
A gift given to one's father is said to be a hundredfold; a thousandfold to one's mother;
a hundred-thousandfold to a sister; and what is given to a uterine brother is inexhaustible.
If, out of greed, negligence, or even delusion, they do not give,
then all those stingy sinners grieve when they have died.
Wealth, acquired through excessive hardship and by its very nature fickle, has but one true course: giving; all other paths lead to misfortune.
Death laughs at the protector of the body who guards his wealth,
just as an unfaithful wife laughs at her own husband who is devoted to his son.
O Tārkṣya, even after acquiring vast wealth, that righteous and gentle man remains indifferent;
he regards both himself and his riches as if they were mere blades of grass.
He shall have no afflictions, nor indeed any web of delusion;
at the time of death, he shall have no fear arising from the messengers of Yama.
Seven thousand years in water, eleven in fire, sixteen in wind,
sixty in great battle, and eighty in a cow-pen— O Kāśyapa, for one who fasts to death, there is an inexhaustible state.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destination of One Who Dies by Fasting," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 37:
Tārkṣya said:
O Janārdana, tell me truly about the gift of the water-pot; by what rite is this practice to be performed?
What are their characteristics, by whom are they fulfilled, and to whom should they be given, O Janārdana?
At what time should those which accomplish the satisfaction of the departed be offered?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall further explain the gift of the water-pitcher (udakumbha).
It should be given for the sake of the deceased, accompanied by food and drink.
Especially do these great birds grant liberation to the departed spirits.
On the twelfth day, or in the sixth month, or even after three fortnights, or at the end of a year,
water-pots should indeed be offered on his path for his happiness.
Day after day, water-pots filled with sesame seeds, cooked food, and water should be offered upon a well-smeared portion of ground.
A vessel should be given there to the preta according to one's inclination;
by that gift, being well-pleased, the preta goes along with the messengers of Yama.
On the twelfth day, one should especially cause water-pots to be offered;
there, according to the prescribed rite, one should consecrate twelve pots.
There, a single vardhanī vessel filled with cooked food and fruit should be given to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa after making a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) dedicated to Viṣṇu.
One [offering] indeed belongs to Dharmarāja; by him, being pleased, one becomes a partaker of liberation.
And one belongs to Citragupta; having gone there, one shall become happy.
The sixteen and the others should be offered, filled with black gram porridge and water.
Starting from the *uktrānti-śrāddha* up to the sixteenth *śrāddha*,
one should assign one Brahmin for each of those sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Starting from the eleventh day, that which is called the "Dṛḍha" should be given daily for as many days as there are in a year, consisting of cooked food and water.
Large water-vessels and small jars were provided;
there was indeed one *vardhanī* vessel among them, and within it was a bowl made of bamboo.
Having worshipped her with fragrant scents, one should cover her with a garment;
one should especially cause vessels filled with water to be given to the Brahmins.
O Lord of Birds, having formed this resolve day after day according to the prescribed rite,
one should give it to a noble-born Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with Vedic knowledge and virtuous conduct.
It should be given to one who possesses both learning and good conduct, but never to a fool;
for one who is capable and rich in Vedic knowledge is able to rescue others and cross over [the ocean of existence] as well.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Śrāddha with a Water-Pot," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the Preta-kalpa, within the second part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Tārkṣya said:
O Lord, tell me of liberation and heaven sought through the ford of giving;
by what means does one attain liberation, and by what means does one dwell long in heaven? (GarP 2.38.1)
By what does the vital energy (tejas) go from the world of light (svarloka) and the world of truth (satyaloka)? By what does one obtain human birth, and by what does one sink into the hells?
O bestower of liberation upon devotees, tell me this after determining it for certain:
upon the death of whom is there no rebirth in heaven? (GarP 2.38.3)
The illustrious Viṣṇu said:
Human birth occurs in the land of Bhārata among the thirteen castes.
Having reached that field, one dies and is not subject to rebirth;
[the sacred fields are] Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, and Avantikā.
The city of Dvāravatī is to be known as one of these seven that bestow liberation;
it is for such a place that one should say "I renounce," even when life-breaths have reached the throat.
He who has uttered even once the two syllables "Ha-ri" goes to the city of Viṣṇu upon death and is not born again on earth.
He has girded his loins for the journey toward liberation—
whosoever constantly remembers me, saying, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa."
Just as a lotus pierces through the water, so do I rescue [the devotee] from hell—
wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone or a Dvāravatī stone.
Where there is a conjunction of these two, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, it brings about the destruction of the defects of sin.
Liberation for a living being is certain through death in its proximity;
by planting, protecting, watering, meditating upon, touching, or glorifying it,
O Bird, Tulasī burns away the sins of men accumulated over lifetimes.
He who has bathed in the mental sacred ford— the lake of knowledge with truth as its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred— is not stained by sins.
The deity is never found in wood, nor is he ever found in stone;
the deity is indeed found in the internal disposition (bhāva). Therefore, one should cultivate that disposition.
Every morning, the fishermen behold the Narmadā;
yet they do not go to the city of Śiva, for the activity of their minds is too heavy.
Whatever the perception of the mind may be, such is the fruit of karma for human beings;
such is the transition to the next world, as subtle as the threading of a needle.
He who is intent on giving up his life for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or to save women from violent slaughter, shall indeed attain liberation.
He who dies by fasting shall indeed attain liberation;
he who dies by fasting is released from all bonds.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, one shall thereafter attain liberation;
these indeed are the paths to liberation as well as the paths to heaven.
During a cattle-raid, the destruction of a country, or at the death of a battle or a sacred pilgrimage site—
for an embodied being who is being oppressed, whether of high, low, or middling status—
by casting off one's self there, one shall obtain a long residence in heaven.
A wise person should train in two things alone: life and death;
life through giving and enjoyment, and death on the battlefield or at a sacred ford.
In Harikṣetra, Kurukṣetra, and likewise in Bhṛgukṣetra;
in Prabhāsa, Śrīsthala, Arbuda, and Tripuṣkara.
The man who dies at Bhūteśvara dwells in heaven for the duration of a day of Brahmā; thereafter, he falls back to the earth.
He who gives the means of subsistence for a year to a Brāhmaṇa free from faults,
having extracted all his impurities, is glorified in the heavenly world.
He who marries off a daughter to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas shall dwell in the world of Indra, surrounded by his own kinsmen.
And by giving great gifts, a man shall obtain their fruit.
One who undertakes the restoration of dilapidated step-wells, wells, tanks, groves, and temples shall obtain the same merit as the original builder;
or, by restoring them when they are decayed, that merit becomes twofold.
Having constructed a leaf-hut that wards off cold and heat,
he gives it to a learned Brahmin who has a family.
A man is honored in heaven for thirty-five million years.
A woman of the same caste who, being virtuous, follows her deceased husband in death,
attains heaven upon her death for as many years as there are hairs on the body.
She who, having abandoned her sons, grandsons, and others, follows her own husband, shall attain heaven;
both of them, adorned by celestial women, shall reach that realm.
She who, though always intent on betraying her husband and having committed many sins,
follows after her own husband, washes away them all.
If her husband should be a doer of evil, practicing great sins,
even a woman who follows his will incurs no sin at all.
He who constantly gives a fixed gift of at least one morsel of food attains a celestial chariot yoked with four chowries.
Whatever sin has been committed by a person until the end of life,
all of that goes to destruction through the granting of the means of subsistence for a year.
The sin accumulated over three lifetimes— past, present, and future—
is entirely washed away by the marriage ceremony of a Brahmin girl.
A large oblong pond is equal to ten wells; a lake is equal to ten such ponds;
and a water-station in a waterless forest is equal to ten lakes.
He who constructs a pond in a waterless region, he who gives a gift to a destitute brahmin,
and he who maintains compassion for all living beings— he shall become the leader of the heavens.
Through these and other such meritorious deeds, one becomes a partaker of heaven;
having attained all that fruit, one shall obtain supreme stability.
Abandoning trivial matters, one should always be devoted to righteousness;
for these three—generosity, self-restraint, and compassion—are the essence on this earth.
Giving to a virtuous person who is poor, honoring one who bears the marks of a mendicant,
and performing funeral rites for a destitute deceased person bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, is the description of the causes for the attainment of the highest worlds, for rebirth, and for liberation as a human being— the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, chapter 39.
Tārkṣya said:
O Lord, having shown compassion toward me, please explain the rules regarding births and deaths (sūtaka),
for the sake of the discernment of the mind and for the welfare of human beings.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Lord of Birds, upon death and birth, there occurs a fourfold impurity (sūtaka) which is generally avoided by all four castes alike.
In both cases, one should avoid the food of the family for ten days;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and the private recitation of sacred texts are suspended.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the means of attainment, and the state, one should perform the ritual action.
In the case of entering a cave or fire, and for those who have died in a foreign land, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on; immediate purification is prescribed.
For those living beings who are still in the womb and those who have emerged from the womb,
there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water-libation rite.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves,
kings, and those learned in the Vedas are proclaimed to be immediately pure.
A sacrificer, one observing a vow, one purified by mantras, and likewise a king who has maintained the sacred fires—
for these there is no impurity from birth, as well as for whomsoever kings so desire.
Upon the birth [of a child], a twice-born man should not cause a confusion of the sapinda relations;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father is pure by bathing.
Manu has declared that wealth previously intended for marriage, festivals, or sacrifices may be used for food even when an impurity due to death or birth occurs in the interim.
For all [relatives], the impurity is thus; however, regarding the birth of a child, the impurity belongs to the mother and father.
The birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual sipping (upaspṛśya).
If death or birth should occur again within ten days,
the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet passed ten days.
When the rule has been established, one should offer gifts to a distressed Brahmin;
likewise, it has been declared by the sages that [this] does not incur fault if performed at the proper time.
However, by bathing with a clay vessel containing water mixed with sesame seeds,
and likewise with clay at the end, a person shall become pure.
One should give a gift to the assembly; to a twice-born man, one should give gold and a bull.
A Kṣatriya should likewise give double that amount, and a Vaiśya three times as much.
A Śūdra must give four times as much wealth to a Brāhmaṇa;
in this very sequence, the four castes are purified.
If [the body] has decayed after seven or eight days and is devoid of the sacraments of the household stage,
his impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many years as the number of years he would have lived.
For those who have perished for the sake of a Brahmin, or in the defense of women or cows,
or those who have perished in battles, there is impurity for only one night.
No misfortune whatsoever shall befall those brahmins who perform auspicious rites for the funeral ceremonies of the destitute and the deceased, O best of men.
Not even the slightest impurity remains for them when they have a Brahmin as their companion;
it is declared that by plunging into the water, their purification is immediate.
When the Śūdras have turned back and reached the edge of the water, then they should not be looked upon by a Brāhmaṇa; so the knowers of the Veda understand.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Period of Impurity and Other Matters," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, within the second Pretakalpa of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 40—
Tārkṣya said:
"Blessed One, some brahmins have fallen under the power of untimely death;
what path would there be for them, what their station, and what their destination?"
Furthermore, what would be appropriate for them, or of what nature is their ritual procedure?
I wish to hear that; tell it to me, O Madhusūdana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Regarding the transformation into ghosts (pretas) of the twice-born, which occurs through the aberration of death,
I shall now describe their path, their destination, and the prescribed rites for them.
Listen, O Tārkṣya, to this supreme secret: when a premature death has occurred—such as that of Brahmins who died from fasting or were killed by fanged beasts.
Those who have drowned while clutching at a neck, those who are emaciated, those killed by a beak,
those [killed] by poison, fire, bulls, or Brahmins, and those who commit suicide through cholera— [these do not attain the path].
Listen to the state of those who have died by falling, by hanging, or by water;
they go to a terrible hell, as do those who have been killed by barbarians and the like.
Those touched by dogs, jackals, and the like; those not cremated; those swarming with worms;
those who died after having transgressed; and those afflicted by great diseases.
Those who have been falsely accused, as well as those who are physically unimpaired yet nourished by sinful food,
[are purified] from the Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, and from the fire of lightning.

Those who have died from fanged beasts, from falling from trees and the like, or those defiled by contact with a woman in her courses, a menstruating woman, a Śūdra woman, or a washerwoman; GarP_2,40.9 //
Released from hell by that sin, they become partakers of the state of hungry ghosts (pretas);
one should not perform their cremation, nor the birth-impurity rites, nor the water-libation ceremony.
One should not perform the funeral rites for them, nor the post-mortem ceremonies such as those beginning with the cremation;
O Tārkṣya, for them one should instead perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali offering.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, listen to that which removes the fear of sin:
burning [the body] for six months is prescribed for a Brahmin, and for three months for a Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, it is prescribed for one and a half months, while for a Śūdra, it is ordained to be immediate;
this applies at the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara.
In a pond full of water, or in a lake of pure water, in a large reservoir, a well, a cow-pen, a house, or a temple; GarP_2,40.14 //
O Brahmin, one should perform the bali offering named Nārāyaṇa before the image of Kṛṣṇa;
the libation for the deceased should be performed with Purāṇic and Vedic mantras.
One should offer libations intended for Viṣṇu with all medicinal herbs mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata),
using either the Puruṣasūkta or Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Facing the south, one should contemplate the deceased as Viṣṇu—
the god who is without beginning or end, and the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The imperishable, lotus-eyed Lord shall become the bestower of liberation upon the deceased;
and at the conclusion of the libation, he is free from passion and devoid of envy.
Having become one whose senses and mind are conquered, pure, devoted to the Dharma,
delighting in the virtue of giving, tranquil, restrained in speech, and purified, he should bow down.
The sacrificer there should be pure and accompanied by his kinsmen;
with devotion, he should perform exactly eleven śrāddhas there.
Through the ripening of all his past actions, he remained concentrated one-pointedly on each [object]:
water, rice, barley, sixty-fold [grains], wheat, and priyaṅgu.
One should cause auspicious sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), a seal (mudrā), an umbrella, a turban,
and a single garment to be offered, as well as all kinds of grain together with milk and honey.
One should give the eightfold gift consisting of garments and sandals;
one should cause this to be given to all the Brahmins and should not form a restrictive seating arrangement.
When the rice-balls are placed upon the ground, one should likewise offer libations separately into a conch vessel or a copper vessel, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains.
Endowed with meditative concentration and mental retention, having knelt upon the ground,
one should give [the gift] to all the Brahmins according to the injunctions of the Vedic scriptures.
In a rite for a single deceased person (ekoddiṣṭa), one should cause the arghya water to be offered separately with a Ṛgvedic verse;
[the water] consisting of the divine waters rich in honey is prepared upon the primary seat.
"Thou art taken with a support; O second [Agni], one should present the offering (argha).
With that purifying eye, O third [Agni], the oblation has been prepared. (GarP 2.40.27)
The *Devāsas* are in the fourth; go to the ocean in the fifth;
*Agnijyotis* likewise in the sixth; and *Hiraṇyagarbha* in the seventh.
On the eighth day, one should know that "yamāya tvā" is used; likewise, on the ninth, "yad jagrat"; on the tenth, "yāḥ phalinī"; and then on the eleventh day, it is used for the funeral ball (piṇḍa).

One should perform the dismissal of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-visarjana) with the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," and having performed the Śrāddha for the eleven deities, one should perform it again on the following day.
One should invite five Brahmins who are experts in the four Vedas,
endowed with learning, virtuous conduct, and good qualities, who are of one's own kin, most excellent in character,
free from physical defects, and highly praised; such persons should never be avoided.
Viṣṇu should be made of gold, and Rudra likewise of copper;
Brahmā should be made of silver, and Yama should be made of iron.
One should place a lead figure, or alternatively one made of darbha grass, facing west; one should install Govinda with the mantra "śanno devī."
One should place Rudra in the north with the mantra "O Agni, come hither" (agna āyāhi),
and Prajāpati in the east with the mantra "I praise Agni" (agnim īḷe).
With the mantra "iṣetvorje," one should place Yama on the right;
having prepared a mandala in the center, a man made of darbha grass should be placed there.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, and the fifth, Preta,
should then be placed in separate jars, accompanied by the five jewels.
Wearing separate garments and sacred threads, and employing distinct mudrās,
one should perform the recitation separately for Brahmā and the other deities therein.
One should perform the five offerings to the deities according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should offer a stream of water separately upon each and every pedestal.
In a conch shell, or a copper vessel, or in the absence of these, even in one made of clay, having taken water with sesame seeds mixed with all medicinal herbs; GarP_2,40.39.
A seat, sandals, an umbrella, a finger-ring, a water-pot, a bowl, a bowl-rest, and garments— this is the eightfold set of requisites.
O Lord of Birds, one should give a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, along with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa in accordance with the prescribed rite.
One should give land with crops grown upon it to a Brahmin who has mastered the Ṛgveda, and one should give a milch cow to a Brahmin whose essence is the Yajurveda. (GarP 2.40.42)
