One should give gold for the sake of Śiva to the chanter of the Sāman;
then one should give sesame seeds and iron for the sake of Yama, and thereafter give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Afterwards, a figurine should be fashioned, provided with all medicinal herbs;
O Kāśyapa, hear now the division of the stalks of the *palāśa* tree.
Having spread out a black antelope skin and a human figure made of kuśa grass,
the collection of bones is said to consist of three hundred and sixty stalks.
Having placed those stalks individually upon these various limbs,
one should place forty in the region of the head and ten in the neck.
One should apply twenty [applications] to the chest, and twenty to the abdomen as well;
one should apply a hundred to the pair of arms, and twenty to the region of the hips.
One should place one hundred bones on the two thighs and thirty on each of the two shanks;
one should assign four to the penis and six to the two testicles;
ten to the region of the toes of the feet—in this manner, one should arrange the bones.
One should place a coconut in the position of the head and a gourd in the palate;
one should place the five jewels in the mouth and a plantain fruit on the tongue.
One should place a tube in the intestines for the child and for the vital breath;
one should provide fat and marrow, and for the urine, one should use cow's urine.
Sulphur, the metallic elements, yellow orpiment, and realgar should be given;
mercury is to be placed in the place of semen, and likewise brass in the place of feces.
Likewise, apply realgar to the limbs, sesame paste to the joints,
barley flour to the flesh, and indeed honey as well.
One should apply the roots of the *vaṭa* tree to the hair, deer-skin to the skin, palm leaves to the ears, and *guñjā* seeds to the breasts. (GarP 2.40.53)
A hundred-petaled lotus on the nose, a lotus at the navel-circle,
an eggplant on the pair of testicles, and auspicious gṛñjana on the penis.
Clarified butter should be applied to the navel, and tin is prescribed for the private parts;
pearls [should be worn] on the breasts, and the head should be anointed with saffron.
With incense of camphor and agallochum, auspicious garlands, and fragrant perfumes,
one should place a silken thread as a garment and a gold ornament upon the heart.
The two arms represent supernatural power and prosperity, the two eyes are [marked with] cowrie shells,
and vermilion is applied to the corners of the eyes, along with offerings such as betel leaf and other gifts.
Having prepared the deceased with all medicinal herbs, one should perform the worship as prescribed;
and according to the ritual involving fire, one should place the sacrificial vessels in their proper sequence.
Having performed the purification of the deceased with the *ṛc* "śīrṣe śrīḥ" and "punantu varuṇa," using water from rice, *śāla* trees, and stone; // GarP_2,40.59 //
A well-behaved, milch cow should be given, dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Sesame seeds, iron, gold, cotton, salt,
as well as the seven grains, land, and cows— each one of these is declared to be an equivalent gift.
Then, having given a vessel of sesame seeds, one should likewise give the gift of the feet.
Great gifts should be given, as well as a vessel of sesame seeds;
thereafter, the Vaitaraṇī river, adorned with all ornaments, should be offered.
A self-possessed person should indeed perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha for the sake of the liberation of the deceased;
then, having envisioned Viṣṇu in his heart, he should effect the release of the deceased.
Having recollected "Oṃ Viṣṇu" with reference to the deceased, his death,
and the cremation by fire, one should then observe the period of ritual impurity for three days.
The performer of the ten-day rites must offer rice balls for the enjoyment of the deceased;
one should perform the entire annual rite in this manner, and thus the deceased partakes in liberation.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Determination of Happiness, Suffering, Gain, and Loss in the Case of Untimely Death," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[End of] the Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*— 41.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord of Birds, one should perform the rite of releasing a bull according to the prescribed rules during the months beginning with Kārttika, on the auspicious day of the full moon."
One should commence the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha for the conclusion of the marriage ceremony;
one should also perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the earth and the installation of the sacred fire.
Then, having duly established the fire in a pond, a well, or a cow-pen,
one should perform everything according to the marriage rite, including the recitation by the Brāhmaṇas.
The placing of the vessels, the cooking, the *upayamana* grass and other implements,
and the sprinkling with water— after these, the twice-born should perform the *homa* with the Brahmin.
One should offer the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions as the two eyes;
furthermore, six oblations (*āhuti*) are to be offered with the mantra beginning "In the first day" (*prathame 'hani*).
The two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) are offered first; then the deities of the limbs are worshipped with milk-rice (pāyasa):
to Agni, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Śiva, Bhava, Mahādeva, Īśāna, and Yama.
One should perform a single oblation with flour paste using the mantra "pūṣā gā anvetu naḥ," and for both [the bride and groom],
there is a *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
First, there is the oblation of the *vyāhṛtis* as an expiation for Prajāpati;
one should then perform the consumption of the remnants and the release of the *praṇītā* water.
Then, having performed the purification rite and offered a sacrificial fee to a Brāhmaṇa, one who is purified by the recitation of the six-limbed Rudra-mantra shall attain liberation.
O Bird, having bathed a single-colored bull and a heifer, one should then adorn them with all types of ornaments.
Having established that pair [of images], the deceased shall attain liberation.
Afterward, an offering of libations (tarpaṇa) should be performed with mantras while the [images] are held aloft;
one should then feed the Brahmins and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha should be performed according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, water and food should be offered for the sake of the liberation of the deceased.
Then, on the twelfth day, one should perform [the rites] month after month individually;
for this procedure, when properly applied, indeed effects the liberation of the deceased.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Release of a Bull," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Viṣṇu said: The glorious Viṣṇu said:
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does previously performed karma follow after its doer.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, Hutāśana,
and the Lord who wields the trident— all these rejoice in the giver of land.
There is no gift equal to the earth; there is no treasure equal to the earth;
there is no teaching equal to truth; and there is no sin greater than falsehood.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu; and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
He who gives gold, a cow, and land has, by that act, bestowed the three worlds as a gift.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī;
these rescue one from hell through recitation, worship, and fire-offerings.
Even after committing many fierce and extensive sins,
one is purified by the gift of land, even if it is only the size of a cow-hide.
Even if it is carrying away [the mind] through greed, one should restrain and ward it off;
he who does not protect it goes to a terrible hell.
That which ought not to be done must not be done, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
that which ought to be done must indeed be done—thus do those who know the Dharma understand.
In causing a change in one's livelihood, the sin is equal to that of killing a thousand cows;
likewise, in cutting off a livelihood, the act is equivalent to the sin of stealing a hundred thousand cows.
A single cow taken away is better than a hundred cows given;
even by giving a hundred after taking one, there can be no equality between the two.
But he who, having given [a gift] himself, himself subverts it,
that sinner goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
And not even by means of a horse sacrifice duly performed with sacrificial fees is there such merit as when a wretched Brāhmaṇa, emaciated by lack of livelihood, is relieved.
That merit which is gained by protecting a weak and terrified Brāhmaṇa is not attained even through the Vedas or through a sacrifice accompanied by very large sacrificial fees.
Vehicles and armies, though well-nourished by the wealth of Brahmā,
crumble at the time of battle like sandcastles.
Whoever seizes land given by himself or given by another shall be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Brahmanical property consumed out of affection destroys the family unto the seventh generation;
that same property, when taken by way of theft, burns [the lineage] as long as the moon and stars exist.
A man might perhaps digest iron filings or stone dust;
but what man in the three worlds could ever digest the sound of the Veda?
By the destruction of the property of the gods, by the seizure of the property of Brahmins,
and by the transgression against Brahmins, entire families fall from their noble status.
There is no sequence of precedence for a Brahmin who is devoid of learning;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
Whatever gifts, whether offerings to the gods (havya) or offerings to the ancestors (kavya), are given at the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
the Sun bestows them again and again until the end of seven kalpas.
Among receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices, they say that receiving gifts is the most desired.
One is purified from receiving gifts by recitation and burnt offerings; the Vedas do not purify the act of officiating at sacrifices.
Always reciting mantras and always performing fire offerings, he avoids food cooked by others;
even if he were to accept the entire earth filled with jewels, he would remain unstained.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Gift of Land and Other Matters," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*) of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 43:
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
Those who have fallen from water, fire, or imprisonment, or those who have failed in their renunciation or died by fasting,
are purified by the two rites dedicated to Indra, as well as by giving a cow and a bull.
For one who is less than twelve years old but more than four years old,
the mother, the father, or even another relative shall perform the penance.
Therefore, even for an ignorant person, there is neither offense nor sin;
he incurs no royal punishment, nor is there any need for expiation.
If a woman who has been bitten is seen with blood [flowing from the wound], she becomes afflicted;
on the fourth day, having abandoned her feet and other limbs and bathed, she becomes pure.
When a person afflicted by disease has become impure, one who is not afflicted should bathe ten times;
having bathed repeatedly, he should touch that patient, and then that afflicted person shall become pure.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Purification," in the *Pretakalpa* of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
In the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 44:
Śrī Viṣṇu said:

O Tārkṣya, those who die by their own will as horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles, or through self-destruction such as that of Cāṇḍālas and others, or by means of poison and the like, or by being beaten; [these go to the hell called Raurava].
Those whose death occurs through falling into water or fire, by wind, or by fasting and other such means, are declared to be doers of evil deeds.
Those belonging to heretical sects and those outside the stages of life, as well as the perpetrators of mortal sins,
women who are unchaste, and likewise those who have fallen after having ascended [to a higher state].
For them there shall be no new śrāddha, nor the consecration rite (saṃskāra), nor the sapindana;
even the sixteen śrāddhas that have been prescribed do not apply to them.
If one should cast his wages into the water, or if he should take the domestic fire to a crossroads,
or if he should burn his vessels in the fire— [this applies] to a sinner who maintains a sacred fire.
When a full year has passed for them, O Kāśyapa, those who are compassionate should perform this rite upon reaching the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings,
one should place ten rice-balls, smeared with ghee and mixed with honey, upon blades of darbha grass.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, meditating upon Viṣṇu and Yama,
he should silently offer each of those [portions] of sesame seeds while facing the south.
Having extracted them and mixed them together, one should subsequently cast them well into the sacred water (tīrtha);
while casting them, one should proclaim the name and the lineage (gotra) of the deceased.
Furthermore, one should again worship Viṣṇu and Yama with flowers and sandalwood,
along with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and delicacies.
On that day of fasting, one should invite Brahmins who are endowed with noble lineage, learning, and austerity, and who are possessed of virtuous conduct.
Nine, seven, or five [offerings], according to one's own capacity;
on the following day at midday, one should likewise worship Yama and Viṣṇu.
He should properly seat those Brahmins facing north;
at the beginning of the invocation and the offering of the *argha* water, he should invoke Viṣṇu together with Yama.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should perform the rite and proclaim the name of the deceased;
remembering the deceased, Yama, and Viṣṇu, one should bring the Śrāddha ceremony to completion.
One should set aside [rice] from all other portions for the purpose of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍas);
or alternatively, one should offer ten separate cakes, or five, in due order.
First, one should offer to Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, and to Śiva;
then to Śiva together with his attendants, and fifthly, to the deceased.
One should remember his name and lineage and proclaim the word "Viṣṇu";
one should offer the fifth funeral cake (piṇḍa) preceded by a salutation.
Remembering that deceased person according to his capacity, he should offer gifts of cattle, land, balls of rice, and so forth;
and with sesame seeds, he should offer sesame to the Brahmins in their hands which are joined with *darbha* grass.
One should give food to the twice-born, as well as betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee;
in this manner, one should worship the most excellent Brahmin with gold.
Recalling the name and lineage [of the deceased], he should give [the gift] while saying, "May there be pleasure for Viṣṇu";
then, having followed behind the twice-born, he should turn away from the water, facing south.
Proclaiming the name and lineage [of the deceased], he should cast [the water] on the ground, saying, "May there be satisfaction.

Together with friends and kinsmen, he should eat the remainder while remaining restrained in speech. This annual rite and others should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* offering.
When this is done, even those who have committed evil deeds will go to the heavenly world;
and once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites have been performed, they truly attain [liberation].
Now, if someone should die through negligence by means of water or other causes,
one should perform for him everything according to the rule, beginning with the rites for the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Out of negligence or by choice, a mortal should not go face-to-face with a serpent;
one should worship the Naga on both fortnights and on the fifth lunar days.
One should fashion an image of the Nāgas out of flour upon the ground;
one should worship it with white flowers, fragrant scents, and sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense and lamps, scatter white rice grains,
and likewise present food made of raw flour as well as milk.
Having approached [the deity], he should speak thus while casting off his garments and ornaments;
on that day he should eat sweet food and conclude the divine *śrāddha*.
Then, according to one's means, one should give a golden serpent to an excellent brahmin;
having given a cow, one should then say: "May the King of Nagas be pleased."
One should perform other rites as previously described according to one's capacity;

thus, one should act exactly in accordance with the injunctions prescribed in one’s own Vedic branch (śākhā). In this manner, one should liberate those beings from the state of a preta and lead them upon the path to heaven.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of What Should and Should Not Be Done Regarding Deaths Occurring Under Unnatural Circumstances," in the *Pretakalpa* (Section on the Departed) within the *Dharmakāṇḍa* (Section on Dharma), the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* (Latter Section) of the *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. —
*Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 45.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
O Lord of Birds, I shall thus describe to you the annual Śrāddha;
every year, both the legitimate son and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) should perform it according to the pārvaṇa rite.
The Ekoddiṣṭa rite is performed by others according to this same procedure; it is not the Pārvaṇa rite.
The two sons of one who is without a sacred fire—the legitimate son and the son born of the wife—shall themselves remain without a sacred fire;
they shall not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite annually, but rather the *pārvaṇa* rite.
But when either the son or the father possesses the sacred fires,
then both the *kṣetraja* and the *aurasa* sons should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite there every year.
Whether they are without sacred fires or possess them, whether they be sons or even fathers,
some say that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed by sons on the anniversary of the death-day (*kṣayāha*).
If one's [ancestral] share is subject to depletion at the time of the new moon or again during the fortnight of the departed (pretapakṣa),
then the annual pārvaṇa rite must be performed for him by all his sons.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed for men who have no sons, and likewise for women.
In the *ekoddiṣṭa*, as well as in sacrificial rites, *kuśa* grass with roots should be taken;
at a *śrāddha* for prosperity (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*) or at death, it should always be cut once and trimmed on the outside.
If impurity (āśauca) should arise when the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha is to be performed,
one should indeed perform that Śrāddha immediately upon the cessation of the impurity.
But if an obstacle should arise when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived,
one should indeed perform that Śrāddha on the very same lunar day of the following month.

The Śrāddha for a Śūdra, for his wife, for his son, for his daughter, for the twice-born who have not yet undergone initiation, and for a twice-born man who has not yet been initiated, should be performed silently.
If one goes to the slaughterhouse at the same time for many or even for two,
one may perform the cooking by way of a single ritual procedure (tantra), but one should perform the śrāddha offerings separately for each.
One should first give [the offering] for the one who died first; then again for the second;
then one should perform it for the third. This is the rule (the sequence) in the event of a simultaneous occurrence of deaths.
He who performs this every year in whatever manner possible, remaining untiring,
shall deliver all his ancestors and attain the supreme goal.
If the day of death is not known, as well as the day of departure,
but the month is known, then the anniversary of the death should be observed on the new moon day (darśa) of that month.
When the month is not known but the day is known,
then that day shall fall in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.
When the day and month of [one's own] death are unknown, however,
the day and month of departure [from home] are to be taken for the śrāddha, as I have declared.
Furthermore, when neither the day nor the month of departure is known,
the news of death should be accepted according to the sequence previously described.
Even in the absence of travel, if those two [the anniversary of death and the anniversary of birth] are forgotten,
they should still be observed at that time, just as in the case of the monthly death-anniversary rite.
If someone dies in the house while the householder is away on a journey, then, upon the conclusion of the period of impurity when the śrāddha rite has been commenced; // GarP_2,45.19 //
If the householder returns and learns of what occurred there,
then the period of impurity for those householders shall apply to them, but not to their property and so forth.
Whatever Śrāddha has been commenced by a son or others should be completed in its entirety according to the truth; even there, one should keep the Śrāddha at a distance from worldly attachment.
Neither the giver nor the eater knows of birth or death;
he never imputes that fault to either of the two.
But when either a birth-impurity (sūtaka) or a death-impurity (mṛtaka) is known only to the eater, then the fault belongs to the eater alone; the other, the giver, does not incur any defilement.
Whoever performs the rite for the day of death in the manner thus described— even if the day of death is unknown— he constantly delivers [the deceased].
Then, in the daily *śrāddha*, having reverently honored the twice-born with perfumes and other offerings,
one should properly join them together while designating all the classes of ancestors.

The invocation, the utterance of *svadhā*, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the ritual of placing food in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and so forth, as well as the observances such as celibacy and the Viśvedevas; // GarP_2.45.26 //
In the daily *śrāddha*, one should avoid these [unfit persons] and prepare food fit for consumption;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should dismiss them with prostrations. (GarP 2.45.27)
Whatever feeding of Brahmins one should give, directed toward the Viśvedevas and other deities, that is to be performed like a Nityaśrāddha; it is called Devaśrāddha.
The śrāddha for the mother should be performed to the east at the beginning of the rite, and likewise that for the paternal ancestors;
however, on the following day, during a festival (vṛddhi), there should be one for the group of maternal grandfathers.
One should perform the three types of *śrāddha* and the *vaiśvadeva* rite according to the Tantric tradition.
One should first prepare for the mothers, immediately after that for the fathers, and likewise offer for the maternal grandfathers; thus indeed should one proceed in this order.
But in the śrāddha for one's mother, in the absence of Brahmins,
one should invite eight virtuous women of noble birth who are accompanied by their husbands and sons.
One should perform the *iṣṭāpūrta* rites, the *śrāddha*, and likewise the *ābhyudayika* [śrāddha];
however, on occasions such as portents, one should perform it exactly like the daily *śrāddha*.
By performing the daily (nitya), ancestral (daiva), prosperity-seeking (vṛddhi), optional (kāmya), and occasional (naimittika) śrāddhas according to the prescribed method, one shall attain success.
Thus has it been told to you, O Tārkṣya; what else do you wish to ask?

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the second part, the Dharma-kāṇḍa, in the section on the Pretas, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, this is the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual Śrāddha and Others. Tārkṣya said:
By the power of their well-performed deeds, various heavens belong to men;
as do enjoyments, exquisite happiness, beauty, strength, wisdom, and valor. (GarP 2.46.1)
O Lord, truth arises for the meritorious both in this world and in the next;
truth, truth, and again truth—this is the word of the Vedas and it is not otherwise.
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood;
forbearance triumphs, not anger; Viṣṇu triumphs, not the asura.
In that same way, truth has been known by me; from good deeds, excellence arises, for merit is most excellent, and likewise, man is most excellent.
Thus, I wish to hear how sinners are born,
by what ripening of karma, and how they come to experience their destined lot.
O best of gods, tell me in brief, as I desire to know, what kind of womb one enters and what form one is born with.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Tārkṣya, O Kāśyapa, hear from me those characteristics by which men here, having experienced the enjoyments resulting from their auspicious and inauspicious deeds, are born again."
The guru is the teacher of those who possess self-control; the king is the teacher of the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the teacher of those who commit sins in secret in this world.
Those who have not performed their penances for various kinds of punishments in the world of Yama go instead to the stream of living beings.
Having entered into human existence, they become marked by signs of evil;
O best of birds, I shall describe those signs to you.
Having endured all the torments and gone to the abode of Vaivasvata,
those who have emerged from their torments go to the world marked by [their merits].
One who speaks falsely becomes stammering; one who lies regarding a cow becomes mute;
a killer of a Brahmin is born with leprosy, and a drinker of liquor has black teeth.

Through the theft of gold one becomes a man with deformed nails; through violating the Guru’s bed, one suffers from skin disease; through sexual union with those of low birth, one is born into a base womb; and through failing to give what should be given, one becomes impoverished.
A twice-born man who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice goes to the state of a crocodile or a pig;
he who performs many sacrifices becomes a donkey, and from eating without mantras, he becomes a crow.
Those who consume without investigation would be like tigers in a desolate forest; a cat is a constant harasser, a firefly is a burner of the undergrowth. (GarP 2.46.15)
He who gives knowledge for the sake of a vessel shall become a bull;
he who gives stale food to a Brahmin shall become a dog.
One who steals a book becomes blind from birth due to stinginess;
the child of one who steals fruit dies—of this there is no doubt. (GarP 2.46.17)
Upon death, he goes to the state of a monkey; he becomes one with a face like that [of a monkey] and a swollen cheek.
He who eats food without having given it away shall be childless.
One who steals clothing becomes a lizard; one who administers poison becomes a wind-eater (a snake); and by abandoning the life of a wandering mendicant, O King, one becomes a desert-dwelling piśāca.
One who steals water becomes a cātaka bird; one who steals grain becomes a mouse;
and by consorting with a girl who has not reached puberty, one becomes a serpent—so says the sacred tradition.
One who lusts after the wife of his guru will certainly become a chameleon;
and a man who breaks a flowing spring of water shall become a fish.
By selling what should not be sold, a man becomes a heron or a vulture;
by violating the womb, he becomes a wolf, and by cheating in trade, an owl.
One who eats on the eleventh day after a person has died will be reborn as a jackal;
likewise, one who promises wealth to the twice-born but does not give it becomes a jackal.
One who goes to the king's enemy becomes a fanged beast; a thief becomes a dog; one who sells *śārivā* becomes a boar; and one who is the husband of a low-caste woman becomes a bull.
A cat that touches fire with its paw becomes diseased and a consumer of other beings' flesh; from approaching a woman in her courses, one becomes impotent, foul-smelling, and a thief of fragrances.
Whether it be this or that, even if it be very small, whoever steals another's property—even if much—he indeed attains the womb of animals after stealing it; there is no doubt in this.
O Lord of Birds, these and other such signs,
which are indeed the expansion of one's own karma,
are seen by those human beings.
Thus, having experienced the hells in succession for their evil deeds,
one is born by the remainder of that karma into these aforementioned wombs.
Then, O Kāśyapa, for a hundred births among all living beings in the mortal world, one is born;
there is no doubt in this matter once the wholesome and unwholesome have been equalized.
When the semen and blood of a woman and a man have been joined through their union,
the being composed of the five elements is born, endowed with those five elements.
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breaths, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, and false egoism— GarP_2,46.31.
But for this self, which seeks a beginning for itself despite being beginningless, its very form, color, passion, hatred, existence, and non-existence are all [conditioned by that].
Then, for one bound by their own karma, there shall be growth within the womb;
indeed, this is the characteristic of a living being as previously described by me to you.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, when this wheel has been set in motion among the fourfold collection of beings,
the birth and destruction of embodied beings occur.
By one's own dharma alone, O bird, upward movement occurs; by unrighteousness, downward movement arises for all castes through deviation from their own dharma.
O Vainateya, whatever actions such as giving and enjoying are seen in the states of divinity and humanity, all that is the fruit born of karma.
One will surely fall again into a terrible, inauspicious hell, earned through desire and anger and not produced by [proper] action; for that person, no crossing back out exists.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious and Inauspicious Destinies of the Soul," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
The Glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—Chapter 47.
Garuḍa said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, please out of supreme compassion tell me of the gift,
the greatness of giving, and the measurement of the Vaitaraṇī.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
That great river named Vaitaraṇī on the path of Yama is bottomless and difficult for sinners to cross; it is terrifying as soon as it is seen.
Abounding with fluids of pus and blood, filled with the mud of flesh, and overwhelmed by various terrors upon seeing the sinners who have arrived; (47.3)
The water boils quickly within the vessel like clarified butter;
it is filled with pus teeming with worms and covered by those with adamantine beaks.
And with crocodiles and sea-monsters equipped with diamond-hard pincers,
as well as other aquatic creatures that are predatory and capable of tearing through flesh.
For at the end of the dissolution, those twelve suns indeed rise;
there, mortals who are evildoers suffer while crying out.
"Alas, brother! Son! Father!"—thus do living beings lament again and again;
they wander about, sink down, and fall into exhaustion.
The great river is seen to be filled with four kinds of hosts of living beings;
they cross over by means of the gift of a cow, but otherwise they fall.
Those fools who despise me, as well as their teacher, their guru, and other elders— their dwelling shall indeed be there.
Those fools who abandon a devoted wife of virtuous character, who is wedded to them and steadfast in her duties, shall dwell perpetually in hell.
Indeed, having committed the murder of those who have placed their trust in them— be they masters, friends, ascetics, women, children, the infirm,
and so forth— the sinners fall there and are cooked in its midst while wailing.
He who approaches to obstruct a peaceful Brahmin who is hungry shall be devoured by worms there until the dissolution of all beings.
If one promises a certain object to a Brahmin and then,
having summoned him, says "it does not exist," his residence shall indeed be there [in hell].
The arsonist, the poisoner, the false witness, the drinker of intoxicants, the destroyer of sacrifices, the one who approaches the king’s wife, and the slanderer; GarP_2,47.14 //
One who interrupts a discourse, one who seizes what has been given by oneself, one who destroys the boundaries of fields, and one who violates the wives of others; GarP_2,47.15 //
A Brahmin who sells liquids, as well as one who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī, and he who causes the breach of a reservoir for cattle afflicted by thirst; GarP_2,47.16 //
One who defiles a maiden, one who regrets a gift after giving it, a Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapilā cow, and a Brāhmaṇa who eats meat; // GarP_2,47.17 //
"These dwell here constantly; do not entertain any doubt about this anywhere.
O bird, that person who dwells there is a wretched, atheistic, and base man."
One who is always resentful, always angry, who treats his own words as the ultimate authority, and who constantly suppresses the speech of others, shall dwell for a long time in the Vaitaraṇī hell.
But he who is full of egoism, sinful, and a self-boaster; he who is ungrateful and causes distress to the fetus—he sinks into the Vaitaraṇī river.
If, by some stroke of fortune, a desire for liberation should ever arise in you,
listen, O Kāśyapa, to that which will make it favorable.
During the solstices, at the meridian equinoxes, on auspicious occasions, at the onset of day,
during lunar or solar eclipses, at the passage of the sun into a new zodiac sign, or on the new moon day.
At other auspicious times, the highest gift is given;
at such times, those who are faithful shall certainly be intent upon giving.
That indeed should be the time for giving, since prosperity is unstable;
bodies are impermanent, and wealth is never eternal.
Death is ever-present; therefore, one should practice the accumulation of dharma.
One should also fashion the auspicious Vaitaraṇī river, either black or pale-red in color.
[One should give] a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel,
covered with a pair of black cloths, and provided with the seven types of grain.
One should fashion a golden image of Yama seated upon a heap of a drona-measure of cotton, holding a copper vessel and equipped with an iron staff;
having constructed a raft made of sugarcane stalks with very firm bindings.
Having placed that cow, born from the body of the Sun,
upon a raft, O Brahmin, he should provide it with an umbrella and sandals.
One should present a ring and garments to a Brāhmaṇa, while holding kuśa grass with water and reciting this mantra: GarP_2,47.29.
Having heard of that Vaitaraṇī at the most terrible gate of Yama, and desiring to cross it, I give this to you; homage to Vaitaraṇī!
May cows be before me; may cows be at my sides;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
O Viṣṇu-form, best of the twice-born, O protector of the earth, deliver me!
This sacrificial fee has been given by me to you; salutations to Vaitaraṇī!
Having circumambulated Dharmarāja, the Lord of All, and the cow named Vaitaraṇī, one should present everything to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having grasped the tail of the cow and placed the twice-born man at her head, [one should say]:
"O cow, wait for me at the gate of Yama, which is full of great terror. (GarP 2.47.34)
"O Goddess, for the sake of deliverance across the Vaitaraṇī, salutations be to you!
One should follow him as he goes and lead him entirely to his home. (GarP 2.47.35)
O Vainateya, when this is done, that river becomes most excellent;
whatever man on earth should give [this gift], he attains all his desires.
By the power of well-performed deeds, there is happiness both here and in the next world;
it is multiplied a thousandfold when one is healthy, and measured at a hundredfold when one is afflicted by illness.
But that gift which is given for one who has already died, when he is out of sight, is considered equal [to giving while he is present].
Therefore, it should be given with one's own hand; for once dead, who will give to whom?
Those devoid of the virtue of giving live as miserable wretches;
therefore, with this unstable body, one should perform deeds that are stable.
The vital breaths will certainly depart, like transient guests.
Thus, O King of Birds, this entire mockery of the multitude of living beings has been described to you.
Therefore, for the sake of the liberation of the deceased and for the welfare and auspiciousness of the world, one should perform these rites both for the hereafter and for this life.
Sūta said:
Thus instructed by the powerful Viṣṇu, O Brahmins,
Garuḍa attained great satisfaction upon hearing the account of the deceased man's conduct.
Having meditated in his mind upon the Lord of All, the cause of all causes, he again questioned Keśava regarding everything, including vows, sacred fords, and so forth.
The sages [know] all this— the origin and so forth of living beings,
as well as death, birth, the state of being a preta, and the funeral rites for the deceased.
I have indeed proclaimed the cause for liberation in its entirety:
"Blessed are they, victorious are they; whence can there be defeat for those in whose hearts Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, resides?"
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood;
forbearance triumphs, not anger; Viṣṇu triumphs, not the asuras.
Viṣṇu is the mother, Viṣṇu is the father, and Viṣṇu is one's own kinsmen and relatives;
for those whose intellect is firmly fixed in this way, there shall be no miserable rebirth.
Auspicious is the Blessed Viṣṇu; auspicious is he whose banner bears Garuḍa;
auspicious is the lotus-eyed one; Hari is the abode of all that is auspicious.
Hari is the Bhāgīrathī, O brahmins; the Bhāgīrathī is the brahmins;
the Bhāgīrathī, Hari, and the brahmins—this is the essence within the three worlds.
Having drunk this nectar of speech belonging to Viṣṇu, which issued from the mouth of the Sūta and was adorned with the meaning of all the scriptures, the sages attained great satisfaction.
Thus the sages, headed by Śaunaka, praised one another and the charioteer who perceives all things; they attained incomparable joy.
Whether impure or pure, or even having reached every possible state,
whoever remembers the lotus-eyed Lord becomes pure both externally and internally.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ripening of Karma and Other Matters," in the second section of the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa concerning the vision of the dead and the nature of dharma.
In the *Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, Chapter 48:
Tārkṣya said:
Those mortals who dwell in the world of men all go to their destruction within their own species at their appointed time according to the measure of their own merit; tell me, O Lord, how this is so.
Established upon the path fashioned by the Creator, they travel along that most difficult road;
by what merit do they attain joy, and by what do they abide with noble lineage, strength, and youth? (GarP 2.48.2)
Sūta said:
Then, having heard this, the Lord remembered his own form and the terrifying nature of his deeds, and spoke to Garuḍa:
"By him the earth was created, by whom the world of moving and unmoving beings was fashioned, and by whom the omnipresent Yama was appointed as the punisher."
The Blessed One said:
Having entered that other second path leading to Yama, which accumulates dharma, artha, kāma, and long-term liberation,
and having reached his own body there in a space the size of a thumb, he [attains] his own abode.
O twice-born one, having taken up the noose and remaining within a body in this most meritorious region, he weeps again and again;
yet, due to delusion, he does not perform the worship of the Lord of Gods nor the gratification of the ancestors and deities, nor does he seek the lineage of sons.

"I have no kinsman who can follow the path of Yama; I have no need for you, desiring as I do the body of a twice-born. Having attained the state of a Brahmin, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, I have not studied the Vedas, Purāṇas, or Saṃhitās.
A supreme jewel, held in the palm of my hand, has slipped away; rescue yourself from wherever you have gone, for that which was done by you is lost."

That Kṣatriya who, in battle, drank blood from the surface of his forehead with his own arms—that indeed constitutes the drinking of Soma in the great sacrifice; though he is as if dead while yet living, he goes to liberation.
Many positions have been taken and many drinks have been consumed that are censured;
yet he who, taking up a weapon, goes face-to-face against his enemies in battle, is liberated from sin.
Whether he belongs to the lineage of the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, or even the low-caste Śūdras;
whether he is a slayer of warriors, gods, brahmins, or children; or a killer of women, the elderly, the wretched, and ascetics.
If one turns his back when these [ancestors] are in distress, all the gods turn their backs upon him;
his ancestors do not drink the water with sesame seeds, nor does the consumer of oblations accept that which was offered.
O Lord of Birds, when battle has arrived, he who takes up a weapon and faces the enemy army out of hatred or fear,
yet does not advance, his kṣatriya strength has likewise departed;
however, having given gold and this earth to a brahmin, he becomes great once again in this world.

He gave gifts during eclipses, performed ablutions at excellent sacred fords, and having gone to Gayā, he constantly offered funeral cakes to his ancestors; such a person who dies in battle [attains liberation].
"O Kṣatriya, having abandoned my body on the field of battle when my master was slain, or during the seizure of cattle,
or upon the slaughter of women and children, or for the sake of a caravan on the road, I have neither failed to strike nor failed to fell my own treasury [of weapons]."
Then the Vaiśya lamented over his own duties, bound by the noose: "Even by me nothing was accumulated;
out of delusion and for the sake of my family, I did not speak the truth in buying and selling. (GarP 2.48.14)

Having attained a Śūdra body that brings constant fame, you never gave gifts to the twice-born nor performed worship of the twice-born; you never constructed a reservoir of water upon the earth, nor did you consecrate an eminent Brāhmaṇa who had not yet been consecrated.

Abandoning my own duties due to intoxication, I remained complacent; I did not cast off my body at a sacred ford, nor was dharma strengthened by me, nor was worship of the gods performed for the sake of liberation.

Having likewise attained a body born of a physical aggregate, as well as those designated as the lowest castes or barbarians, these beings enter a body composed of air; they do not desire this while on the path crowded with dharma.
Cutting through their own dharma and wandering on the path toward their respective goals, listen to those words of the Lord of Birds which he speaks so delightfully. (GarP 2.48.18)
For among all worlds, the three realms are indeed the essence; among all continents, that named Jambū;
among all lands, the land of the gods; and among all living beings, human beings alone.
In this world, the four castes are praised, and among the castes, those men who are most righteous are praised;
by means of dharma one attains all happiness, and standing upon the great path, one acquires knowledge.
When my life has ended and I have cast off this body, O bird, I shall exist as a worm or an insect;
I shall be fashioned as a reptile, a mosquito, a quadruped, or a wild boar.
For while still situated in the womb, one knows everything; yet as soon as born, one may forget this very thing.
Whatever was indeed thought by one who had entered the womb, [one remembers] having become a child, a youth, and an old man.
If that which was conceived in the womb is lost through delusion, and is remembered again once the body has passed away;
and when that [body] has perished, what was conceived in the heart is gone, yet it is remembered again once the body has entered the womb.
When that [thought] had vanished from my heart, I reflected again: "I have practiced deceiving others for the sake of my own treasury;
I have transgressed righteousness by means of gambling, trickery, and even the profession of theft, all for the protection of my body."
Wealth was acquired by me with great hardship, yet I did not personally enjoy the riches desired by my mind;
instead, I gave betel, food, sweets, and products of the cow to the fire-god, the deities, guests, and my circle of kinsmen.
O embodied one, even during lunar or solar eclipses, you did not resort to this most excellent and supreme of holy places;
rather, you have filled your own treasury with filth and urine—extricate yourself from that which you have done!

I have neither seen, nor bowed to, nor worshipped the form of the Three-Strider standing here upon this earth; nor has the Lord Prabhāsa been praised with devotion anywhere, O Dehin—consider what you have done! GarP_2,48.27 //
Having gone to the most excellent places on earth near sacred fords, I did not place wealth in the hands of the learned;
having bathed my body according to the rules before the twice-born preceptor, I have somehow emerged from that which was done by you.
There is no worship of the Mother, nor Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, nor Gaṇeśa and Caṇḍī, nor even the Sun;
nor are there any services with offerings, oblations, or sandalwood paste—whatever you have done, O embodied one, by that alone cross over.
O King, out of delusion I obtained all this which was like that of a god among men;
yet that person of utterly confused intellect did not foresee his destiny. Therefore, cross over wherever you have been bound by your own actions.
Having reflected in their minds upon these words which bring about dharma, purpose, and fame,
those birds who dwell in a noble land and are devoted to dharma attain liberation in the world of men.

Thus being struck by the throngs of Yama’s messengers who speak these words and by hammers made of Time, he indeed remembers with cries of "Alas, Fate! Alas, Fate! the wealth that he himself earned but failed to give away.
Neither the gift of land, nor the gift of cows, nor the gift of water, nor the gift of clothing;
nor even the fruit of betel-leaves or ointments was given by you on this earth—why do you lament now?
Your father is dead, as is your grandfather—he who once held you within his own womb;
even all those kinsmen are dead. You have seen all this with your own eyes as it passed away.
Your treasury has been consumed by fire, and the accumulation of wealth and grain has been seized by your sons;
only that which you have made into a collection of Dharma through well-spoken words shall follow after you.

Not a single dead person is seen who has returned—whether it be a king, an ascetic, or even a preeminent brahmin; for that mortal who was reckless has met his destruction, even as he stood upon the surface of the earth.
Thus those hosts, including the kinnaras, spoke while maintaining their composure though filled with grief;
having heard the most wonderful words of the hosts, the lord of birds, who had attained human form, replied: GarP_2,48.37 //

By the power of generosity, Dharma is his father, established in celestial palaces; Speech, speaking words of sweet meaning, is his wife, corresponding to his compassion for his mother; bathing at sacred fords and a circle of good kinsmen are his.
Whatever merit has been offered by the hand, all that shall become heaven for you;
he who is righteous shall attain supreme happiness, while the sinner shall experience every kind of manifold suffering.
That man who is virtuous in dharma, who has conquered pride and anger, who is disciplined by knowledge, who does not harm others,
who is content with his own wife and stays far from the wives of others— he indeed is not merely worthy of veneration on earth.
The giver of sweet food, one who has maintained the agnihotra fire, a knower of Vedānta, one who lives for a thousand moons,
one who observes the month-long fast, and a devoted wife— these six are worthy of my salutation in the world of the living.

A man endowed with such conduct likewise constructs a well with a water-wheel, a pond filled with water, a beautiful water-station, or a temple for the heart-god; by that very act, he performs the highest dharma.
A year's worth of food was given to one learned in the Vedas, and the marriage of a daughter served as the discharge of debt to a twice-born man;
even well-tilled land was given for the sake of relieving the pain of thirst—thus, all this constitutes my accumulated merit.
He who hears or even chants this chapter, the essence of meritorious deeds, with purity of heart, is indeed noble and endowed with dharma; he shall surely go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharma and Adharma that Bring about Happiness and Suffering for Human Beings," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Śrī-Gāruḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
— *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*: 49.
Garuḍa said:
"O ocean of compassion, I have heard from you how the cycle of existence for living beings arises from ignorance;
now I wish to hear the eternal means for liberation."
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
in this essence-less, terrible saṃsāra, which is defiled by all forms of suffering.
Infinite multitudes of living beings, residing in various kinds of bodies, are born and die; there is no end to them.
They are always afflicted by suffering; no friend whatsoever exists for them.
O Lord of Liberation, tell me, O Master, by what means are they liberated? 49.4.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Tārkṣya, I shall declare that which you ask me;
by the mere hearing of which a person is liberated from saṃsāra.
There exists the Lord Śiva, whose nature is the supreme Brahman;
he is partless, omniscient, the creator of all, the lord of all, stainless, and non-dual.

He is self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; those who are His portions are known as individual souls (jīvas).
Afflicted by beginningless ignorance, like sparks within a fire,
they are differentiated by the limiting adjuncts of the body and so forth, through beginningless karmas.
Restrained by various types of merit and demerit which bestow pleasure and pain,
they obtain a body, lifespan, and experience born of karma, endowed with their respective species.
O bird, even for them, that supreme [state] is attained again in every birth,
along with the subtle liṅga-body, until liberation from the imperishable.
Immovable beings, worms, goats, birds, cattle, trees,
the righteous gods, and likewise those destined for liberation, follow this sequence respectively.
Having assumed and discarded thousands of fourfold bodies,
if one becomes wise after being born anew from well-performed deeds, one shall attain liberation.
Among the eighty-four hundred thousand bodies of embodied beings,
the knowledge of reality is not obtained anywhere else except in a human body.
In this world, even after thousands or tens of millions of births,
a living being may at some point obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit.
Having attained this human state, which is so difficult to find and serves as a staircase to liberation,
who in this world could be more sinful than he who does not deliver himself?
A man who, having obtained this birth and having acquired the excellence of the senses,
does not know what is beneficial for the self— he would be a slayer of Brahman.
Without a body, the human goal (puruṣārtha) of anyone does not exist;
therefore, one should protect the body and wealth, and accomplish meritorious deeds.
One should always protect oneself, for the self is the vessel of everything;
one should apply effort toward its protection, for while living, one beholds auspicious things.
Again there is a village, again a field, again wealth, and again a house;
again there is wholesome and unwholesome karma, but the body is not [reborn] again and again.
The wise always employ means for the protection of the body,
and even those afflicted by leprosy and other such diseases do not wish to abandon it.
That [teaching] should be guarded for the sake of Dharma; Dharma is for the sake of knowledge alone, and knowledge is for the sake of the yoga of meditation, whereby one is swiftly liberated.
If the self itself does not restrain itself from harmful things,
what other benefactor is there who will bring happiness to the self?
He who does not seek treatment for the disease of hell while still here— once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, what will he do when afflicted by disease?
Old age approaches like a tigress, and life passes away like water from a broken jar;
diseases strike like enemies; therefore, one should practice that which leads to the highest good.
As long as one does not experience suffering, as long as calamities do not arrive,
and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should one practice for the highest good.
As long as this body remains, one should practice the essential truth;
otherwise, the fool is like one who digs a well while his house is on fire.
Time is not perceived due to the various activities arising from cyclic existence;
alas, people do not understand pleasure, pain, or what is truly beneficial for themselves.
Seeing those born afflicted, those dead, and those fallen into calamity— all suffering—
the world, having drunk the wine of delusion, never fears.
Prosperity is like a dream, youth is comparable to a flower, and life is as fleeting as lightning; for one who knows this, how could there be any steadfastness?
A hundred-year lifespan is exceedingly short; half of it is spent in sleep and lethargy.
What remains is diminished by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age—and even that is fruitless.
Alas, what man is not destroyed who is devoid of effort when action must begin, who sleeps when he should be awake, and who is full of trust where there is cause for fear? (GarP 2.49.31)
When the body, which resembles the foam of water, stands occupied by the life-force,
how can one remain fearless in this impermanent abode of exertion?
One who perceives what is harmful as beneficial, one who perceives the impermanent as permanent,
and one who perceives the non-beneficial as beneficial— he is one who does not understand his own true interest.
Though seeing, he stumbles; though hearing, he does not understand;
though reciting, he does not know—deluded by the divine illusion.
This world, sinking into the deep ocean of time,
is not perceived by anyone as it is seized by the crocodiles of death, disease, and old age.
Time, which brings fear at every moment, is not perceived as it wanes;
like a raw clay pot submerged in water, it is not noticed until it has shattered.
It is as reasonable to attempt to wrap the wind or to break the sky,
as to tie together waves or place one's trust in life.
By that [fire] the earth is consumed and even Mount Meru is shattered;
the waters of the ocean dry up—what need is there to speak of the body?
"Offspring are mine, my wife is mine, wealth is mine, and my kinsmen are mine"—while the mortal speaks thus, the wolf of Time forcibly slays him. (GarP 2.49.39)
"This has been done, this is to be done, and this other thing is half-finished"—
Kṛtānta brings under his control one who is thus occupied with such worldly striving.
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what belongs to the afternoon;
for death does not wait to see whether a task is finished or yet unfinished.
Why does he not see a savior— one who has been shown the path by old age, whose soldiers are fierce diseases, and who is presided over by the enemy Death?
Pierced by the needle of craving, sprinkled with the ghee of sense objects,
and cooked in the fire of passion and hatred, Death devours the human being.
Death enters all—those who are children, those established in youth, the elderly, and even those still in the womb; such is this world of living beings.
This living being goes even to the abode of Yama, leaving behind its own body;
for what reason, then, should there be attachment to relations such as wife, mother, father, or son?
For cyclic existence is the root of suffering; whoever possesses it is one who suffers.
He by whom its abandonment has been accomplished is happy, and no other anywhere.
One should abandon saṃsāra in an instant— it is the source of all sufferings, the abode of all calamities, and the refuge of all evils.
A man bound by fetters made of iron or wood may be released;
but he is never released from the fetters consisting of son and wife.
As many dear relationships as a living being forms with the mind,
so many spikes of sorrow are driven into his heart.
The world has been constantly ruined by those who have stolen all its wealth—alas, by the thieves of the senses dwelling within the body that feed upon sense-objects! GarP_2,49.50.
Just as a fish greedy for flesh does not see the iron hook,
so too the embodied being greedy for pleasure does not see the affliction of Yama.
O Bird, those men who do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful, who constantly follow the wrong path,
and whose sole aim is the filling of their bellies, are denizens of hell.
Sleep, fear, sexual intercourse, and food are common to all living beings;
a human being is said to be possessed of knowledge, while one devoid of knowledge is considered a beast.
At dawn they are afflicted by excrement and urine; at midday by hunger and thirst;
and at night by passion and sleep—thus are foolish men tormented.
All living beings are intent upon their own bodies, wealth, wives, and so forth;
they are born and they die—alas! indeed, deluded by ignorance.
Therefore, attachment should always be abandoned; if it cannot be abandoned, one should associate with the great, for the virtuous are the remedy for attachment.
He who possesses neither the company of the virtuous nor discernment—those two stainless eyes—is blind; how could such a man not stray from the path?
All human beings devoted solely to the conduct of their own respective castes and stages of life do not know the supreme Dharma; these hypocrites perish in vain.
Why do some people, devoted to exertion and engaged in the practice of vows and other observances,
wander about as itinerant teachers while their very selves are shrouded in ignorance?
Men who are satisfied with mere names, devoted to the ritualistic section [of the Veda],
are deluded by the recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and the extensive performance of sacrifices.
Deluded and bewildered by my māyā, fools desire that which is beyond perception through restrictive practices such as eating once a day or fasting, which merely wither the body.
What liberation can there be for the undiscriminating merely through the punishment of the body?
Does a great serpent die simply from being struck by an anthill?
Bearing masses of matted hair and deer skins, these hypocrites who merely assume outward appearances wander through the world as if they possess true knowledge, leading others astray as well.

One who is attached to the pleasures born of saṃsāra, who claims "I am a knower of Brahman," and who has fallen away from both karma and Brahman— one should abandon such a person as one would an outcaste.
In this world, donkeys and other such animals roam about naked and devoid of shame, treating their homes and the forest as equal; are they, therefore, truly dispassionate? 65.65.
If human beings were liberated simply by smearing themselves with clay and ashes,
then would a dog that constantly dwells in clay and ashes ever become liberated?
Subsisting on grass, leaves, and water, constantly dwelling in the forest—do jackals, mice, deer, and the like become ascetics? (GarP 2.49.67)
From birth until the end of death, do those dwelling on the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā—beginning with frogs and fish—become yogins? (GarP 2.49.68)
Do pigeons, stone-eaters, and even cātaka birds ever drink water from the earth? Are they not practitioners of vows? (GarP 2.49.69)
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, rites such as the daily obligatory ones (nitya) merely serve to please the world; the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
O Bird, like animals fallen into the great well of the six perceptions, they do not know the ultimate reality, being constrained by the bonds of the bound (paśu-pāśa).
Carried hither and thither by the deep oceans of the Vedic scriptures,
the false logicians remain indeed swallowed by the suppression of the six waves.
He who knows the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, yet does not know the ultimate truth— for such a person, all that is merely the prattling of a crow, like the mockery of a buffoon.
Agitated by the thought, "This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge," they study the scriptures day and night, while turning their backs on the supreme reality.
Bound by the composition of sentences and meters, adorned with poetic ornaments, these deluded ones remain with their senses agitated, suffering from anxiety. (GarP 2.49.75)
People suffer by conceiving the supreme reality in one way, while the true nature of the scriptures is otherwise; yet they provide explanations in yet another way.
Some speak of the state of being free from egoism, yet they do not experience it themselves; they are devoid of it as if by mere instruction. (Garuda Purāṇa 2.49.77)
They recite the Vedas and Shastras and instruct one another,
yet they do not know the supreme reality, just as a ladle does not know the flavor of the food it stirs.
The head bears flowers; the nose perceives fragrance;
one recites the Vedas and Shastras; but rare is the one who awakens to the true nature of reality.
Not knowing the reality that resides within oneself, the fool is deluded by the scriptures; like a foolish cowherd who, while his goat is right in his armpit, looks for it in a well. (GarP 2.49.80)
Verbal understanding is indeed not capable of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra;
darkness would never be dispelled merely by talk of a lamp.
The recitation of one devoid of wisdom is like a mirror for the blind;
therefore, the scripture of those possessed of wisdom is the defining characteristic of the knowledge of reality.
"This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge"— desiring to hear all of this,
he does not reach the end of the treatise even after a thousand divine years.
There are many treatises and millions of obstacles to a short life;
therefore, one should discern the essence from them, just as a swan extracts milk from water.
Having studied the Vedic scriptures and understood their essential truth, the wise man should abandon all the scriptures, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (GarP 2.49.85)
Just as one who is satiated by nectar has no need for food,
O Tārkṣya, so one who knows reality has no need for scripture.
Liberation does not come from the study of the Vedas, nor even from the recitation of the Shastras;
for absolute isolation comes only from knowledge, and not otherwise, O son of Vinata.
The stage of life is not the cause of liberation, nor are the philosophical systems the cause;
likewise, all ritual actions are not the cause—for knowledge alone is indeed the cause.
The single word of the Guru bestows liberation; all other sciences are mere mockery. Indeed, among thousands of burdensome scriptures, this alone is the supreme means of revival.
For non-duality is declared to be auspicious and devoid of ritual action;
it is obtained through the mouth of the Guru, not by those who have studied millions of scriptures.
They declare that knowledge is twofold: that which is spoken in the scriptures and that which arises from discernment;
the former consists of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), while the latter is the Supreme Brahman born of discernment.
Some desire non-duality, while others desire duality;
they do not know the reality that is equal and devoid of both duality and non-duality.
There are two words for bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine.
By thinking "mine," a living being is bound; by thinking "not mine," one is liberated.
That action which does not lead to bondage is ignorance; that which bestows liberation is knowledge.
One kind of action leads to weariness, while the other kind of knowledge is skill in the arts.
As long as karmas burn, as long as the latent impressions of saṃsāra persist,
and as long as the senses remain restless, how can there be talk of reality?
As long as there is the conceit of "I" regarding the body, and as long as there is the sense of "mine-ness";
as long as there is the force of effort, and as long as there is the conceptualization of volitions.
As long as there is no stability of mind, as long as there is no reflection upon the scriptures,
and as long as there is no compassion from the guru, how can there be discourse on reality?
Austerity, vows, pilgrimage, recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like,
as well as the discourses of the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas, are all for that long until one finds the ultimate reality.
Therefore, O Tārkṣya, if one desires liberation for oneself, one should at all times and in all circumstances remain devoted to reality with every effort.

One who is scorched by the three types of suffering and other afflictions should take refuge in the shade of the tree of liberation, which bears the flowers of the knowledge of dharma and the fruits of heaven and liberation.
Therefore, the reality of the Self should be understood through knowledge from the mouth of a venerable guru;
by this, a living being is easily liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra.
Listen now as I shall tell you the final duty of one who knows reality,
by which he attains liberation known as the Nirvāṇa of Brahman.
But when the end has arrived, the person, free from fear,
should sever with the weapon of non-attachment both the desire for the body and that which follows it.
Having renounced the household life, the wise one, bathed in the waters of sacred fords,
sits in a pure and secluded place upon a seat prepared according to the rules.
One should practice with the mind the pure, threefold, supreme, imperishable Brahman; having conquered the breath, one should restrain the mind, never forgetting the seed-syllable of Brahman.
The charioteer, which is the intellect, should restrain the senses from their objects by means of the mind;
and one should hold with wisdom the mind, which is drawn away by actions, toward the goal of virtue.
"I am Brahman, the supreme abode; I am Brahman, the highest state.
Having thus perceived the Self, one should establish it within the partless Self.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering me,
he who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal.
I shall describe to you that goal which the wise attain— a goal where those who are hypocritical and devoid of knowledge and dispassion do not go.
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, constantly established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, those who are undeluded go to that imperishable state.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford— the lake of knowledge with truth as its water, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred— shall indeed attain liberation.
Resorting to mature dispassion, he who worships me with undivided devotion,
possessing perfect vision and a tranquil soul, shall indeed attain liberation.
Having abandoned his home and dwelling at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with a longing for death,
he who dies in places of liberation will indeed attain emancipation.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā,
and the city of Dvāravatī— these seven should be known as bestowers of liberation.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, I have declared to you the eternal dharma of liberation;
by hearing this, which is accompanied by knowledge and dispassion, one shall attain liberation.
Those who know reality attain liberation; righteous men go to the heavenly realm;
sinners go to an evil destiny; and birds and other creatures transmigrate.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard from the mouth of the Blessed One the final conclusion regarding his own question, Tārkṣya, his body thrilled with joy, bowed down to the Lord of the World.
"My great doubt has vanished through the illumination of your words.
Having said this and taken leave of Viṣṇu, he went to the hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Just as one goes to another body immediately or as one goes with delay,
there is likewise no contradiction between these two views for you.
"O dear one, he related everything exactly as it was heard from the Blessed One;
even Mārīca attained joy upon hearing the words of the Lord of Ramā."
O Brahmins, your doubt has been dispelled by me;
I have related this most wonderful Purāṇa known as Suparṇa. (GarP 2.49.121)
Hari received this from Tārkṣya, Tārkṣya received it from him, and from him Bhṛgu obtained it;
Vasiṣṭha received it from Bhṛgu, and from him again Vāmadeva obtained it.
From him Parāśara Muni obtained it, from him Vyāsa, and from him indeed I;
by me, however, this supreme secret of Hari has been proclaimed to you.
Whatever mortal hears this, or whoever recites it,
shall obtain happiness everywhere, both in this world and in the world beyond.
Whatever suffering has been described here regarding one traveling to Saṃyamanī,
merit arises from hearing this, and from that, one becomes liberated.
Furthermore, because hearing about the ripening of karma and other such matters as described here brings about detachment in men in this world, it is indeed to be heard.
Worship this Kṛṣṇa, the lord of sages, who has conquered his senses; from whom, alas, there has arisen a stream of showers of nectar in the form of sacred speech.
By drinking even a single drop of his color and form with the ladle of one's ears, one may attain identity with the Self.
Vyāsa said: Having drunk this nectar-like speech of Viṣṇu, adorned with the meaning of all the scriptures, which issued from the mouth of Sūta, the sages attained great satisfaction.
Thus they praised one another and the charioteer who perceives all matters;
the sages, headed by Śaunaka, attained incomparable joy.

Having heard these words of Hari, spoken through the voice of the Sūta and capable of dispelling the doubts of the Lord of Birds, that sage, the chief of the Śaunakas, considered himself even more highly honored.
Then those sages repeatedly honored the Sūta with shouts of joy, exclaiming, "O Sūta, you are blessed here! And when the sacrifice was concluded, they sent him back on his way.
The Gāruḍa Purāṇa is meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of sins.
For those who listen, that which is to be heard always fulfills their desires.
Having heard [the scripture], all gifts should be given to the reciter, including the previously mentioned bed and other items; otherwise, it will not be fruitful.
One should first worship the Purāṇa, and immediately thereafter the reciter,
with due respect, by means of gifts of clothing, ornaments, cows, and sacrificial fees.
One should worship the reciter with devotion through abundant gifts of food, gold, and land, for the sake of attaining the fruit of great merit.
Whatever mortal should hear this, or likewise proclaim it,
shall leave behind terrible torment and, with sins shaken off, go to heaven.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means to Liberation," in the *Pretakalpa* section of the *Dharmakāṇḍa*, within the second part of the *Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Thus ends the second *Dharmakāṇḍa* of the *Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
